\chapter{Replacing an ideal distance-nine quadrilateral
payment}\label{replacing-an-ideal-distance-nine-quadrilateral-payment}

\textbf{Final, internally checked local theorem.} Let Q be an actual
quadrilateral face of a finite-sided finite-volume hyperbolic Coxeter
polytope, with no simplicity assumption at ideal vertices. Suppose an
ideal corner has its two marked roots at graph distance9 in the varying
irreducible affine factor F, of order greater than17. Then either a mark
lies within14 steps of a feature of F, or an adjacent black pair of Q is
joined by a path of length at most8 whose internal vertices are
supporting white roots. A feature means a vertex of degree at least3 or
an endpoint of a bond with label at least4.

There is no global exclusion of small affine diagrams. The theorem is
compatible with arbitrarily many spectator factors and supporting
whites. It is a local replacement lemma, not a new ambient dimension
bound.

The
\href{../scripts/fresh_distance8_ideal_corner_replacement_20261017.py}{checker}
and
\href{fresh_distance8_ideal_corner_replacement_20261017.json}{certificate}
verify the exact weak-profile inequalities. Their all-rank
classification and geometric interpretation are proved below. The
corresponding affine graph rule has the separately proved
\href{fresh_affine_distance8_feature_payment_20261017.md}{cost at most8m
on a factor of order m}.

\section{Actual corner and spectator
reduction}\label{actual-corner-and-spectator-reduction}

Write the face star as H=W+a+b+c+d, with opposite pairs \{a,c\} and
\{b,d\}. All roots have square2. The white diagram W is positive
definite; W plus any one black supports an actual edge and is also
positive definite. Each adjacent corner is positive semidefinite. The
full star has rank n+1 and corank1: its four side normals project to a
spanning three-dimensional Lorentz space perpendicular to W.

At the chosen ideal corner W+a+b, the
\href{fresh_cusp_factor_payment_framework_20261017.md}{factor-fiber
lemma} gives the varying affine component F containing a,b, plus a
positive-definite spectator forest Z orthogonal to F. This statement
concerns the actual face star, not the entire set of facets at a
nonsimple cusp.

Assume for contradiction that there is no path of length at most8 from
\{a,c\} to \{b,d\} with white interior. In particular b.c=a.d=c.d=0. Let
nu be the positive affine kernel combination of F. It is a nonzero
future null vector representing this actual ideal corner. Neither
opposite side c nor d contains that corner, so

\begin{verbatim}
h=-c.nu>0,  k=-d.nu>0.
\end{verbatim}

The opposite contacts x=-a.c and y=-b.d may be zero, any finite Coxeter
magnitude, parallel2 or dotted. Every nonzero magnitude is at least1. No
upper label or distance cutoff is imposed on x,y.

Eliminate the whites of F first. The frozen
\href{fresh_simple_cusp_affine_a_quadrilateral_20261017.md}{four-root
determinant identity} applies. Eliminating Z afterwards subtracts a
positive-semidefinite matrix {[}{[}p,q{]},{[}q,r{]}{]} from the c,d
block. By the
\href{fresh_cusp_factor_payment_framework_20261017.md}{spectator
identity}, this changes the normalized determinant by

\begin{verbatim}
alpha*(p/h² - 2q/(h*k) + r/k²) >= 0,
\end{verbatim}

where alpha\textgreater0. The heights are unchanged because Z is
orthogonal to F. Thus a strictly positive determinant before the
spectator subtraction contradicts the required corank1 afterwards as
well.

\section{Affine cycles: complete weak
profiles}\label{affine-cycles-complete-weak-profiles}

Suppose F is affine A. Its two a-to-b arcs have edge lengths P,Q≥9,
since a,b have graph distance9. Deleting a leaves A\_(P+Q−1), of rank at
least17. Its complete one-root positive-semidefinite extensions give the
following c profiles: isolated; one simple bond at either endpoint; one
doubled bond at either endpoint; one simple bond at the second node from
either endpoint; or simple bonds at both endpoints. In ranks at least17,
finite exceptional diagrams cannot occur. The connected finite
extensions are A, B and D, and the only connected affine extension of
the entire path is its simple cycle. Disconnected spectators do not
enlarge this list, because the principal old path plus c is itself
positive semidefinite. This is the same full finite/affine
classification used in the
\href{fresh_simple_cusp_affine_a_quadrilateral_20261017.md}{previous
cycle proof}; here none of its small-affine exclusions is used.

For an attachment to an arc, let j=1 at an endpoint and j=2 at its next
node. Let l=(l1,l2) be attachment magnitude times j on the two arcs. The
norm constants, heights and weak bounds are:

{\def\LTcaptype{none} % do not increment counter
\begin{longtable}[]{@{}lrllr@{}}
\toprule\noalign{}
Profile & c0 & l & h & Minimum h \\
\midrule\noalign{}
\endhead
\bottomrule\noalign{}
\endlastfoot
isolated & 2 & (0,0) & x & 1 \\
endpoint3 on arc i & 1 & unit vector i & x+1 & 1 \\
endpoint4 on arc i & 0 & sqrt(2) times unit vector i & x+sqrt(2) &
sqrt(2) \\
second-node3 on arc i & 0 & 2 times unit vector i & x+1 & 1 \\
both endpoints3 & 0 & (1,1) & x+2 & 2 \\

}

The isolated minimum follows from h\textgreater0 and the native Coxeter
gap. All other minima use only x≥0. Define analogous d0,m,k for d, and
u=1/h, v=1/k.

There is one additional necessary length inequality. If c and d both
attach on the same arc, at positions j\_c,j\_d from its opposite ends,
their path through that arc has length P−j\_c−j\_d+2. It has white
interior because j\_c,j\_d≤2 and P≥9. The no-short-path assumption
therefore implies

\begin{verbatim}
P >= max(9,7+j_c+j_d).
\end{verbatim}

Apply the corresponding inequality to Q. If one attachment is absent,
the original bound9 suffices. This refinement is essential for two
second-node attachments: their common arc must have length at least11.

Put A=1/P, B=1/Q, L=u\emph{l1+v}m1 and M=u\emph{l2+v}m2. The normalized
four-root determinant is exactly

\begin{verbatim}
F=1-2*(A*L+B*M)
    -(A+B)*(c0*u²+d0*v²)-A*B*(L-M)².
\end{verbatim}

For fixed u,v≥0, F is nonincreasing in A and B. For fixed A,B≥0 it is
jointly concave in u,v: its quadratic terms are negative diagonal
squares and one negative square. It therefore attains its minimum on the
permitted height rectangle at a rectangle vertex. For each of the64
ordered profile pairs, the checker uses the largest permitted reciprocal

All256 values are at least5/81. Hence F≥5/81\textgreater0 for every
actual arc length and every allowed height. This is an arbitrary-rank,
continuous-height inequality, not extrapolation from finitely many
lengths.

Consequently an ideal affine-A corner of marked distance9 cannot occur
in an unpaid quadrilateral. Additional spectator contacts only increase
this positive determinant.

\section{Feature-free classical tree
corridor}\label{feature-free-classical-tree-corridor}

In order greater than17, the other affine factors are the classical
B/C/D trees. Suppose both marks are farther than14 from every feature.
They lie on the undecorated simple-bond spine, at distance P=9. Beyond
each mark, the outer component is a finite B or D diagram attached at
its long endpoint and has rank at least9. Indeed a fork feature is at
least15 simple steps away, and a doubled bond's nearer endpoint is also
at least15 steps away; retaining the entire end decoration only
increases the outer order. Deleting either mark therefore leaves two
large finite B/D components.

A complete one-root positive-semidefinite extension of these two old
components has eight possible profiles: isolated; an endpoint3,

\section{Domain and the unbounded order-three
family}\label{domain-and-the-unbounded-order-three-family}

A connected core of order k containing two black roots has marked radius
at most k−2. The complete high-order catalogue has maximum radius seven.
If both cores have order at most five, every possible cross edge gives a
path of length at most seven, and every overlap gives a still shorter
path. With no cross edge their two indefinite blocks already give two
negative directions. Thus only a small/high pairing needs attention.

A minimal order-two core has only its two black nodes. Every contact
with a high core gives a path of length at most eight; otherwise the
indefinite blocks are orthogonal. It cannot occur in an unpaid
configuration.

An order-three core has a single white w, at distance one from its black
pair. An overlap is impossible, because1+7=8. Any disjoint cross edge
must meet a high port at distance seven. The strict actual-edge inverse
test leaves precisely L25 node9, with high black pairs \{1,2\}, \{1,3\},
\{2,3\}. Its full inverse diagonal is exactly

\begin{verbatim}
(G_L25 inverse)99 = 0.
\end{verbatim}

Write the small Gram as

\begin{verbatim}
[[2,-x,-a],[-x,2,-b],[-a,-b,2]].
\end{verbatim}

The black-black magnitude x can have an unbounded finite label or be
parallel. A truly minimal order-three core has x≤2: a dotted black-black
pair would already be an indefinite proper order-two subdiagram. Its two
black deletions are positive definite. If one also applies the low port
inverse test, a²,b²\textless3, so the white-incident labels are
right,3,4 or5. No finite bound on the black-black label follows or is
assumed.

The high core supplies one negative direction and the small indefinite
core supplies another. This holds for \textbf{every real x,a,b and cross
magnitude for which the small core is indefinite}, including the
physical unbounded-label family. It also covers zero cross contact. The
proof is a symbolic identity, not a sampled angle limit.

\section{Why smaller cores enter

Disjoint joins are different. Order-four radius-two ports can meet

Each reconstructed core H has inertia(order(H)−1,1,0). Consequently its

blocks permit no external contact: their positive null relation and
acuteness force all such products to vanish. Finite blocks give the

Write J for the inverse normalized full-core Gram. Suppose the
short-path alternative has not already paid the face. The saved end
partition has maximum left distance plus maximum right distance plus2 at
most9. A supporting white root contacting both ends therefore supplies a
short path. Within either end, all entries of J are positive, and the
exact minimum projection for any two distinct contacts is greater than2.
Since every nonzero acute Coxeter contact has magnitude at least1, no
multicontact root remains. Thus every core-contact root has a single
contact. The candidate nodes satisfy1≤J\_ii≤2. If J\_ii\textgreater1,
only a simple bond is possible; if J\_ii=1, a simple or doubled bond is
possible. Larger labels have projection square greater than2.

For a simple-contact root at node i, write its core projection as v\_i
and its positive-space residual as g\_i. Then

\[
v_i^2=J_{ii}=p_i,\qquad g_i^2=2-p_i=\rho_i,
\qquad r_i\cdot r_j=J_{ij}+g_i\cdot g_j.
\]

Cauchy bounds the residual product. The exact pair tests either force a
positive actual product, force a nonzero native edge giving a path of

last case the discrete Coxeter gap and acuteness force the product to

separately checked: their residual vanishes, so the sign of the exact

These checks also exclude simultaneous relevant roots, apart from the
single relevant root being analysed.

Let G be that relevant root, with0≤rho\textless1. There is at most one
other allowable core-contact type C when G is present, and C contacts a
node outside the marked component. The actual roots G,C must be
orthogonal. If its simple-contact projection is p\_C\textgreater1, two

complement gives inverse diagonal1/(2−sum of rooted child inverse

magnitudes.

including roots having no direct contact with G. It is not merely a
bound on the first attached node. In the present cases the maximum
alone-tail rank is3.

\section{Complete forest domain and exact
certificates}\label{complete-forest-domain-and-exact-certificates}

Separate all D10 through D16 components and all A17 components. Their
multiplicities form 753 complete count vectors of total rank at most 64.
All remaining components have ranks1--9 or at least17, with E6 as the
rank6 representative and D\_r as the representative for r≥17.

For counts d10,\ldots,d16,a17, the five-coordinate interaction key is

\begin{verbatim}
(2d10+3(d11+...+d16)+2a17, d11+d12, d13, d11, d14).
\end{verbatim}

There are 348 keys. Let the coordinates be (b,u,a,d,e). The residual
item of rank r has its doubled same-component cost plus these cross
terms:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  rb when r≤5;
\item
  an additional 2u+e for r=1;
\item
  an additional 4d+2e for r=2;
\item
  an additional 2a for r=4;
\item

The last term is the upgraded E6/D11 cost. The new B10 coupon disappears

neighbor halves, A17 coupons and all broad small-component coupons. The
source compares the compressed formula with literal typed component
interactions 42,921 times.

The saved verifier does not rerun that optimization. For every residual
rank n it checks all last-item upper inequalities

\begin{verbatim}
V[n] ≥ V[n−r]+w[r],
\end{verbatim}

and one saved attaining predecessor with equality. Induction on n proves
both the upper bound for every residual forest and attainment by a typed
forest. There are 597,168 inequalities and 22,272 predecessors.

Each of the 753 large-component vectors is then combined with the exact
residual value at its remaining rank. Its attaining typed forest is
reconstructed and its full same-component plus cross-component cost is
recounted literally. This covers every rank64 forest after domination.
The largest doubled value is 928, hence cost 464, and four D16
components attain it. They carry no cross coupons, so this attainment is
unchanged by either addition. It is attainment in the formal
finite-forest domain, not an assertion that such a vertex occurs in an
actual chamber.

Let a\_i count representative A\_i components
for1\textless=i\textless=5, let \texttt{a=sum\_i\ i*a\_i}, let t count

respectively. For a representative forest the cost is exactly

\begin{verbatim}
sum_components base(rank)

\end{verbatim}

There are three broad eligible marks on each D and two on each A17, each

\section{Complete exact maximization}\label{complete-exact-maximization}

Enumerate all count vectors of the eight large coupon ranks10 through17
whose total rank is at most75. There are1,608 such vectors. For fixed
large counts the cost of each remaining connected component is additive:
its rank is1 through9 or at least18, and its entire cross-payment
contribution is fixed by the large counts.

Only the tuple \texttt{(t,u,b10,b12,b13)} matters for this residual
additive problem. There are377 distinct tuples. Double every cost to use
integers. For each tuple k let w\_k(r) be the doubled residual component
cost, including all its cross-payments, and define

\begin{verbatim}
F_k(0)=0,
F_k(s)=max_(allowed r<=s) [F_k(s-r)+w_k(r)].
\end{verbatim}

Allowed ranks are1,\ldots,9 and18,\ldots,75. A rank greater than s
cannot occur. This Bellman identity is an induction proof of
completeness: removing any one component of a residual forest leaves a
lower-rank residual forest; conversely every maximizing predecessor may
be extended by that component. The positive component ranks make the
recursion finite. The certificate stores all76 values and an attaining
last rank for every tuple.

For each ambient rank n, maximize the doubled large-component base cost
plus F\_k(n minus their rank) over every large vector of rank at most n.
This covers every representative forest. The source also reconstructs an
attaining forest for each n and checks its full cost directly using the
displayed coupon formula.

\chapter{Finite-eight and marked-leaf-nine
replacements}\label{finite-eight-and-marked-leaf-nine-replacements}

\textbf{Completed internally checked local theorem; verification scope
is recorded below.} Let Q be an actual quadrilateral of a finite-sided
finite-volume hyperbolic Coxeter polytope. No arithmetic or simple-cusp
hypothesis is imposed. Use the following corner payments:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  A finite corner pays one if its marked roots are connected at distance
  at most8, or at distance9 with one mark a leaf of its \textbf{whole
  actual connected component}.
\item
  An ideal corner pays one at marked distance at most6, or at
  distance7,8,9 with a mark within6 steps of a feature of its varying
  affine factor. Features are vertices of degree at least3 and endpoints
  of bonds of label at least4.
\item
  The already proved half-coupon between a whole A1 component and the
  unique middle of a whole A15 component is retained.
\end{itemize}

Then an ideal corner in an affine cycle of order at least15 at marked
distance7,8 or9 is replaceable by these payments at the other corners.
The only equality case uses two of the stated half-coupons. The same
replacement holds for a classical affine tree at those distances if both
marks are farther than6 from its features.

Adding the existing unit payments on whole finite components of order at
most17 and whole affine factors of order at most14 preserves this
statement. This package repairs a specific finite-distance-nine
dependency of the
\href{fresh_ideal_distance6_mixed_replacement_20261017.md}{mixed
ideal-six proof}. It does \textbf{not} establish the complete
distance-eight high-core overlap theorem, cover every preferred
small-factor pattern, prove a total finite budget, or improve the
ambient dimension bound.

The
\href{../scripts/fresh_finite8_cycle_replacement_20261017.py}{source}
and \href{fresh_finite8_cycle_replacement_20261017.json}{certificate}
contain740 exact cycle rectangle values,66 single-profile finite
diagrams, three isolated exceptional analyses and192 tree cases.

\section{Actual star, profiles and
spectators}\label{actual-star-profiles-and-spectators}

Write the actual face star as H=W+a+b+c+d, with opposite black pairs
\{a,c\},\{b,d\}. The white diagram W and each actual edge diagram W+one
black are positive definite. At the chosen ideal corner W+a+b, the
\href{fresh_cusp_factor_payment_framework_20261017.md}{factor-fiber
lemma} gives the varying irreducible affine factor F containing a,b and
a positive-definite diagram Z orthogonal to F. This remains true at
nonsimple cusps.

Normalize roots to square2. A direct adjacent black bond gives a unit
payment, so in the unpaid analysis b.c=a.d=c.d=0. Let nu be the positive
affine kernel representing the actual chosen cusp. The opposite sides do
not contain this cusp, so h=-c.nu and k=-d.nu are strictly positive.
Every nonzero native contact magnitude is at least1.

For a cycle of order m, let the two old marked arcs have lengths P,Q,
with P the marked distance and Q\textgreater=P. Here P is7,8 or9 and
m\textgreater=15. Deleting a leaves the long A\_(m-1) path. The complete
one-root positive-semidefinite extension list is isolated; endpoint3 or
endpoint4 on either end; second-node3 on either end; or both-end3.
Finite exceptional extensions are too small. The
\href{fresh_distance8_ideal_corner_replacement_20261017.md}{weak-profile
theorem} supplies this classification, exact heights, Schur identity and
its all-rank interpretation. Nothing here assumes absence of small
affine diagrams elsewhere in the polytope.

For a single attachment at position j=1 or2 on an arc of length L, the
adjacent marked distance is L-j+1. The old endpoint opposite this
attachment is a simple leaf whose neighbor has degree2. Both remain
fixed under all spectator contacts, because Z is orthogonal to the old
cycle. The adjacent connected component has at least m\textgreater=15
nodes. No classical affine A/B/C/D graph has such a fixed simple leaf
with a degree2 neighbor; exceptional affine graphs are too small. By the
actual factor-fiber theorem, a connected component containing both marks
of an ideal corner would have to be affine. Therefore this adjacent
corner is finite, including after all supporting whites have been
restored.

Distances at most8 now pay immediately. The new issue is precisely
distance9.

\section{Which distance-nine marks remain
leaves?}\label{which-distance-nine-marks-remain-leaves}

An endpoint4 profile is a finite B\_m component with the new mark c at
its doubled terminal. A second-node3 profile is a finite D\_m component
with c a short fork leaf. Every spectator is orthogonal to every old
path root, so a spectator touching this component can touch only c.

The exact inverse diagonal at c is

\begin{verbatim}
B_m doubled terminal:  m/2,
D_m short fork leaf:   m/4.
\end{verbatim}

These follow by one Schur complement of A\_(m-1): its endpoint inverse
diagonal is (m-1)/m and its second-node diagonal is 2(m-2)/m. The native
attachment squares are2 and1 respectively. Since m\textgreater=15, both
displayed values exceed2. Any spectator with nonzero contact magnitude
at least1 would give negative Schur norm in the principal extension by
that root, contradicting positive semidefiniteness of the actual corner.
Hence every spectator is orthogonal to c.~The new mark remains a leaf of
the whole actual component, and the distance-nine leaf rule pays.

An endpoint3 profile instead gives A\_m, with inverse diagonal m/(m+1).
It may extend. If c has no spectator neighbor it remains a
whole-component leaf and again pays. Thus an unpaid endpoint3 profile at
distance9 \textbf{must} have a spectator neighbor. This necessary
contact supplies a useful determinant correction; no finite list of
spectator forests is needed.

\section{An unequal-height spectator
bound}\label{an-unequal-height-spectator-bound}

Let G be the positive-definite norm-two Gram matrix of Z, and let
x,y\textgreater=0 be the native contact-magnitude vectors from c,d to Z.
If they share a nonzero coordinate, c-e-d is an actual white-interior
path of length2, which pays at that adjacent corner. Otherwise their
supports are disjoint.

Suppose c is the unpaid endpoint3 profile just described, and choose one
of its spectator neighbors i. Then x\_i\textgreater=1 and y\_i=0. For
z=x/h-y/k, Cauchy in the positive-definite Gram metric gives

\begin{verbatim}
z^T G^(-1) z >= (z^T e_i)^2/(e_i^T G e_i)
                = x_i^2/(2h^2) >= 1/(2h^2).
\end{verbatim}

This uses no equality between h and k and no lower bound on other
coordinates of z. The analogous bound holds for d.~If both sides require
neighbors, use \textbf{one fixed side only} throughout the height
rectangle; two coordinate bounds are not added.

Write A=1/P, B=1/Q, u=1/h, v=1/k and use the inherited profile moments
l,m and norm constants c0,d0. Put L=u\emph{l1+v}m1 and M=u\emph{l2+v}m2.
Before the spectators, the normalized determinant is

\begin{verbatim}
F=1-2(A*L+B*M)-(A+B)(c0*u^2+d0*v^2)-A*B*(L-M)^2.
\end{verbatim}

Spectator elimination adds (A+B) z\^{}T G\^{}(-1)z. The new bound
therefore replaces c0=1 by c0=1/2 for one required-contact endpoint3
profile, or replaces d0 analogously. The modified constants remain
nonnegative. Consequently this lower bound is still nonincreasing in A,B
and concave in u,v. Its minimum over the permitted height rectangle
occurs at a vertex, exactly as in the inherited determinant proof. A
strictly positive lower bound contradicts the actual star's corank1.

\chapter{Compact simplex ports and exact cusp truncation in finite
volume}\label{compact-simplex-ports-and-exact-cusp-truncation-in-finite-volume}

The disjoint-port theorem extends to \textbf{compact simplex faces
through finite vertices} of a finite-volume acute Coxeter polytope, even
when its ideal vertices are nonsimple. It does not extend to triangles
containing ideal vertices. The exact square pyramid below demonstrates
the distinction.

Truncating the ideal vertices produces a simple projective polytope and
gives explicit face-count identities. This is not, by itself, a route to
a better dimension bound: the artificial cusp faces already exceed the
usual simple polytope corner-payment budget. A more useful starting
point is Khovanskii's inequality on the original polytope, with the cusp
contributions retained. It leaves a precise missing noncompact-face
incidence inequality.

The
\href{../scripts/fresh_finite_volume_simplex_truncation_20261017.py}{standalone
Fraction checker} and
\href{fresh_finite_volume_simplex_truncation_20261017.json}{exact
certificate} verify the identities against 914 product links, all-rank
polynomial coefficients, and the literal pyramid. The proofs for
arbitrary ranks are given here; bounded checks are not used as
extrapolation. No new dimension bound, external review, or novelty claim
is made.

\section{Geometric scope and primary
inputs}\label{geometric-scope-and-primary-inputs}

Let P be a finite-sided, finite-volume acute Coxeter polytope in
hyperbolic n-space, n \textgreater= 3, and use its closed projective
polytope in the Klein model. Write v\_f for its number of finite
vertices. Finite vertices are simple. At an ideal vertex v the link is
combinatorially

\[
 L_v=\prod_{i=1}^{s_v}\Delta^{r_{vi}},\qquad
 r_{vi}\ge1,\quad \sum_i r_{vi}=n-1.
\]

The projective polytope is simple at edges. These local facts and the
later average-face formula are stated in
\href{https://ems.press/content/serial-article-files/43032}{Potyagailo--Vinberg,
printed pp.64--65}. The graph-connectivity input is
\href{https://msp.org/pjm/1961/11-2/pjm-v11-n2-p03-s.pdf}{Balinski's
original theorem, printed p.432}. Khovanskii's original
\href{https://www.math.utoronto.ca/askold/1986-Faa-1-english.pdf}{Theorem
10, printed p.49, and §6} apply the average-face estimate to polytopes
simple at edges, explicitly including finite-volume reflection chambers.
All three primary sources were opened on 2026-10-17.

\section{Transfer of the compact-simplex port
theorem}\label{transfer-of-the-compact-simplex-port-theorem}

At a finite vertex a, the incident edges are its ports. Simplicity at a
gives a Boolean face interval: any d ports generate a unique d-face.
Relate two ports only when their two-face is a \textbf{compact}
triangle.

Suppose the triangles abc and abd share the edge ab. They lie in the
three-face generated by their three ports at a. Their vertices a,b,c,d
are finite. In that three-face a and b each have degree three, with
neighbors exactly the other three displayed vertices. If there were
another vertex, deleting c and d would disconnect \{a,b\} from it,
contrary to Balinski's three-connectivity. The three-face is therefore a
tetrahedron, and it is compact. This argument does not require any
undisplayed vertex to be simple. Compact-triangle adjacency of ports is
consequently transitive.

Let a class have d \textgreater= 2 ports, and let F be their generated
d-face. The neighbors a1,\ldots,ad of a are finite because they belong
to compact triangles. Every pair ai,aj is an edge of F. Thus
a,a1,\ldots,ad form a complete graph, and each already has degree d in
F. All these vertices are finite and hence simple in F. There can be no
edge to another vertex. Graph connectivity implies that F has exactly
these d+1 vertices, so F is a compact simplex.

Conversely, a compact simplex through a gives a clique, hence lies in
one class. It follows that distinct maximal compact simplex faces of
dimension at least two through a use disjoint ports. The
\href{fresh_simplex_disjoint_ports_20261017.md}{frozen compact
disjoint-port proof} therefore supplies the same one-port capacities at
every finite vertex. An isolated port ending at an ideal vertex is not a
compact simplex edge; it must not be silently included in this
conclusion.

The theorem gives no port capacity at a nonsimple ideal vertex, and no
partition of all triangles into compact simplex aggregates. Those are
separate obligations in any finite-volume charge argument.

\section{Exact counterexample to including noncompact
triangles}\label{exact-counterexample-to-including-noncompact-triangles}

In the Lorentz form diag(-1,1,1,1), take outward normals

\[
 b=(0,0,0,-1),\quad
 s_1=(1,2,0,1),\ s_2=(1,0,2,1),\
 s_3=(1,-2,0,1),\ s_4=(1,0,-2,1).
\]

Their squares are 1,4,4,4,4. Base/side products are -1, successive side
products are zero, and opposite side products are -4. Thus the chamber
has base/side dihedral angle pi/3, right successive sides, and parallel
opposite sides. H=(2,0,0,1) has square -3 and product -1 with every
normal, so it is a strict common future center.

In the affine chart t=1 the closed polytope is exactly

\[
 0\le z\le1,\qquad |x|,|y|\le(1-z)/2.
\]

It has four finite base vertices (1,+/-1/2,+/-1/2,0) and the ideal apex
nu=(1,0,0,1). Its cusp link is the bounded square Delta1 x Delta1, so
this is a finite-volume Coxeter square pyramid. At the finite vertex
(1,1/2,1/2,0), the two triangular side faces share the edge to nu,
whereas the third two-face through its ports is the square base.
Triangle adjacency is not transitive if these noncompact triangles are
allowed.

The checker reconstructs all vertices, active sets, edges and faces from
the inequalities, not from an assumed incidence table. Cutting by z
\textless= 1/2 gives a combinatorial cube. Its new outward normal
(1,0,0,2) has product +1 with every old side normal: even this
elementary truncation is not acute. Accordingly no Coxeter-angle or
acute local-face theorem is imported to the truncated polytope.

\section{Exact truncation counts}\label{exact-truncation-counts}

Take sufficiently small disjoint projective vertex cuts at all ideal
vertices, and call the result Q. Each new vertex belongs to a truncation
facet and corresponds to a vertex of L\_v. Since L\_v is simple, this
new vertex is simple. The old finite vertices are unchanged, so Q is a
simple Euclidean/projective polytope.

For one cusp suppress v and put d=n-1, V=f0(L), E=f1(L). Let T and R be
the numbers of triangular and square two-faces of L. Then

\[
\begin{aligned}
 V&=\prod_i(r_i+1),& E&=\tfrac12 dV,\\
 T&=\tfrac16V\sum_i r_i(r_i-1),&
 R&=\tfrac14V\sum_{i<j}r_ir_j,\\
 f_2(L)&=T+R,&3T+4R&=\binom d2 V.
\end{aligned}
\tag{1}
\]

Indeed a two-face of a product is either a triangular two-face in one
simplex factor or an edge in each of two factors. The other factors
supply vertices. This proves (1) for all ranks, including a
two-dimensional link whose full polytope itself is counted as its one
two-face.

Every old positive-dimensional face persists after truncation. The new
positive-dimensional k-faces are precisely the k-faces of the links,
while an old ideal vertex is replaced by V vertices. Therefore

\[
\begin{aligned}
 f_0(Q)&=f_0(P)+\sum_v(V_v-1)=v_f+\sum_vV_v,\\
 f_1(Q)&=f_1(P)+\sum_vE_v,\\
 f_2(Q)&=f_2(P)+\sum_v(T_v+R_v).
\end{aligned}
\tag{2}
\]

Let N\_\{k,s\} count old k-gonal two-faces having s ideal vertices. An
ideal corner contributes one additional side after truncation, so

\[
 f_{2,\ell}(Q)=\sum_{k+s=\ell}N_{k,s}
  +\mathbf1_{\ell=3}\sum_vT_v+\mathbf1_{\ell=4}\sum_vR_v.
\tag{3}
\]

In particular triangles(Q)=N\_\{3,0\}+sum T\_v, while
quadrilaterals(Q)=N\_\{4,0\}+N\_\{3,1\}+sum R\_v. A noncompact triangle
with two or three ideal corners becomes a pentagon or hexagon,
respectively.

Counting old incidences also gives

\[
 2f_1(P)=nv_f+\sum_vV_v,\qquad
 S(P):=\sum_{F^2\subset P}|F^2|
       =\binom n2v_f+\sum_vE_v.
\tag{4}
\]

Here E\_v counts old two-faces through v, because they correspond to
edges of its link. The polygon side count equals its vertex count,
including ideal vertices. These formulas do not replace E\_v by
binom(n,2), which would incorrectly assume ideal vertices simple.

For D\_j(P)=sum\_F(j-\textbar F\textbar), (2)--(4) yield

\[
 D_4(Q)=D_4(P)+\sum_v(T_v-E_v),\qquad
 D_5(Q)=D_5(P)+\sum_v(2T_v+R_v-E_v).
\tag{5}
\]

The demand on the surviving old faces, without the new link faces, is

\[
 D_5^{\rm old}(Q)=5f_2(P)-\binom n2v_f-2\sum_vE_v.
\tag{6}
\]

Each old ideal corner is counted twice here: once as its old vertex and
once as the extra side created by truncation.

\section{Why simple truncation does not close the charge
argument}\label{why-simple-truncation-does-not-close-the-charge-argument}

For n \textgreater= 4 write

\texttt{
\ \textbackslash{}eta\_n=\textbackslash{}begin\{cases\}4(n-1)/(n-2)\&n\textbackslash{}text\{\ even\},\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}4n/(n-1)\&n\textbackslash{}text\{\ odd\},\textbackslash{}end\{cases\}
\ \textbackslash{}quad
\ b\_n=\textbackslash{}begin\{cases\}n(n-6)/8\&n\textbackslash{}text\{\ even\},\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}(n-1)(n-5)/8\&n\textbackslash{}text\{\ odd\}.
\ \textbackslash{}end\{cases\}
}

The strict simple-polytope inequality S(Q)/f2(Q)\textless eta\_n gives
D5(Q)\textgreater b\_n f0(Q), since S(Q)=binom(n,2)f0(Q).

Consider the usual nonnegative corner-payment scheme in which every
triangle receives at least 2 and every quadrilateral at least 1; this
suffices to dominate 5-\textbar F\textbar{} on all two-faces. The
artificial faces of one cusp alone require at least 2T+R, all supported
on its V new vertices. Formula (1) gives the exact all-rank lower bound

\[
 \frac{2T+R}{V}
 =\frac{5\sum_i r_i^2+3d^2-8d}{24}
 \ge\frac{d(d-1)}8,
\tag{7}
\]

because sum r\_i\^{}2 \textgreater= sum r\_i=d.~Its excess over b\_n is
at least

\[
 \frac{(n-1)(n-2)}8-b_n
 =\begin{cases}(3n+2)/8&n\text{ even},\\3(n-1)/8&n\text{ odd}.
 \end{cases}
\tag{8}
\]

It is strictly positive for every cusp partition. Thus a nonnegative
corner-payment model on Q with total budget at most b\_n at
\textbf{every} new vertex is impossible already on the new link faces.
This is an algebraic obstruction to this particular uniform-budget
method, not an existence claim about high-dimensional reflection
polytopes.

Subtracting those known demands instead leaves

\[
 D_5^{\rm old}(Q)>b_n v_f
       -\sum_v\bigl(2T_v+R_v-b_nV_v\bigr).
\tag{9}
\]

Every displayed cusp deficit is positive. Finite-vertex compact-simplex
port savings alone provide no bound on their sum; finite-volume chambers
can even have no finite vertices. A proof using truncation would
therefore need an additional aggregate bound relating cusp mass to
genuine old-face incidences. It cannot discard the new faces while
retaining the original simple-polytope lower bound.

\section{A usable original-polytope budget, and the missing
theorem}\label{a-usable-original-polytope-budget-and-the-missing-theorem}

Khovanskii's Theorem 10 avoids the artificial faces altogether. Using
its estimate in the conservative weak form S(P)/f2(P) \textless= eta\_n,
(4) gives

\[
 D_5(P)\ge\alpha_n S(P)
 =b_n v_f+\alpha_n\sum_vE_v,
 \qquad \alpha_n=5/\eta_n-1.
\tag{10}
\]

No strictness for this nonsimple-at-vertices application is needed or
claimed here. For a prospective nonnegative original-face payment rule,
let B(a) bound the total payment at a finite vertex a, and C(v) the
total payment over original two-face corners at the ideal vertex v. A
necessary condition for all face lower bounds to hold is

\[
 \sum_{a\ {
m finite}}(B(a)-b_n)
 +\sum_{v\ {
m ideal}}(C(v)-\alpha_nE_v)\ge0.
\tag{11}
\]

Consequently a strictly negative right-hand upper bound would give a
dimension contradiction. This retains the exact cusp factors and is a
concrete target for a future incidence theorem. It is not yet an
inequality bounding C(v) from above.

The transferred simplex capacities apply only to compact triangles and
their compact maximal simplex aggregates. A complete application of (11)
still needs payments for noncompact triangles and quadrilaterals, their
interaction with the affine product at each cusp, and simultaneous
global incidence restrictions. Local affine classification or the
individual port theorem alone supplies none of these missing
inequalities.

There is a published model of the stronger kind of argument needed:
Potyagailo--Vinberg's §§4--5 couple cusp counts across neighboring faces
to obtain a lower bound on the number of facets of a five-dimensional
right-angled polyhedron, then apply the higher-face average inequality.
The right-angle assumptions are essential there; that result is not an
unrestricted estimate. This package changes neither the repository's
\href{fresh_nikulin_two_budget_frontier_20261015_dimension163.md}{dimension163
proof package} nor any arithmetic bound.

\chapter{Depth17 suffices for the full high-domain corridor
alternative}\label{depth17-suffices-for-the-full-high-domain-corridor-alternative}

For every corner of the complete frozen 6,703-context high-overlap
domain, the following statement holds. If the actual whole finite A/B/D
component has its two marked roots at distance 8, and both marks have
distance at least 17 from every endpoint, branch and endpoint of a
nonsimple bond, then the full actual supporting star has an
opposite-black path of length at most 7.

This is a \textbf{short-path alternative}. Only in the branch with no
such path anywhere in the full supporting star does it exclude the deep
corridor. The absence of a path in the saved old core alone is
insufficient. There is no new pair weight, complete payment system or
dimension bound here.

The
\href{../scripts/fresh_full_a39_corridor_high_domain_20261017.py}{source}
and \href{fresh_full_a39_corridor_high_domain_20261017.json}{exact
certificate} cover all 26,812 corners of the
\href{fresh_distance7_high_supporting_frontier_20261017.md}{inherited
high domain}, including all four corners of the 251 formerly unresolved
contexts and all earlier structural outputs. No old principal matrix is
required to be nonsingular or Lorentzian. The proof instead uses a
forced positive definite path in the proposed actual completion.

\section{The forced path and every possible old
embedding}\label{the-forced-path-and-every-possible-old-embedding}

Normalize all actual wall roots to squared norm 2. A feature of a finite
A/B/D diagram is a vertex of degree other than 2, or either endpoint of
a bond whose label exceeds 3. Depth at least 17 at each mark, together
with marked distance 8, gives two outward simple arms of length 17 and
the simple path joining the marks. All vertices other than the two marks
are supporting whites. The two omitted black roots do not belong to this
actual corner.

Keep the first 15 outward whites on each arm. Together with the marks
and the seven whites between them, these form an induced A39 diagram.
Number its vertices 0 through 38; the left and right marks are at 15 and
23. The unused two outward whites on each side are retained as geometric
inputs for the A17 contact estimates below, but are not needed in the
final matrix. A feature at outward distance exactly 17 is harmless: all
bonds inside the displayed A17 arm are simple.

The 342 old native cores are reconstructed from their frozen diagrams
and positive diagonal gauges. They have order at most 19, so any
displayed corner has at most 17 roots. Their gauges are 1 or 2; dividing
by the square roots of the gauges puts every relevant product in
Q(sqrt(2)). The source checks all four left/right choices in every old
context and independently reconstructs the displayed component
partitions.

A displayed component containing a mark must be a simple path. An
existing branch or nonsimple bond remains a feature in the actual
component and is at distance at most 16 \textless{} 17 from the mark. An
existing cycle cannot occur inside a finite A/B/D tree. The checker
saves one such witness for each rejected nonsimple marked block.

If the two marks are in the same displayed path, that path must already
give distance 8: a tree cannot acquire a second, shorter route. Its
embedding in A39 is then fixed once the two marks are placed at 15 and
23. If the marks lie in different displayed paths, orient each path from
its outward endpoint toward the eventual joining segment. Let t\_L,t\_R
be the inward distances from the marks to the chosen endpoints. The
connecting segment must contain exactly

\begin{verbatim}
k = 7 - t_L - t_R
\end{verbatim}

additional whites, with k at least 1. The two displayed components are
orthogonal, so no zero-white connection is possible. Every orientation
of both paths is enumerated, with singleton orientations counted once. A
connected displayed path has at most 17 roots and already spans 8 edges
between the marks, so its two outward tails together use at most 8
roots. For disconnected marked paths, their combined order is at most 17
and each is nonempty; either path has at most 16 roots and outward
extent at most 15. Thus every old embedding fits inside the 15 retained
outward whites on each side. The source asserts these distinct bounds
before checking every old pair product against the corresponding A39
entries. This also covers paths joined through old spectator roots:
those roots may occupy positions not selected in the reduced old
embedding. Their identities and extra contacts are not assumed away. The
Gram tests use a necessary subset of actual roots only.

\section{All-label restrictions leave three white slots per omitted
black}\label{all-label-restrictions-leave-three-white-slots-per-omitted-black}

Write b for the omitted left black root and d for the omitted right
black root. The full-star no-short7 hypothesis implies b·d=0 and forbids
any contact from b to the right mark, or from d to the left mark. Their
products with their own marks are fixed native products and remain in
the calculation.

For a norm-2 A17 arm, the inverse is positive and its diagonal at
outward distance j is j(18-j)/18. The omitted black and all these whites
belong to an actual edge diagram, which is strictly positive definite.
Hence:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  At outward distance 1, only nonzero contacts of labels 3 or 4 are
  possible. A label at least 5 has squared magnitude greater than 5/2,
  and (17/18)(5/2)\textgreater2.
\item
  At distance 2, only label 3 is possible, since (16/9)·2\textgreater2.
\item
  At distances 3 through 15, even a unit contact gives projection
  greater than 2, so no contact is possible.
\end{itemize}

Additional nonpositive products cannot lower these projection bounds,
because the inverse is positive. Strictness excludes equality as well.
The retained path stops at outward distance 15. Contacts to the unused
outer whites at distances 16 and 17 are not claimed to vanish: those
whites supply the A17 inverse bound and are omitted from the final
principal matrix. These statements have no finite label cutoff.

In the inner A7 segment, b contacting a white at distance j at least 2
from the left mark gives a route to the right mark of length 9-j, at
most 7. Only the first inner white can therefore meet b in the no-short7
branch. Its A7 inverse diagonal is 7/8, which excludes label 5 and every
larger label by the same squared-magnitude comparison. Contacts to the
first two outward whites beyond the opposite mark also give short paths;
more distant contacts are already excluded by the other A17 arm. The
argument for d is the reflection of this argument.

Thus b can contact, apart from its own mark at 15, only positions
14,13,16, with allowed nonzero labels respectively (3 or 4), 3, (3 or
4). Root d has the reflected slots 24,25,22. The source first checks
every fixed old contact. A forbidden one supplies either a recorded
short path, an A17 projection obstruction, or a strict edge label
obstruction. Four orientations are rejected by the last reason; the
remaining fixed-contact exclusions use the former two reasons.

One omitted black cannot contact both consecutive outer whites. The
positive A2 inverse is (1/3){[}{[}2,1{]},{[}1,2{]}{]}, and two unit
contacts already have projection square 2, contrary to strict edge
positivity. The remaining slot products are enumerated exactly as
0,1,sqrt(2), respecting every old fixed contact. They are an
overestimate of realizable completions, which suffices for an
obstruction.

\section{Two necessary Gram tests}\label{two-necessary-gram-tests}

For a norm-2 simple path of order n, the inverse entries, using indices
from 0, are

\begin{verbatim}
J_n[i,j] = (min(i,j)+1)(n-max(i,j))/(n+1).
\end{verbatim}

The source verifies this inverse formula by multiplication for
n=2,7,15,17,39. Deleting the two marked roots from A39 gives three
independent white blocks A15+A7+A15. Let J\_W be their inverse. For the
positive contact vectors x,y of b,d with the A39 path, strict positive
definiteness of each actual edge requires

\begin{verbatim}
2 - x_W^T J_W x_W > 0,     2 - y_W^T J_W y_W > 0.
\end{verbatim}

Every profile violating either strict inequality is impossible.
Otherwise eliminate the full positive definite A39 block. Because b·d=0,
the remaining two-by-two Schur matrix is

\begin{verbatim}
[ 2 - x^T J_39 x       -x^T J_39 y     ]
[   -x^T J_39 y      2 - y^T J_39 y    ].
\end{verbatim}

In every surviving enumerated profile its first diagonal is strictly
negative and its determinant strictly positive. It therefore has two
negative directions. By congruence the full Gram matrix would have two
negative directions, impossible for actual vectors in a real Lorentz
space. This argument requires no assumption on the old core's signature.
Adding further actual roots or spectator contacts cannot repair a
principal Gram matrix with two negative directions.

All signs and products use the
\href{../scripts/fresh_quadratic_sqrt2_exact_20261017.py}{exact
Q(sqrt(2)) helper}. No floating-point tolerance or optimizer is used.

\chapter{A full corridor settles the deep-pair question throughout the
high
domain}\label{a-full-corridor-settles-the-deep-pair-question-throughout-the-high-domain}

For every corner of the complete frozen 6,703-context high-overlap
domain, the following statement holds. If the actual whole finite A/B/D
component has its two marked roots at distance 8, and both marks have
distance at least 20 from every endpoint, branch and endpoint of a
nonsimple bond, then the full actual supporting star has an
opposite-black path of length at most 7.

This is a \textbf{short-path alternative}. Only in the branch with no
such path anywhere in the full supporting star does it exclude the deep
corridor. The absence of a path in the saved old core alone is
insufficient. There is no new pair weight, complete payment system or
dimension bound here.

The
\href{../scripts/fresh_full_a43_corridor_high_domain_20261017.py}{source}
and \href{fresh_full_a43_corridor_high_domain_20261017.json}{exact
certificate} cover all 26,812 corners of the
\href{fresh_distance7_high_supporting_frontier_20261017.md}{inherited
high domain}, including all four corners of the 251 formerly unresolved
contexts and all earlier structural outputs. No old principal matrix is
required to be nonsingular or Lorentzian. The proof instead uses a
forced positive definite path in the proposed actual completion.

\section{The forced path and every possible old
embedding}\label{the-forced-path-and-every-possible-old-embedding-1}

Normalize all actual wall roots to squared norm 2. A feature of a finite
A/B/D diagram is a vertex of degree other than 2, or either endpoint of
a bond whose label exceeds 3. Depth at least 20 at each mark, together
with marked distance 8, gives two outward simple arms of length 20 and
the simple path joining the marks. All vertices other than the two marks
are supporting whites. The two omitted black roots do not belong to this
actual corner.

Keep the first 17 outward whites on each arm. Together with the marks
and the seven whites between them, these form an induced A43 diagram.
Number its vertices 0 through 42; the left and right marks are at 17 and
25. The unused three outward whites on each side are retained as
geometric inputs for the A20 contact estimates below, but are not needed
in the final matrix. A feature at outward distance exactly 20 is
harmless: all bonds inside the displayed A20 arm are simple.

The 342 old native cores are reconstructed from their frozen diagrams
and positive diagonal gauges. They have order at most 19, so any
displayed corner has at most 17 roots. Their gauges are 1 or 2; dividing
by the square roots of the gauges puts every relevant product in
Q(sqrt(2)). The source checks all four left/right choices in every old
context and independently reconstructs the displayed component
partitions.

A displayed component containing a mark must be a simple path. An
existing branch or nonsimple bond remains a feature in the actual
component and is at distance at most 16 from the mark. An existing cycle
cannot occur inside a finite A/B/D tree. The checker saves one such
witness for each rejected nonsimple marked block.

If the two marks are in the same displayed path, that path must already
give distance 8: a tree cannot acquire a second, shorter route. Its
embedding in A43 is then fixed once the two marks are placed at 17 and
25. If the marks lie in different displayed paths, orient each path from
its outward endpoint toward the eventual joining segment. Let t\_L,t\_R
be the inward distances from the marks to the chosen endpoints. The
connecting segment must contain exactly

\begin{verbatim}
k = 7 - t_L - t_R
\end{verbatim}

additional whites, with k at least 1. The two displayed components are
orthogonal, so no zero-white connection is possible. Every orientation
of both paths is enumerated, with singleton orientations counted once.
All retained embeddings fit inside A43; all old pair products are
checked against the corresponding A43 entries. This also covers paths
joined through old spectator roots: those roots may occupy positions not
selected in the reduced old embedding. Their identities and extra
contacts are not assumed away. The Gram tests use a necessary subset of
actual roots only.

\section{All-label restrictions leave three white slots per omitted
black}\label{all-label-restrictions-leave-three-white-slots-per-omitted-black-1}

Write b for the omitted left black root and d for the omitted right
black root. The full-star no-short7 hypothesis implies b·d=0 and forbids
any contact from b to the right mark, or from d to the left mark. Their
products with their own marks are fixed native products and remain in
the calculation.

For a norm-2 A20 arm, the inverse is positive and its diagonal at
outward distance j is j(21-j)/21. The omitted black and all these whites
belong to an actual edge diagram, which is strictly positive definite.
Hence:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  At outward distance 1, only nonzero contacts of labels 3 or 4 are
  possible. A label at least 5 has squared magnitude greater than 5/2,
  and (20/21)(5/2)\textgreater2.
\item
  At distance 2, only label 3 is possible, since (38/21)·2\textgreater2.
\item
  At distances 3 through 18, even a unit contact gives projection
  greater than 2, so no contact is possible.
\end{itemize}

Additional nonpositive products cannot lower these projection bounds,
because the inverse is positive. Strictness excludes equality as well.
These statements have no finite label cutoff.

In the inner A7 segment, b contacting a white at distance j at least 2
from the left mark gives a route to the right mark of length 9-j, at
most 7. Only the first inner white can therefore meet b in the no-short7
branch. Its A7 inverse diagonal is 7/8, which excludes label 5 and every
larger label by the same squared-magnitude comparison. Contacts to the
first two outward whites beyond the opposite mark also give short paths;
more distant contacts are already excluded by the other A20 arm. The
argument for d is the reflection of this argument.

Thus b can contact, apart from its own mark at 17, only positions
16,15,18, with allowed nonzero labels respectively (3 or 4), 3, (3 or
4). Root d has the reflected slots 26,27,24. The source first checks
every fixed old contact. A forbidden one supplies either a recorded
short path, an A20 projection obstruction, or a strict edge label
obstruction. Four orientations are rejected by the last reason; the
remaining fixed-contact exclusions use the former two reasons.

One omitted black cannot contact both consecutive outer whites. The
positive A2 inverse is (1/3){[}{[}2,1{]},{[}1,2{]}{]}, and two unit
contacts already have projection square 2, contrary to strict edge
positivity. The remaining slot products are enumerated exactly as
0,1,sqrt(2), respecting every old fixed contact. They are an
overestimate of realizable completions, which suffices for an
obstruction.

\section{Two necessary Gram tests}\label{two-necessary-gram-tests-1}

For a norm-2 simple path of order n, the inverse entries, using indices
from 0, are

\begin{verbatim}
J_n[i,j] = (min(i,j)+1)(n-max(i,j))/(n+1).
\end{verbatim}

The source verifies this inverse formula by multiplication for
n=2,7,17,20,43. Deleting the two marked roots from A43 gives three
independent white blocks A17+A7+A17. Let J\_W be their inverse. For the
positive contact vectors x,y of b,d with the A43 path, strict positive
definiteness of each actual edge requires

\begin{verbatim}
2 - x_W^T J_W x_W > 0,     2 - y_W^T J_W y_W > 0.
\end{verbatim}

Every profile violating either strict inequality is impossible.
Otherwise eliminate the full positive definite A43 block. Because b·d=0,
the remaining two-by-two Schur matrix is

\begin{verbatim}
[ 2 - x^T J_43 x       -x^T J_43 y     ]
[   -x^T J_43 y      2 - y^T J_43 y    ].
\end{verbatim}

In every surviving enumerated profile its first diagonal is strictly
negative and its determinant strictly positive. It therefore has two
negative directions. By congruence the full Gram matrix would have two
negative directions, impossible for actual vectors in a real Lorentz
space. This argument requires no assumption on the old core's signature.
Adding further actual roots or spectator contacts cannot repair a
principal Gram matrix with two negative directions.

All signs and products use the
\href{../scripts/fresh_quadratic_sqrt2_exact_20261017.py}{exact
Q(sqrt(2)) helper}. No floating-point tolerance or optimizer is used.

at its other E8 ideal corners fixed, its actual faces force all136 D16
pair weights to be at least1 under any rule invariant under the
intrinsic D16 diagram automorphisms. The resulting factor cost
is136=8·17. This is a local obstruction to reducing that particular
diagram-based budget, not a new dimension theorem.

from that frozen chamber package, not inferred from a partial list of
proposed corners.

The D16 cusp is simple. Every pair among its17 incident facets

face vertices and actual side facets from the saved cone rays, then
checks agreement with the frozen exhaustive face ledger. It computes

The fixed comparison rule is:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist

\item

\item
  at the D16 cusp, leave the weight as an arbitrary nonnegative real
  variable for its marked pair.
\end{itemize}

A triangle requires total payment2 and a quadrilateral requires1. The
exact required D16 payment is the positive part of that demand minus the
fixed payments at all other corners. Every resulting deficit is0 or1.

\section{Diagram invariance forces all136
pairs}\label{diagram-invariance-forces-all136-pairs}

The D16 diagram has two fork-leaf interchanges and the reversal of its
unique double-fork spine. These generate its full group of8
automorphisms. The checker verifies every generator against the literal

Consequently any intrinsic-diagram-invariant nonnegative real weighting
satisfying the stated fixed-baseline face demands must give every pair

Without diagram invariance, the109 primary mandatory pairs may receive

Under the distance9-only comparison the corresponding counts are122

Every one of the64 quadrilaterals through the D16 cusp has all19 roots

\chapter{Independent local transfer for the nine dropped D16
pairs}\label{independent-local-transfer-for-the-nine-dropped-d16-pairs}

The nine pairs between the two fork triples of the17-node affine D16
diagram can be removed in a literal shared-L25 H17 quadrilateral star if
the stated finite half-payments are added. The transfer survives
arbitrary additional supporting whites: either they give an immediate
length-two payment, or they are orthogonal to the entire19-root core and
preserve its finite component types.

exact checker} and

verify the core signature, radical, affine positive kernel and all27
finite corners in the nine cases. They use Fraction elimination and
literal graphs, without importing the proposed global producer's
arithmetic. The actual small chamber is the frozen
\href{fresh_nonincident_carrier_incidence_20261017.md}{known
finite-volume H17 pyramid}; the transfer below concerns any actual
quadrilateral with this same literal core and role assignment.

\section{Local hypotheses and finite
coupons}\label{local-hypotheses-and-finite-coupons}

Let the19-node core be two copies of L25 sharing node9, with the
numbering of the \href{fresh_h17_d16_payment_bottleneck_20261017.md}{D16
bottleneck audit}. Its opposite black pairs are

\texttt{\{a,3\}} and \texttt{\{b,13\}}, with a in\{0,1,2\} and b
in\{10,11,12\}.

All other core roots are supporting whites. Further supporting whites E
are allowed, and their Gram is positive definite because the face has an
interior hyperbolic point. The four displayed blacks are the actual four
sides. The Gram on the displayed19 roots is assumed to be the literal
core, including its zero contacts; obtaining that literal core from a
general classification is a separate obligation.

Retain a unit finite payment when the two marks have distance at most9
or lie in a connected component of order at most17. Add weight1/2 at
either of the following kinds of finite corner:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  the marks lie in distinct A1 and D16 components, with the D16 mark at
  its fork center or either short fork leaf;
\item
  the marks lie in distinct A2 and D14 components, with either A2 mark
  allowed and the D14 mark at its fork center or either short fork leaf.
\end{itemize}

The component names here are finite types: D16 has16 roots and D14 has14
roots. These half-payments are disjoint from the retained finite rule,
since their marks lie in different components. This note proves the
required local transfer, not a universal bound on the sum of all such
coupons.

\section{Extra supporting whites cannot change the required
components}\label{extra-supporting-whites-cannot-change-the-required-components}

Write F for the17-node affine D16 subdiagram obtained by omitting3 and13
from the core. The actual corner retaining a,b contains F. It is
necessarily ideal, since a finite corner cannot contain a singular
principal diagram. Its positive affine kernel has coefficients1 at the
four leaves and2 elsewhere. Every supporting white e in E lies at that
corner. The positive kernel and nonpositive Coxeter contacts force e to
be orthogonal to every root of F.

The exact19-root Gram has signature(17,1,1) and radical

\texttt{(-6,-3,-4,-2,-5,-4,-3,-2,-1,0,6,3,4,2,5,4,3,2,1)}.

This radical is an actual linear relation in the ambient Lorentz
realization. Indeed, its represented vector is null and orthogonal to
the indefinite core, hence to a timelike vector; a timelike vector's
orthogonal complement is positive definite, so the represented vector
must be zero.

Since e is already orthogonal to F, pairing that relation with e leaves

\texttt{-2(e·n3)+2(e·n13)=0.}

If these equal contacts are nonzero, the actual corner with marks3,13
contains the white-interior path3--e--13. That corner has a unit payment
under the finite distance9 or ideal distance7 rules. At an ideal corner
the actual factor-fiber lemma places this path in the varying affine
factor. Thus this case already pays the quadrilateral.

Otherwise every e in E is orthogonal to all19 core roots. The finite
corner stars then split as the displayed finite core corner plus the
positive-definite diagram E. They remain finite, and the marked core
components cannot be enlarged or joined by E. Consequently their literal
A1/D16 or A2/D14 coupon types, and their existing connected-component
payments, persist unchanged.

This argument concerns the supporting whites in the actual face star. It
does not assume a simple ideal vertex or claim that all ambient facets
incident to the ideal corner are among them. Those extra ideal facets
are irrelevant to the finite coupon corners.

The

diagrams}, retains 84 labelled attachments, and identifies \textbf{26
diagrams up to labelled graph isomorphism}. The
\href{fresh_high_rank_quasilanner_census_20261017.json}{saved census}
records every retained attachment, its explicit isomorphism, every
vertex deletion and the relevant diagonal-decrease thresholds.

These are \textbf{classical diagrams, not new examples or a new
classification}. The result reproduces the higher-order part of
\href{https://www.numdam.org/item/M2AN_1969__3_3_3_0.pdf}{M. Chein's
1969 classification, printed pp.15--16}. Chein's printed p.4 states the
order-ten ceiling, attributing it to Vinberg, and describes the
finite/affine principal-subdiagram criterion. Those classification facts
are published mathematical inputs here; a search restricted to ten nodes
would not itself establish the ceiling. A
\href{../data/references/fresh_finite_edge_cusp_tradeoff_20261017_chein.pdf}{repository
copy of the primary PDF} is also available through the separately frozen
finite-edge package.

\section{Why the finite search covers these
orders}\label{why-the-finite-search-covers-these-orders}

Use the usual norm-two Gram convention: diagonal entries are 2, a
missing edge denotes label 2, label 3 has product −1, and label 4 has
product \texttt{-sqrt(2)}. A minimal indefinite diagram has indefinite
full Gram matrix and positive-semidefinite every proper principal
submatrix. It is connected, since otherwise a smaller connected
component would already be indefinite.

For orders six through ten, the compact Lannér branch is absent: the
published compact classification has at most five nodes. Consequently at
least one proper principal submatrix is singular positive semidefinite
and contains a connected affine component A. Its kernel has strictly
positive coordinates. If another node is joined to A, the enlarged block
cannot be positive semidefinite: its affine kernel has a nonzero pairing
with the new node. Indeed a vector of zero quadratic form in a
positive-semidefinite matrix must lie in its full kernel, while the
positive coefficients and nonpositive Coxeter contacts make this pairing
strictly negative.

Connectivity supplies such an adjacent outside node. Minimal
indefiniteness therefore forces A together with that node to be the
whole diagram. Thus every diagram under consideration is an irreducible
affine diagram of order \texttt{n-1} with one additional, nonorthogonal
node. This also explains why an arbitrary disconnected affine forest is
not needed as a source.

There are no edge labels 5 or larger. Any edge in a connected diagram
with at least six nodes can be extended to a connected induced
subdiagram on five nodes, by adjoining adjacent vertices. This is a
proper principal subdiagram and must be finite or affine. The standard
finite/affine classification has no connected five-node diagram
containing an edge label at least 5. The smaller exceptions, such as the
noncrystallographic finite diagrams or the rank-two families, cannot
survive this extension.

Dotted pairs are already indefinite two-node subdiagrams, so are
excluded immediately. A parallel pair is a connected affine two-node
subdiagram; adjoining any adjacent node makes a proper indefinite
subdiagram by the same positive-kernel argument. Parallel bonds are
therefore also excluded at these orders. The attachment alphabet is
exactly \texttt{2,3,4}, including orthogonality; there is no numerical
cutoff on a hidden label or dotted distance.

The complete affine source list has ranks four through eight:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  rank 4: affine A4, B4, C4, D4 and F4;
\item
  rank 5: affine A5, B5, C5 and D5;
\item
  ranks 6, 7 and 8: affine A, B, C, D and the corresponding E type.
\end{itemize}

These are the 24 source models. For a source on \texttt{n-1} nodes the
program tests all \texttt{3\^{}(n-1)-1} nonzero attachment vectors.
Their total is 146,262.

\section{Exact acceptance, signature and isomorphism
checks}\label{exact-acceptance-signature-and-isomorphism-checks}

Every one-node deletion is decomposed into connected components. Each
component must be a recognized finite or affine Coxeter diagram. Finite
and affine trees are recognized by their complete labelled tree codes;
the affine A cycles are recognized separately. This supplies exact
positive semidefiniteness of every one-node deletion, and hence of every
proper principal submatrix. Rejection depends on this classification,
not on approximate eigenvalues.

For every newly encountered isomorphism type the source reconstructs the
full Gram matrix over exact rational numbers and \texttt{sqrt(2)} and
proves its determinant negative. Interlacing with the
positive-semidefinite one-node deletions then gives precisely one
negative eigenvalue. The nonzero determinant excludes a radical, so the
full signature is \texttt{(n-1,1,0)}.

Refinement is used only to select possible isomorphism matches; the
actual merges use a complete labelled graph-isomorphism test. All 84
retained attachments have an explicit saved map to one of the 26 final
diagrams. The classical order counts are asserted only after
enumeration, as a comparison check; they are not used to prune or accept
candidates.

The export distinguishes finite from affine node deletions. For a
diagram with a unique affine deletion j, it also records, for every
other deleted node b, the exact threshold

\[
 \tau_b=\frac{1}{(G_{\widehat b}^{-1})_{jj}}.
\]

All these thresholds are checked positive and rational. They describe
positive-semidefinite rank-one diagonal decreases at j. Applying them to
an actual simplex face with additional white supporting roots still
requires the appropriate geometric and Schur-complement argument.

\section{Scope and frozen validation}\label{scope-and-frozen-validation}

The finite/affine classifications, compact Lannér order bound and
general order-ten ceiling are explicit published inputs. The computation
exhausts the stated attachment domain and reproduces the classical
higher-order diagrams. It does not identify an induced geometric simplex
face with a Coxeter simplex, settle arbitrary extra supporting roots or
black/white partitions, or establish a new ambient dimension bound.

\chapter{Complete finite9 and ideal5 face
payments}\label{complete-finite9-and-ideal5-face-payments}

For every finite-sided finite-volume hyperbolic Coxeter polytope of
dimension n≤80, the rules below give each triangular two-face total
corner payment at least2 and each quadrilateral at least1. Finite-vertex
payment is at most9n. At an ideal vertex the exact factor costs have the
piecewise envelope stated below. This is a complete local-payment and
counting composition, including nonsimple cusps and arbitrary supporting
white roots. The ambient dimension comparison is separate.

The
\href{../scripts/fresh_ideal5_combined_payments_20261017.py}{checker}
and \href{fresh_ideal5_combined_payments_20261017.json}{certificate}
bind the frozen proofs and check their interfaces. The complete core
classification used here is the finite9 classification. No claim of
complete finite8 overlap coverage is needed or made.

\section{The rules}\label{the-rules}

At a finite vertex, pay1 when the marks lie in the same whole
irreducible component and either their graph distance is at most9 or
that component has order at most17. In addition, pay one half between
distinct whole components when one has rank at most5 and the other is
one of:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  D11 through D16, marked at its fork center or either short fork leaf;
\item
  A13 or A15, marked at its unique middle;
\item
  A17, marked five steps from one endpoint and eleven from the other.
\end{itemize}

Each qualifying pair receives one half, with no duplicate coupon for
multiple descriptions. The unit and coupon conditions use the full
actual finite vertex diagram, not a selected subdiagram.

At an ideal vertex, use the full varying affine factor containing the
two marks, as supplied by the
\href{fresh_cusp_factor_payment_framework_20261017.md}{actual
factor-fiber theorem}. Pay every pair when its order is at most13. At
orders14--17 use the exact automorphism-invariant pair sets in the
\href{fresh_ideal5_small_factor_payments_20261017.md}{571-pattern
census}. At larger orders pay distance at most5, and distances6--9 if an
endpoint is within5 of a branch or a nonsimple-bond endpoint. All these
ideal payments are zero or one.

\section{Triangle coverage is
retained}\label{triangle-coverage-is-retained}

The \href{fresh_ideal5_finite8_triangle_payments_20261017.md}{complete
finite8/ideal5 triangle theorem} already pays every triangle twice by
finite distance at most8, ideal factors of order at most9, or ideal
distance at most5 and feature-near distances at most8. The present
finite rule contains that finite rule. The source checks the inclusion
of every elementary triangle pair in every order14--17 target.
Conceptually, cycles have no features, so their removed distances
greater than5 were never elementary triangle payments. The nine removed
D pairs have minimum distance9 at order14 and larger minimum distances
in higher orders, whereas the triangle theorem's feature-near paths have
length at most8. Factors of order at most13 are wholly retained. Thus no
replacement of one triangle corner by only one total quadrilateral
payment is used.

\section{Quadrilateral coverage from the complete finite9
domain}\label{quadrilateral-coverage-from-the-complete-finite9-domain}

Start with an actual quadrilateral. If it has a finite marked corner
path of length at most9, its unit payment remains. Suppose an ideal
corner has such a path. It pays immediately at distance at most5 or
within the radius5 feature neighborhood, unless it is one of the
explicitly removed pairs.

For a classical tree factor outside that neighborhood, the complete
\href{fresh_finite8_ideal5_local_replacement_20261017.md}{finite8/ideal5
local theorem} replaces marked distances6--9 by retained units or sealed
finite coupons. The same theorem treats cycles of order at least15,
including the sealed A1/A15 and A1/A17 equalities. The separate
\href{fresh_cycle14_ideal5_transfer_20261017.md}{cycle14 theorem} treats
its remaining distances6 and7 using the strict spectator spectrum and
the sealed A13-middle coupons. Smaller factors are wholly paid.

All D pairs deliberately deleted from the basic rule are handled by the
specific transfers below. Therefore, when no corner has yet paid and no
transfer has already supplied a total unit, there can be no adjacent
marked path of length at most9. This is exactly the original hypothesis
of the complete
\href{fresh_selective_distance9_dimension108_20261017.md}{dimension108
core classification}, not a silently weakened no-short8 hypothesis.

That classification includes its complete all-label low-core supplement
and949 high-core overlap contexts. The low-core selected component
bounds are at most12. At a finite selected corner, the retained small17
rule pays. At an ideal selected corner, the whole varying factor has the
proved bound at most17. Orders at most13 pay. For orders14--17 the
actual marked principal component gives an induced labelled embedding
into the full factor; all such maps are in the571-pattern census, with
its extension-bound filter. Thus its pair is in the union before the
certified deletions. No arbitrary provenance, favorable map, or minimum
across incompatible realizations is selected.

\section{Every deleted pair has a retained
alternative}\label{every-deleted-pair-has-a-retained-alternative}

The cycle transfers above directly use the present short/feature rule
and the listed whole finite coupons. They do not leave an unexamined
ideal distance6 or7 obligation behind.

For order14 affine D13, the
\href{fresh_affine_d13_long_pair_transfer_20261017.md}{universal
long-pair transfer} replaces all nine cross-fork pairs. Its immediate
ideal alternatives are paths of length at most3 or the two literal
affine components of order12; these all pay. Its other conclusions are
sealed whole finite components or small components of ranks1,2,4,5
paired with D11 or D13 fork marks, all in the finite rule.

For order15 affine D14, the
\href{fresh_affine_d14_long_pair_transfer_20261017.md}{preceding
universal transfer} has only two immediate whole-small ideal
alternatives, both of order13. They arise from the center deletion D12
plus the new root, with either an endpoint4 or a second-node3
attachment. They are wholly paid. A possible order14 affine component
after another outer attachment is \textbf{not} an immediate paid
alternative in that proof: it remains among the bounded nonextreme
profiles and is eliminated by the strict determinant gap. The only short
ideal alternatives used are the adjacent-product or common spectator
paths of length1 or2, not an arbitrary distance6 pair. Its sealed
small-rank≤3 against D12/D14 coupons are included.

For orders16 and17, the nine affected preferred-core contexts at each
order are matched exactly to the saved
\href{fresh_order16_finite_cross_payments_20261017.md}{order16} and
\href{fresh_ideal7_finite_cross_payments_20261017.md}{order17}
replacements. Those are literal sealed-core arguments, not a new
universal center-profile extension. A nonorthogonal supporting white
gives a retained length2 path; otherwise the saved finite unit/coupon
corners sum to at least1. The source checks that every nonzero terminal
payment in all18 cases is finite. There is consequently no hidden
order14 ideal payment inherited from their older global rules. Their
core matching is applied only after the original no-short9 reduction has
been restored.

These implications complete quadrilateral coverage. They are direct
contradictions to a face whose total new payment is less than1: a direct
new ideal unit, a direct finite unit, or two sealed halves resolves it.
No cyclic chain of ideal transfers is assumed to terminate without
proof.

\section{Finite and ideal budgets}\label{finite-and-ideal-budgets}

The \href{fresh_finite8_a17_d11_coupon_budget_20261017.md}{finite8
coupon budget} already covers exactly the stated coupons together with
distance≤8, distance9 at a whole-component leaf, and whole finite

To restore all finite distance9 pairs, nothing is added in ranks at

n.~The new finite total is therefore at most9n with all enlarged coupons

The small-factor costs and the all-rank ideal5/R5 spine proof give the
factor rank envelope

polytope receives total payment at least2 under the following rule:

supporting white roots. The

\chapter{Unrestricted finite-volume dimension at most
74}\label{unrestricted-finite-volume-dimension-at-most-74}

The completed local three-pair replacement and the exact global
comparison give the following computer-assisted conclusion:

\textbf{Every finite-sided, finite-volume real hyperbolic Coxeter
polytope has dimension at most 74.}

There is no arithmetic, compactness, simple-cusp, cusp-factor or
facet-count restriction. This strengthens the completed
\href{fresh_ideal5_piecewise_dimension75_20261017.md}{dimension-75
proof}. The
\href{../scripts/fresh_ideal5_piecewise_dimension74_20261017.py}{source}
and \href{fresh_ideal5_piecewise_dimension74_20261017.json}{certificate}
check the new local interfaces and all 999 reduced profiles at dimension
75. The
\href{fresh_ideal5_piecewise_dimension74_20261017_review.md}{independent
review} reconstructs every profile and agrees on every exact row.

\chapter{Complete finite9/ideal6 payments and piecewise cusp
budgets}\label{complete-finite9ideal6-payments-and-piecewise-cusp-budgets}

This package combines the local arguments into a single payment rule for
arbitrary finite-sided finite-volume hyperbolic Coxeter polytopes. Every
triangle receives at least2 and every quadrilateral at least1. For
n\textless=108 every finite vertex costs at most9n. At an ideal vertex
with simplex-factor ranks r\_i and V link vertices, the cost is at most
V*sum\_i b(r\_i), where

\begin{verbatim}
b(r)=r/2 for1<=r<=13;
b(14)=20/3; b(15)=111/16; b(16)=127/17;
b(r)=95/13 forr>=17.
\end{verbatim}

The \href{../scripts/fresh_ideal6_combined_payments_20261017.py}{binder}
and \href{fresh_ideal6_combined_payments_20261017.json}{certificate}
retain the complete source dependencies. A global dimension comparison
is separate.

\section{The rule}\label{the-rule}

At finite vertices retain unit payments for same-component marked pairs
of distance at most9 or whole-component order at most17, together with
the \href{fresh_broad_finite_half_coupons_20261017.md}{broad finite
half-coupons}. Those coupons apply to whole components, with one of rank
at most4 and the other a specified fork-marked D12,\ldots,D16 or
middle-marked A13,A15.

At ideal vertices pay every pair in a varying factor of order at most14.
For larger factors the basic unit rule is distance at most6, or
distance7--9 with an endpoint within6 of a branch or nonsimple bond
endpoint. At orders 15,16,17 add all induced marked images of the
complete inherited preferred components. Remove the nine D pairs at each
of those orders: the two fork centers and the eight pairs spanning the
two fork triples. Their finite replacements are proved separately,
including all supporting whites.

The exact resulting A/B/C/D costs are

\end{longtable}
}

The \href{fresh_ideal6_small_factor_frontier_20261017.md}{small-factor
census} enumerates every relevant induced labelled map of437 preferred
contexts. The new

transfer} handles all nine order15 pairs universally, so it handles
