\section{Every face is paid}\label{every-face-is-paid}

The \href{fresh_ideal6_triangle_payments_20261017.md}{triangle theorem}
applies directly: its short paths and feature witnesses remain paid, and
its sole affine-E8 exception uses a whole factor of order at most9. None
of the nine removed D pairs at orders15--17 belongs to these
short/feature payments.

For a quadrilateral, suppose first that some actual corner has a path of
length at most9. A finite corner pays immediately. An ideal factor of
order at most14 pays in full. An unpaid pair in a larger classical
factor has distance7,8 or9 and lies outside the relevant feature
neighborhood. The
\href{fresh_ideal_distance6_mixed_replacement_20261017.md}{mixed6
replacement} handles distance7 cycles and tree distances7--9. For cycles
of distance8 or9, the
\href{fresh_ideal_distance7_mixed_replacement_20261017.md}{preceding
mixed7 theorem} gives another finite-distance9 or ideal-distance7
payment when the factor order is at least17. If that ideal-distance7
corner is still unpaid, the new mixed6 theorem applies there. Since the
whole face was assumed unpaid, each such transfer directly contradicts
that assumption; no iteration or termination premise is needed. The
antipodal order16 cycle case is handled by its
\href{fresh_cycle16_half_coupon_transfer_20261017.md}{finite A15-center
coupons}. No cycle of order15 has distance8 or9. These cases cover every
short path.

Otherwise there is no short9 path at any corner, precisely the
hypothesis of the inherited preferred-component theorem. Its complete
small-core classification gives a preferred component of order at
most12; the complete high-core classification gives one of order at
most17. A finite preferred corner pays by its whole-component rule. At
an ideal corner, order at most14 pays in full, and every possible image
at orders15--17 was included above. Only the nine removed D pairs can
remain; their universal finite transfer pays the face. Thus every
quadrilateral receives at least1. Polygons with at least5 sides need no
positive lower payment for the D5 comparison.

\section{Vertex budgets and scope}\label{vertex-budgets-and-scope}

The broad finite-coupon theorem proves the9n bound for every
n\textless=108, using only whole-component ranks, slack and at most
three eligible large marks. At factor order m\textless=14,
binom(m,2)/m=(m-1)/2. The table gives the exceptional normalized
maxima20/3,111/16,127/17. For order at least18 the preferred component
bound allows no extra pair. The mixed6 all-rank spine formulas and
their12 linear branches give a common normalized bound95/13; cycles
cost6 per node. These are all-rank arguments, not extrapolation from a
finite graph sample.

The \href{fresh_cusp_factor_payment_framework_20261017.md}{actual
cusp-factor theorem} counts each pair in a rank-r factor with
multiplicity V/(r+1). This gives the stated ideal cost V*sum\_i b(r\_i),
without a simple-cusp, arithmetic or minimum-factor-rank assumption.

\section{Reduction to the finite
census}\label{reduction-to-the-finite-census}

Let W be the elliptic supporting diagram of an actual triangular
two-face, and let its sides be a,b,c.~Its full star is indefinite. Every
W together with two sides is a finite or ideal corner and hence has
positive-semidefinite Gram matrix. Consequently any minimal indefinite
subdiagram contains all three sides. Such a diagram has order at most10
by the stated classification. For order at most7, a Steiner tree on the
three marked nodes has at most6 edges. At least two of its
marked-to-marked paths avoid the third mark. Each gives a paid corner,
including at an ideal vertex.

For orders8,9,10, remove the third mark for each corner and find its
marked path and branch/bond features. There are224,336,360 triples
respectively. Only nine triples fail the pure distance6 test. The
feature rule pays at least two corners in all920 triples except
diagram25 with marks(1,2,9). Every saved feature witness persists under
additional supporting whites: an existing branch or nonsimple bond
cannot disappear, and an existing path cannot become longer. At an ideal
corner the connected marked core lies in its varying affine factor. At a
finite corner every saved path has length at most9. Thus these are
witnesses in the full corner, not assumptions that a small finite
subdiagram remains a whole finite component.

\section{The one exceptional triple}\label{the-one-exceptional-triple}

Diagram25 is simply laced, with edges

\begin{verbatim}
0-1, 0-2, 0-4, 2-3, 4-5, 5-6, 6-7, 7-8, 8-9.
\end{verbatim}

corner(1,2). The exact checker verifies its positive kernel, rank8 and a
positive-definite eight-node principal matrix. Every extra supporting
white is orthogonal to this entire affine diagram: positive
semidefiniteness at corner(1,2) forces its pairing with the positive
kernel to vanish, and all individual pairings are nonpositive.
Corner(1,2) already pays through its path1-0-2.

At corner(1,9), deleting2 leaves A8+A1, with marked path

\begin{verbatim}
1-0-4-5-6-7-8-9
\end{verbatim}

and isolated node3. The checker verifies this labelled path and positive
definiteness exactly. The preceding orthogonality forces node1 to remain
a simple-bond leaf and its neighbor0 to retain degree2 in the full
corner. No classical irreducible affine diagram has a simple-bond leaf
whose neighbor has degree2: affine A has no such leaf, affine C has
nonsimple end bonds, and the simple leaves of affine B and D meet branch
vertices. The remaining irreducible affine diagrams have at most9 nodes.
This uses the standard finite/affine classification already assumed by
the census.

Therefore, if corner(1,9) is finite, its length7 path pays1. If it is

\section{Independent exact scalar
reconstruction}\label{independent-exact-scalar-reconstruction}

For each link dimension d=91,\ldots,96, the checker chooses the
exceptional large part b in\{0,16,\ldots,d\} and small part a

For a rank profile, sliding-window multiplication independently

\begin{verbatim}

expands only the numerator product\_i(1−t\^{}(r\_i+1))=sum\_l a\_l

where out-of-range binomial terms are zero. It agrees with the
coefficient calculation in all477 profiles and the boundary profile. The

\chapter{Mixed finite-nine and ideal-six quadrilateral
replacements}\label{mixed-finite-nine-and-ideal-six-quadrilateral-replacements}

\textbf{Completed local proof; final verification status below.} Use
unit finite payments for marked distance at most9. At ideal corners use
unit payments for marked distance at most6, or for distance7,8,9 when an
endpoint is within6 graph steps of a feature. A feature is a vertex of
degree at least3 or an endpoint of a bond of label at least4.

The following statements hold for actual quadrilaterals in finite-sided
finite-volume hyperbolic Coxeter polytopes, without an arithmetic or
simple-cusp assumption.

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  An ideal marked pair at distance7 in an affine cycle of order at
  least15 has another corner paid by finite distance9 or ideal
  distance6.
\item
  At cycle order14, the same conclusion holds unless the face has two
  sealed finite corners of types A1/A13 and A2/A13, with the A13 mark
  its unique middle. A half-payment at each of these whole-component
  pairs pays the face.
\item
  For a classical affine tree, an ideal marked pair at distance7,8 or9
  whose endpoints are farther than6 from all features has another corner
  paid by the rule above.
\end{itemize}

The
\href{../scripts/fresh_ideal_distance6_mixed_replacement_20261017.py}{source}
and
\href{fresh_ideal_distance6_mixed_replacement_20261017.json}{certificate}
also give the all-rank costs of this basic ideal rule. They do
\textbf{not} establish a new dimension bound or remove the separate
preferred-component obligations in small factors. In particular the
remaining order15 D-factor payment obstruction is not resolved here.
Triangle payments and the total finite budget are separate tasks.

\section{Actual face setup and inherited
classification}\label{actual-face-setup-and-inherited-classification}

Write the face star as H=W+a+b+c+d, with opposite pairs \{a,c\},\{b,d\}.
If a corner has a nonzero adjacent black product it already pays, so in
the unpaid analysis all adjacent black products are zero. At a chosen
ideal corner, W+a+b is a varying affine factor F plus a
positive-definite spectator diagram Z orthogonal to F. The
\href{fresh_cusp_factor_payment_framework_20261017.md}{actual
factor-fiber theorem} gives this description even at nonsimple cusps.

The positive affine kernel represents the actual ideal point. The
opposite sides c,d do not contain it, so their heights h,k are strictly
positive. We retain the complete finite/affine one-root profile lists
and normalized Schur determinant from the frozen
\href{fresh_distance8_ideal_corner_replacement_20261017.md}{weak-profile
proof} and
\href{fresh_ideal_distance7_mixed_replacement_20261017.md}{mixed
finite-nine/ideal-seven proof}. These classification inputs do not
assume a global exclusion of small affine subdiagrams.

Eliminating the spectator block changes the normalized determinant by

\begin{verbatim}
alpha * (x/h-y/k)^T G_Z^(-1) (x/h-y/k) >= 0,
\end{verbatim}

where alpha\textgreater0 and x,y are nonnegative native
contact-magnitude vectors of c,d with Z. Thus a strictly positive
spectator-free determinant contradicts the actual face star's corank1. A
negative relaxed determinant alone proves nothing; the small-cycle
analysis below handles its equality condition exactly.

\section{Cycle factors of order at
least17}\label{cycle-factors-of-order-at-least17}

Choose the shorter old marked arc as P=7. The other arc has
Q\textgreater=10. The complete long-A profiles are isolated, endpoint3
on either arc, endpoint4 on either arc, second-node3 on either arc, and
both-end3.

A single-attachment profile gives an adjacent component containing the
old A\_(m-1) path and the new root. The old endpoint opposite the
attachment stays a simple leaf with a degree2 neighbor, since spectators
are orthogonal to the old factor. No large affine A/B/C/D diagram has
this configuration, and exceptional affine diagrams are too small.
Therefore this adjacent marked component and its actual corner are
finite. This is the fixed-leaf argument already proved in the
\href{fresh_cycle16_half_coupon_transfer_20261017.md}{cycle16 transfer};
it applies here to old paths of rank at least13.

For an attachment at position j=1 or2 on an arc of length L, the finite
marked distance is L-j+1. Under unpaidness it must exceed9, forcing
L\textgreater=9+j. Thus all single profiles on the short arc7 are
excluded. On the long arc an endpoint profile requires Q\textgreater=10
and a second-node profile Q\textgreater=11.

Only five profiles remain. The normalized determinant is nonincreasing
in the reciprocal arc lengths and concave in the reciprocal heights, as
in the frozen formal identity. For every ordered profile pair, use
Q\textgreater=11 if a second-node profile occurs and Q\textgreater=10
otherwise. The checker evaluates all100 height-rectangle vertices, with
exact minimum1/35. Positive heights and arbitrary positive-definite
spectators therefore cannot produce a zero determinant. This proves the
cycle statement for every order at least17, not just for tested orders.

\section{The exact spectator gap at
orders14,15,16}\label{the-exact-spectator-gap-at-orders141516}

Here P=7 and Q=7,8,9. Every single profile already yields a finite
marked distance at most9. The checker verifies the18 literal
positive-definite single-profile diagrams, their marked distances and
their fixed opposite leaf. Only isolated and both-end3 profiles remain.
The12 ordered profile pairs give48 exact rectangle values. Every pair
involving both-end3 has a strictly positive minimum. Hence only
isolated/isolated can remain.

For isolated profiles the heights are exactly the native opposite
contact magnitudes. They are1 or at least sqrt(2). If either height is
at least sqrt(2), the normalized determinant has lower bound

\begin{verbatim}
1-3*alpha > 0,       alpha=1/7+1/Q <=2/7.
\end{verbatim}

Consequently h=k=1. This step precedes the contact gap: no lower bound
on coordinates of a divided contact vector is being assumed. The
normalized determinant equation now requires

\begin{verbatim}
D = (x-y)^T G_Z^(-1)(x-y) = 4-1/alpha.
\end{verbatim}

Its required values are

{\def\LTcaptype{none} % do not increment counter
\begin{longtable}[]{@{}rrr@{}}
\toprule\noalign{}
Cycle order & Q & Required D \\

Any common nonzero coordinate of x,y gives a path c-e-d of length2,
already paid. Otherwise their supports are disjoint. Each nonzero native

If both vectors are nonzero, choose i in the support of x and j in the
support of y. Cauchy in the positive-definite Gram metric gives

\begin{verbatim}
D >= (x_i+y_j)^2 / (4-2G_ij) > 1/2.

Indeed x\_i+y\_j\textgreater=2, while positive definiteness of the

If just one vector is nonzero, say x, Cauchy with the coordinate vector

Thus orders15 and16 are impossible in the unpaid analysis. Order14

case are universal positive-definite Gram arguments, not finite

\section{The sealed order14 equality

\section{Classical trees outside feature
radius6}\label{classical-trees-outside-feature-radius6}

Both marks are on the simple spine. At a doubled end, distance greater

Each profile has cost g=2*l/h+c0/h\^{}2 at most4. The unique cost4

determinant is

\begin{verbatim}
F = 1-(g_c+g_d)/P.
\end{verbatim}

For P=7, an inner second-node attachment produces an adjacent path of

profile leaves F\textgreater=1/4. For P=9, no removal is needed:
F\textgreater=1/9.

The source checks192 ordered profile/distance cases:30 immediate
payments and162 positive gaps. Spectators only increase the determinant.
This proves the tree statement in every rank satisfying the actual
distance-from-features condition.

\section{All-rank costs of the basic ideal
rule}\label{all-rank-costs-of-the-basic-ideal-rule}

For order m\textgreater=18, the exact counts are

\begin{verbatim}
A: 6m,
C: 6m-21+min(m-7,16)+min(m-8,16)+min(m-9,16),
B: 6m-14+min(m-9,15)+min(m-10,15)+min(m-11,15),
D: 6m-7+min(m-11,14)+min(m-12,14)+min(m-13,14).

The A cycle has exactly m pairs at each distance1,\ldots,6 and no
features. For C, the path contributes6m-21 short pairs. At each
distance7,8,9, the allowed start positions lie in two endpoint intervals
of length8, so their union has min(m-k,16) positions.

For B, the simple spine has m-2 nodes. Short pairs total6m-20, including
the one extra pair between the two fork leaves. At each of the three
long distances there are two fork-leaf pairs, plus two spine start
intervals of lengths7 and8. This gives the constant6m-14 and the three

pairs, and two spine intervals of length7. For m\textgreater=18 no
opposite-fork leaf pair has distance at most9. This gives6m-7 and the
cap14 minima. The interval-union formulas cover their overlap exactly.

Each expression has successive linear slopes9,8,7,6. Its normalized
maximum is85/12 at C order24,36/5 at B order25, and95/13 at D order26.
The checker records all12 finite/infinite linear branches and proves the
bound on each from its endpoint or positive infinite-tail slack. The332
literal graph counts at orders18,\ldots,100 corroborate the formulas;
the proof of the infinite tail is the spine count and linear-branch
analysis, not extrapolation.

These are costs of the basic rule only. The inherited
preferred-component images may require additional pairs at small orders,
and the order14 coupon needs a total finite-budget proof if used
globally. This package makes neither inference automatically.

\chapter{Mixed finite-nine and ideal-seven local
payments}\label{mixed-finite-nine-and-ideal-seven-local-payments}

\textbf{Completed internally reviewed local results.} The following
statements concern actual faces of finite-sided finite-volume hyperbolic
Coxeter polytopes, with no arithmeticity or simple-cusp assumption.

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  Every triangle has two distinct adjacent black pairs joined by
  white-interior paths of length at most7.
\item
  Suppose an ideal corner of an actual quadrilateral has marked
  distance8 or9 in a varying affine factor of order at least17. Either
  one mark is within7 graph steps of a feature, or some corner is paid
  by finite distance at most9 or ideal distance at most7. A feature is a
  vertex of degree at least3 or an endpoint of a bond of label at
  least4.
\end{enumerate}

The
\href{../scripts/fresh_ideal_distance7_mixed_replacement_20261017.py}{source}
and
\href{fresh_ideal_distance7_mixed_replacement_20261017.json}{certificate}
prove the finite exact parts below. These are local payment statements,
not an ambient dimension bound. In particular they do not replace the
old whole-component payments on factors of order16 or17 without an
additional argument.

There is also an exact order16 obstruction to the naive local rule: an
actual quadrilateral in an infinite-volume H16 Coxeter chamber receives
no payment from finite distance9 and ideal distance7 with whole
components only through order15. Its complete cone and strict escape are
certified below. It is \textbf{not} a finite-volume counterexample to
statement2 or to a proposed global theorem.

\section{Two length-seven paths at every
triangle}\label{two-length-seven-paths-at-every-triangle}

The triangle star has the supporting positive-definite white diagram W
and three black roots. It is indefinite, while deleting any black gives
the positive-semidefinite star at an actual corner. Consequently a
minimal indefinite principal subdiagram L contains all three black
roots. The inherited Lanner/quasi-Lanner classification bounds its order
by10, as in the
\href{fresh_selective_distance9_dimension108_20261017.md}{completed
dimension108 proof}.

If L has order at most9, take a minimal spanning tree connecting its
three marks. Its three arms have total length at most8. If the branch
point is one of the marks, the two nonempty arms each have length at
most7. Otherwise all three arms are positive; adjoining the shortest arm
to either other arm gives two paths of length at most7. These paths
contain no third mark internally, so their interiors consist of whites.
This argument also covers every lower-order minimal core, independently
of labels.

Only the three order10 diagrams in the
\href{fresh_high_rank_quasilanner_census_20261017.md}{complete frozen
catalogue} remain. The checker tests all360 black triples in these three
literal graphs. For each pair it deletes the third black before finding
a shortest path. Every triple has at least two such paths of length at
most7. The largest second-smallest length is exactly7. These paths lie
in the corresponding actual corner diagrams. At an ideal corner the
factor-fiber theorem puts both marks and the path in the varying affine
factor. Thus two triangle payments survive lowering ideal short distance
to7.

\section{Quadrilateral setup and cycle
factors}\label{quadrilateral-setup-and-cycle-factors}

Use H=W+a+b+c+d with opposite pairs \{a,c\},\{b,d\}, and square-two
normals. Assume that no corner receives finite-distance9 or
ideal-distance7 payment. In particular there is no adjacent black bond:
such a bond would have distance1 at its actual corner. Hence
b.c=a.d=c.d=0.

At the selected ideal corner, W+a+b is its varying affine factor F plus
a positive-definite spectator forest Z orthogonal to F. The positive
affine kernel gives the actual future ideal point nu. The opposite sides
c,d do not contain it, so h=-c.nu and k=-d.nu are positive. These facts
hold at nonsimple cusps by the
\href{fresh_cusp_factor_payment_framework_20261017.md}{actual
factor-fiber theorem}.

We use the complete eight long-A profiles, weak height bounds and
four-root determinant from the frozen
\href{fresh_distance8_ideal_corner_replacement_20261017.md}{ideal
distance-nine replacement}. No small-affine exclusion is restored here.
For a cycle, write its two old marked arcs as P,Q. Their minimum is8
or9, and P+Q≥17. It is safe to relax this to P,Q≥8 and P+Q≥17.

A single endpoint3/endpoint4/second-node3 profile for c has an important
extra consequence. In the adjacent corner W+b+c, the old cycle minus a
is a path of rank at least16. The old endpoint opposite the attachment
remains a simple leaf, and its neighbor remains degree2: both are old F

connected affine A/B/C/D diagram. Exceptional affine diagrams are too
small to contain the old path. Thus the full component containing b,c is
finite, even after arbitrary spectators are restored. The actual
factor-fiber theorem then prevents this corner from being ideal: at an

Let the attachment be on an arc of length P, at position j=1 for an
endpoint or j=2 for a second node. The finite marked distance from c to
b is P−j+1. If it were at most9 this corner would already pay. Therefore
an unpaid single profile forces

\begin{verbatim}
P >= 9+j:  P>=10 at an endpoint,  P>=11 at the second node.
\end{verbatim}

This handles attachments on a long arc as well as on a short one; it
does not incorrectly assume that every single-profile corner has
distance at most9. The same reasoning applies to d.~Isolated and
both-end3 profiles impose no such additional lower bound.

Use the weak heights h\textgreater=1 for isolated, endpoint3 and
second-node3; h\textgreater=sqrt(2) for endpoint4; and h\textgreater=2
for both-end3. For each ordered profile pair, impose its arc lower
bounds. If both lower bounds remain8, the integer condition
P+Q\textgreater=17 splits the domain into
P\textgreater=8,Q\textgreater=9 or P\textgreater=9,Q\textgreater=8.
Otherwise the lower bounds already sum to at least17.

With A=1/P, B=1/Q, u=1/h, v=1/k, and the inherited moment data, the
normalized determinant is

\begin{verbatim}
F=1-2*(A*L+B*M)
    -(A+B)*(c0*u²+d0*v²)-A*B*(L-M)².
\end{verbatim}

It is nonincreasing in A,B and jointly concave in u,v. The checker
evaluates the four height-rectangle vertices for every resulting
reciprocal-arc box. All272 exact values are at least1/18. Therefore

As before, eliminating arbitrary spectator whites changes this

\begin{verbatim}
alpha*(p/h² - 2q/(h*k) + r/k²) >= 0
\end{verbatim}

for a positive-semidefinite {[}{[}p,q{]},{[}q,r{]}{]} and
alpha\textgreater0. It cannot remove the contradiction. Thus the cycle
part of statement2 is complete for every factor order at least17.

\section{Classical trees away from
features}\label{classical-trees-away-from-features}

In these orders only affine A/B/C/D types occur. For a B/C/D factor
suppose both marks lie farther than7 from every feature. They are on its
simple spine. At a doubled end, the nearer doubled-bond endpoint is a
feature, so the outer finite B component has rank at least9. At a fork
end, the fork center is a feature, so the outer finite D component has
rank at least10. These are literal node counts, not distances that
accidentally count a doubled edge as a simple extension.

The eight complete large-B/D extension profiles and their all-rank Schur
constants are those proved in the
\href{fresh_distance8_ideal_corner_replacement_20261017.md}{preceding
replacement lemma}. They include both one-component affine alternatives,

g=2*l/h+c0/h² is at most4; the only profile attaining this bound is
inner second-node3. The next-largest maximum is3 for inner endpoint3.
The determinant after eliminating the factor whites is

\begin{verbatim}
F=1-(g_c+g_d)/P,
\end{verbatim}

where P is the old marked spine distance.

For P=9, F\textgreater=1/9 directly. For P=8, an inner second-node3
attachment gives a path from the new root to the opposite old mark of
length P−1=7. That actual corner is already paid, whether finite or

g\_c,g\_d\textless=3, so F\textgreater=1/4. The checker records all128
ordered profile/distance cases:15 immediate length-seven paths and113

This proves the tree part, and therefore statement2 with feature

\section{Exact local obstruction at cycle
order16}\label{exact-local-obstruction-at-cycle-order16}

Take a simple cycle on0,\ldots,15, add a simple leaf16 at0 and a simple
leaf17 at8, and set every other contact to zero. Let G be its norm-two
Gram. Its exact signature is(16,1,1), so the quotient by its radical is

and h²=-204. Thus there is a strict common interior. For every root i,
h+e\_i/2 is a timelike witness on its wall and strictly inside every
other wall, proving that all18 walls are actual facets.

Set W=\{1,\ldots,7,9,\ldots,15\}, with black order(0,8,16,17). W is
positive definite. Its four projected side normals have Gram

\begin{verbatim}
[[ 1/4,-1/4,-1, 0],
 [-1/4, 1/4, 0,-1],
 [-1,    0,  2, 0],
 [ 0,   -1,  0, 2]].
\end{verbatim}

The complete face cone has four rays: three finite vertices and one

the marked roots0,8 are antipodal at distance8 in the16-node affine A

finite-distance9 does not pay any of them. The
ideal-short7/whole-factor15 rule pays no corner of this actual

The full chamber is nevertheless \textbf{infinite volume}. In dual

radical relation. Its extreme rays are the two zero-coordinate axes and
the64 balanced pairs of positive and negative radical coordinates. The
exact census gives35 finite,7 ideal and24 exterior rays. This is a

balance equation decomposes into those axes and balanced pairs.

For a particularly explicit escape, let v be the ray with y=e4. Then

\begin{verbatim}
t=(sqrt(285)-9)/204>0,
\end{verbatim}

the vector v+t*h is null, pairs negatively with h and has strictly

example shows exactly why the local mixed replacement theorem cannot

\chapter{Quadrilateral payment at a large affine factor with
spectators}\label{quadrilateral-payment-at-a-large-affine-factor-with-spectators}

\textbf{Final internally reviewed ideal-corner payment lemma.} Let P be
a finite-sided finite-volume hyperbolic Coxeter polytope. Suppose its
diagram has no connected affine subdiagram of order at most9. If an
actual quadrilateral has an ideal corner whose varying irreducible
affine factor has order m\textgreater=18, that quadrilateral receives
payment at least1 under the finite Vinberg rule and the affine rule
described below. Other irreducible factors at the cusp may be present.
This statement does not assert payment for quadrilaterals with four
finite corners, or an ambient dimension bound.

The affine rule pays a marked pair at graph distance at most3 or in a
fork-invariant end segment of order at most6. Its cost is at most three
times the factor order in every rank, by the
\href{fresh_cusp_spectator_role_payments_20261017.md}{role-payment
package}. The finite rule is the original published Vinberg rule. The
new
\href{../scripts/fresh_large_affine_factor_quad_payment_20261017.py}{checker}
and \href{fresh_large_affine_factor_quad_payment_20261017.json}{data}
verify the additional scalar and inverse-entry calculations below.
Complete extension lists and unbounded parameters are handled in the
proof, not by a rank or label cutoff.

\section{The original face star and the spectator
correction}\label{the-original-face-star-and-the-spectator-correction}

Write the four corners as W+a+b, W+b+c, W+a+d and W+c+d.~The supporting
white diagram W has order n-2 and is positive definite. Each W+one black
supports an actual edge and is positive definite, even if an endpoint is
ideal. The full star has rank n+1 and corank1, by projecting its four
side normals to the three-dimensional Lorentz space perpendicular to W.

At the chosen ideal corner, W+a+b consists of the varying affine factor
F, containing both a and b, together with a positive-definite spectator
forest Z orthogonal to F. This is the
\href{fresh_cusp_factor_payment_framework_20261017.md}{actual
factor-fiber description}; it does not assume the ideal vertex is
simple. The full cusp may have other incident normals not in the face
star. Every normal has square2.

The positive kernel of F gives a nonzero vector nu representing this
actual ideal vertex. Since c and d are opposite sides of the
quadrilateral, neither contains that vertex. Therefore h=-c.nu and
k=-d.nu are strictly positive. This argument replaces orthogonality to
the entire simple-cusp normal span; a single factor need not span that
null hyperplane.

First eliminate only the white roots of F, leaving the spectators. The
frozen cycle and tree formulas give a four-root Schur determinant.
Eliminating Z subsequently subtracts a positive-semidefinite matrix
{[}{[}p,q{]},{[}q,r{]}{]} from the c,d block. The normalized determinant
changes by

\begin{verbatim}
alpha*(p/h^2 - 2q/(h*k) + r/k^2) >= 0,
\end{verbatim}

where alpha\textgreater0 is the old marked-pair residual diagonal. The
heights h,k are unchanged. This is the exact
\href{fresh_cusp_factor_payment_framework_20261017.md}{PSD spectator
identity}. Consequently every strictly positive scalar contradiction
remains valid with any number of spectator roots and arbitrary allowed
contacts to them. A finite-component payment requires a separate check
that its marked roles remain paid; those checks appear below.

If any of b.c, a.d or c.d is negative, the corresponding adjacent marked
pair is paid. In the remaining analysis all three products are zero. The
opposite contacts x=-a.c and y=-b.d are arbitrary Coxeter contacts:
zero, a finite cosine magnitude, parallel2, or dotted. No field
restriction is imposed.

\section{Cycle factors}\label{cycle-factors}

For an affine A factor, deleting a leaves the connected A\_(m-1) path.
Its complete one-root finite/affine extensions are exactly the five
classes in the
\href{fresh_simple_cusp_affine_a_quadrilateral_20261017.md}{frozen cycle
proof}. Spectators do not enlarge this principal-diagram list: every
connected component of a positive-semidefinite Coxeter diagram is finite
or affine.

All height exclusions in that proof use only affine diagrams of
orders3,4 and9. They therefore hold under the present hypothesis. The
old cycle has m\textgreater=18, so its unused arc supplies the same
induced affine-E8 leaf witness. Both arc lengths are at least4 at an
unpaid corner. The all-rank reciprocal-arc argument gives a strictly
positive determinant before spectator elimination, and the PSD identity
preserves that contradiction. Thus the complete cycle branch transfers.

\section{A bounded affine witness for every excluded simple
leaf}\label{a-bounded-affine-witness-for-every-excluded-simple-leaf}

Consider a classical affine tree with main-path marks a,b, distance
P\textgreater=4, and outer ends B\_r or D\_r. D2 denotes the two fork
leaves. The factor order is m=r+s+P+1. A new simple leaf at a, its first
inner neighbor, or its second inner neighbor has available opposite
all-3 path lengths

\begin{verbatim}
L=r-1+j,  R=m-3-L,  j=0,1,2.
\end{verbatim}

These lengths stop before a doubled terminal bond and may end at one
chosen fork leaf. If L,R\textgreater=2, their sum m-3\textgreater=15
ensures that one is at least5. The leaf together with path arms of
lengths2 and5 induces affine E8, of order9. Extra fork leaves are
omitted and introduce no additional edge among the selected vertices.

Only the following near-end exceptions have L\textless2. At j=0 they are
B1, B2 and D2; the whole short end, a, the new leaf and the first inner
neighbor give respectively an affine four-node doubled star, affine B4,
or affine D4. At j=1 the only exception is B1, giving affine B4 on five
nodes. There is no exception at j=2. The right path has length at
least4-j. Thus every simple-leaf exclusion needed here uses an explicit
induced affine diagram of order at most9, even when the outer end is
arbitrarily long. This replaces the older proof's use of a possibly long
affine B/D witness.

\section{Complete main-path replacements and their
bounds}\label{complete-main-path-replacements-and-their-bounds}

Deleting a separates its outer B/D end from the inner B/D component
containing b. A connected one-root extension contains whole old
components. The original finite/affine classification in the
\href{fresh_simple_cusp_affine_tree_short_ends_20261017.md}{short-end
proof} still gives every join touching both components. The one addition
is a D2 join using one outer leaf by a bond4 and the inner long port by
a bond3, leaving the second A1 separate. It has outer projection data
q=1,t=1/sqrt(2), hence g\textless=2/(1+1/sqrt(2))\textless14/9. Other
extra doubled joins would put a doubled bond in the interior of a large
classical component and are excluded by the finite/affine
classification.

An outer-only extension is still strictly spherical: outer+c is a
subdiagram of the actual edge W+c.~Thus q\textless2, and the
arbitrary-contact Cauchy--Schwarz argument from the short-end proof
applies unchanged. Its small F4/E8 exclusions have order at most9. The
D2 arbitrary-contact bound is unchanged. These give g\textless=14/9,
with no contact-label cutoff.

The inner component may now acquire its own affine extension while the
outer end remains separate. For a large B/D inner component, the
complete additional profiles are a bond4 at its long endpoint and a
bond3 at its next node. Together with isolated and ordinary endpoint3,
their residual data are:

{\def\LTcaptype{none} % do not increment counter
\begin{longtable}[]{@{}lrrlr@{}}
\toprule\noalign{}
Profile & c0 & l & h & Bound on g=2l/h+c0/h\^{}2 \\
\midrule\noalign{}
\endhead
\bottomrule\noalign{}

isolated & 2 & 0 & x & 1 \\
inner endpoint3 & 1 & 1 & x+1 & 1 \\

For isolated x=1 and endpoint3 x=0, the preceding leaf argument applies.

\begin{verbatim}
g <= g_* = 4(sqrt(2)-1).
\end{verbatim}

\begin{verbatim}
det(S)/(h^2*k^2) = 1-(g_c+g_d)/P

\end{verbatim}

The complete small-inner exceptions remain D6→E7 and D7→E8. This is the
same finite/affine deletion classification: exceptional affine
extensions have order at most9 and are excluded, while the newly allowed
classical affine profiles are the two rows just added. Because
m\textgreater=18, at most one inner component is small; the other has
rank at least9.

\section{Finite exceptional roles and the extra E8 scalar
rows}\label{finite-exceptional-roles-and-the-extra-e8-scalar-rows}

For D6→E7, the added d is the leaf at the end of the length-two arm. Its
inverse diagonal is2. Spectators can touch that E7 only at d; the
\href{fresh_cusp_spectator_role_payments_20261017.md}{role lemma} makes
every nonzero extension affine E7, which is forbidden here. Thus no
spectator touches it, and the original finite E7 payment persists.

For D7→E8, d is again the end of the length-two arm, now with inverse
diagonal4. A nonzero spectator contact costs at least4, exceeding
square2. Thus every spectator is orthogonal to d and to this entire E8
component. In the D2/P5 case the marked branching vertex is paid by
Vinberg's published special-vertex lemma. This argument uses the actual
d position, not an arbitrary embedding of E7 or E8.

For the main-path D3/P4 exception, retain the old notation with outer A3
roots L,0,L', a the next main node, and d attached to L'. The frozen
formulas give alpha=1/4, A=1/2, D=5/4 and v=1/k\textless=2/3. All old
scalar contradictions survive the PSD correction. There are two new
inner profiles and the formerly directly paid outer-only profiles to
check.

The complete outer-only finite extensions of A3 are an endpoint bond3,4
or5, or a middle bond3. An endpoint5 cannot coexist with d in the
positive-semidefinite opposite corner: its connected five-node diagram
contains a bond5 and is neither finite nor affine. Endpoint4 at the same
leaf as d gives the forbidden affine doubled star. The remaining cases

\chapter{Multi-ideal triangle obstructions and a bound on simplex-face
size}\label{multi-ideal-triangle-obstructions-and-a-bound-on-simplex-face-size}

Two exact finite-volume Coxeter square pyramids show that triangle-port
transitivity can fail for triangles with exactly two ideal vertices, and
also for triangles with three ideal vertices. In both examples the
chosen cusp is simple and its whole link is a single simplex factor.
Thus choosing a simplex-factor face at that cusp does not repair the
argument: the other endpoint of the shared edge can still be a nonsimple
ideal vertex.

A separate original-wall-star argument does give a justified bound on
aggregate size: \textbf{any actual simplex face of a finite-volume
hyperbolic Coxeter polytope has dimension at most9}. This does not
assume that the induced face angles are Coxeter angles. It sharpens the
one-ideal cusp block budget, without bounding the ambient dimension or
covering the remaining multi-ideal triangles.

The
\href{../scripts/fresh_multi_ideal_triangle_scope_20261017.py}{standalone
checker} and
\href{fresh_multi_ideal_triangle_scope_20261017.json}{certificate} use
exact Fraction pairs in Q(sqrt2). They reconstruct both pyramids, all
vertices, active sets, face incidences, Gram gates, and ideal-support
semidefiniteness. They also check the block maximum below by dynamic
programming through 256 ports. Its proof for all port counts is given
separately here.

\section{Two literal Coxeter
counterexamples}\label{two-literal-coxeter-counterexamples}

Use the Lorentz form diag(-1,1,1,1). Put

\[
 b=(0,0,0,-1),\quad
 s_1=(a_1,1,0,a_1),\quad s_2=(a_2,0,1,a_2),\quad
 s_3=(a_3,-1,0,a_3),\quad s_4=(a_4,0,-1,a_4).
\]

All five normals have square1. Their products are

\[
 b\cdot s_i=-a_i,\qquad
 s_i\cdot s_{i+1}=0,\qquad s_1\cdot s_3=s_2\cdot s_4=-1.
\]

Indices on the successive sides are cyclic. Choose a\_i=cos(pi/m\_i)
with m\_i in \{3,4\}. Then all native contacts are right, pi/3, pi/4 or
parallel. The common future center H=(2,0,0,1) has square-3 and pairs
strictly negatively with every normal.

In the chart t=1 these inequalities give the rectangular pyramid

\[
 0\le z\le1,\qquad
 -a_3(1-z)\le x\le a_1(1-z),\qquad
 -a_4(1-z)\le y\le a_2(1-z).
\]

Its apex is nu=(1,0,0,1). Its base vertices are the four combinations of
x in \{a\_1,-a\_3\} and y in \{a\_2,-a\_4\}, with z=0. Both choices
below put all vertices in the closed ball, with bounded Euclidean links
at the ideal vertices, hence give finite-volume Coxeter chambers.

\textbf{Two-ideal triangles.} Set (m\_1,m\_2,m\_3,m\_4)=(4,4,3,3). The
base vertex

\[
 v=(1,1/\sqrt2,1/\sqrt2,0)
\]

is ideal; the other three base vertices are finite. The faces on s\_1
and s\_2 are triangles, each with precisely the ideal vertices v and nu
and one finite vertex. They share edge v--nu. The third two-face through
the three ports at v is the quadrilateral base. Thus the two relations
at v do not complete to a third triangular relation.

\textbf{Three-ideal triangles.} Set every m\_i=4. All five vertices are
ideal. The same two side triangles and base square give the same
failure, now with all three vertices of each triangle ideal.

In both cases v is incident with exactly three facets. Its link is the
affine (4,4,2) triangle and is combinatorially Delta2, so the selected
factor fiber is the entire link. The apex nu is incident with four
facets; its link is Delta1 x Delta1. Positive null relations include

\[
 \sqrt2\,b+s_1+s_2=\sqrt2\,v,\qquad
 s_1+s_3=(a_1+a_3)\nu,\qquad
 s_2+s_4=(a_2+a_4)\nu.
\]

The shared ideal edge therefore has a nonsimple endpoint nu. This is
exactly where the degree-three/Balinski argument fails. No inference
from a numerical near-ideal point or an unverified Gram signature is
involved.

These examples rule out unrestricted transitivity and a disjoint-port
capacity1 for multi-ideal simplex blocks even within a simplex cusp
fiber. They do not rule out a different incidence inequality using
additional endpoint data.

\section{A simplex-face bound from the original Coxeter
star}\label{a-simplex-face-bound-from-the-original-coxeter-star}

Let A be an actual k-dimensional simplex face of an n-dimensional
finite-volume Coxeter polytope P, with k \textgreater= 2. Every vertex
of A is finite or ideal. Let W be the n-k original ambient facet normals
supporting A. They are independent and span a positive-definite
subspace.

Each facet of A is positive-dimensional, of dimension k-1. Simplicity at
edges gives exactly n-k+1 ambient facets containing it. Hence each facet
of A supplies \textbf{one} additional original normal b\_i beyond W.
These k+1 black normals are distinct. This produces the original star

\[
 \Sigma=W\cup\{b_0,\ldots,b_k\},\qquad |\Sigma|=n+1.
\]

This does not say that an ideal vertex of P has only n incident facets.
The n normals obtained by deleting b\_i are merely a selected subset of
the walls through the corresponding vertex of A.

Project the black normals orthogonally off W. The projected normals are
positive multiples of the geometric facet normals of A. Since A is a
nondegenerate projective k-simplex, its k+1 vertex rays are independent;
its facet normals form the corresponding dual basis. Their span is the
full Lorentzian (k+1)-space. Thus the Gram matrix of Sigma has signature
(n,1) and in particular is indefinite. No assertion about the projected
angles being Coxeter angles is used.

For every i, the star Sigma minus b\_i consists of normals through an
actual vertex of A. It is positive definite at a finite vertex and
positive semidefinite at an ideal vertex, since the latter normals lie
in the orthogonal complement of a null vector. Therefore any indefinite
principal subdiagram of Sigma must contain \textbf{all k+1 black nodes}.

Choose an inclusion-minimal indefinite principal subdiagram L. It is
connected and every proper principal submatrix is positive semidefinite.
If every proper submatrix is positive definite, L is Lanner. Otherwise a
proper connected affine component C has a positive null vector. An
outside node adjacent to C makes C plus that node indefinite by its
nonzero coupling to that null vector. Minimality forces these to be all
of L. This also excludes a proper affine component accompanied by extra
orthogonal spherical or affine components. Thus L has precisely the
Lanner/quasi-Lanner scope of the standard classification.

The classification input is Prokhorov's
\href{https://www.mathnet.ru/links/1e830e3298f5df6e148b8dc52fd64e1c/im1484_eng.pdf}{§2,
Proposition1, printed p.407}: the largest quasi-Lanner diagrams have
order10. The primary \href{https://www.mathnet.ru/eng/im1484}{article
record} identifies the original paper and translation. Its indexed
primary PDF text was retrieved during this check; a fresh full-PDF fetch
timed out. The same exact input and the minimal-indefinite reduction
were already explicitly reviewed in the
\href{fresh_nikulin_narrow_20261015_compact_facet.md}{frozen
compact-facet proof}. This package does not independently reclassify
those diagrams.

Since L contains all black nodes,

\[
 k+1\le |L|\le10,\qquad\boxed{k\le9.}
\tag{1}
\]

For k=1 the same conclusion is trivial. The local face-incidence facts
used to obtain W and the black normals are stated in
\href{https://ems.press/content/serial-article-files/43032}{Potyagailo--Vinberg,
printed p.64}.

If the \textbf{ambient P is compact}, it has no affine subdiagram, so L
is Lanner and the familiar order-five bound instead gives k\textless=4.
Compactness of A alone does not justify that improvement: deleting a
white node from L can still leave an affine subdiagram containing all
black nodes, even when all black deletions are positive definite. The
report makes no order-five claim in that case.

\section{Sharper one-ideal cusp
budget}\label{sharper-one-ideal-cusp-budget}

The \href{fresh_cusp_one_ideal_simplex_capacity_20261017.md}{one-ideal
factor-fiber theorem} gives disjoint blocks of k ports in a fiber with
m=r\_i+1 ports. By (1), every nontrivial block has 2 \textless= k
\textless= 9. Define

\[
 F_9(m)=36\lfloor m/9\rfloor+\binom{m\bmod9}{2}.
\tag{2}
\]

Then sum binom(k,2) \textless= F9(m). To prove this for every m, move a
port from a smaller nonempty block to a largest block of size below9.
The objective does not decrease, and increases when both blocks have
size at least2. A leftover block of size1 is an unused port and
contributes zero. Repeat until all blocks except the last have size9;
the remainder has size m mod9. This proves (2) without a rank cutoff.
The exact dynamic-programming check is an independent finite
confirmation of this elementary optimization.

For a cusp with factor ranks r\_i and V=product(r\_i+1), every triangle
with exactly one ideal vertex belongs to one such block. Hence

\[
 \boxed{\quad
 2N_{3,1}(v)\le V\sum_i\frac{2F_9(r_i+1)}{r_i+1}.
 \quad}
\tag{3}
\]

For r\_i\textless=8 the summand equals r\_i. For larger factors it is at
most8, so in particular

\[
 2N_{3,1}(v)\le V\sum_i\min(r_i,8)
 \le\min((n-1)V,8s_vV).
\tag{4}
\]

This improves the previous worst-case bound 2E\_v=(n-1)V when the cusp
has large factors. It does not pay for triangles with two or three ideal
vertices, or by itself provide the alpha\_n E\_v budget required by the
original-face inequality. The exact counterexamples above show why that
missing scope cannot be filled by simply repeating the transitivity
proof.

The complementary
\href{fresh_finite_ended_simplex_ports_20261017.md}{finite-ended-port
theorem} groups triangles having at least two finite vertices into
maximal simplex faces, which may have several ideal vertices. Those
blocks are not the same as the maximal one-ideal blocks in (3), so their
incidence variables must not be identified without an additional
allocation argument.

\textbf{FINAL/FROZEN.} Generation and a fresh saved replay passed, as
did source hash, syntax and report-link checks. Exact\_hub\_counts
independently read the original-star/minimal-indefinite argument and the
block-filling proof; the primary classification was not independently
re-enumerated. This is an internally checked face-size lemma and two
exact local counterexamples, not a new ambient dimension ceiling,
external review or novelty claim.

\chapter{Avoiding the narrow-facet node at a cost of
2/9}\label{avoiding-the-narrow-facet-node-at-a-cost-of-29}

\textbf{Uniform local lemma.} In every irreducible affine Coxeter factor
of rank r, and for every forbidden node s, one can prescribe two
omissions i,j different from s, before either terminating contact row is
known, such that

\begin{verbatim}
σ τ E / M + 2C ≥ 2(r−1)/9.                    (1)
\end{verbatim}

Here the roots have square two, C is the sum of the two retained-support
Schur costs, σ,τ are the positive affine null heights, M=max(σ/τ,τ/σ),
and E is the normalized-row energy. The rows satisfy the actual endpoint
hypotheses from the frozen product proof: they are nonnegative, every
nonzero entry is at least one, and each endpoint's total Schur cost is
at most two. No upper contact or Coxeter-label bound is imposed.

Together with the reviewed non-narrow estimate, this gives a
\textbf{research proof candidate n≤181} for finite-sided finite-volume
real hyperbolic Coxeter polytopes. The new lemma is not yet
independently reviewed. The
\href{fresh_nikulin_dimension_189_candidate_20261015.md}{189 checkpoint}
stays frozen and remains the preceding reviewed result. No novelty,
publication-priority, or current-best claim is made.

The \href{../scripts/fresh_nikulin_avoid_node_20261015.py}{checker} and
\href{fresh_nikulin_avoid_node_20261015.json}{data} rebuild all 34
exceptional forbidden-node cases, the 16 modified classical cases in
ranks 2 through 9, the three E8 inexpensive-contact identities, and the
all-rank scalar comparisons. The unbounded-rank localization and
geometric framing inputs are explicitly inherited from the frozen proofs
and their reviews; finite computations are not substituted for those
arguments.

\section{Definitions and fixed
choices}\label{definitions-and-fixed-choices}

For an affine Gram matrix G with positive kernel δ, use the
normalization min δ=1. For the two prescribed omissions i,j let
S\_i,S\_j be the retained supports and put

\begin{verbatim}
C = p_Siᵀ G(S_i)⁻¹ p_Si + q_Sjᵀ G(S_j)⁻¹ q_Sj,
σ = δ·p,   τ = δ·q,   M=max(σ/τ,τ/σ).
\end{verbatim}

For normalized point rows define

\begin{verbatim}
R_ab = (e_a/δ_a−e_b/δ_b)ᵀ G⁺ (e_a/δ_a−e_b/δ_b).
\end{verbatim}

The normalized rows p/σ and q/τ have difference of energy E. In
particular,

\begin{verbatim}
σ τ E/M = min(σ,τ)² E.                       (2)
\end{verbatim}

The inverse retained Grams are entrywise nonnegative. A retained nonzero
entry therefore costs at least the corresponding inverse diagonal. A
terminating row cannot vanish on a whole affine factor, since all affine
null sums are positive multiples of the initial cusp ray and its null
height is positive.

Use these fixed rules in the single factor containing the forbidden
narrow-facet node:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  A\_r, r≥2: rotate an opposite pair of cycle nodes to avoid s. The
  existing estimate is rotation invariant.
\item
  D\_r, r≥4: use leaves from opposite fork ends, switching to the other
  leaf if necessary to avoid s.
\item
  B\_r: use a left fork leaf and the right short end. Switch left leaves
  if necessary. If the short end is forbidden, replace that omission by
  its adjacent interior node.
\item
  C\_r: use both ends, replacing a forbidden end by its adjacent
  interior node. The two endpoint cases are diagram reversals.
\item
  A\_1: both omissions are the only node other than s; coincident
  omissions are allowed in this factor.
\item
  E6: choose the first two of leaves 2,4,6 not equal to s.
\item
  E7: choose 4,7, except when s is 4 or 7, when the pair is 2,5.
\item
  E8: choose 3,7, except when s is 3 or 7, when the pair is 1,6.
\item
  F4: choose 1,3, except when s is 1 or 3, when the pair is 0,4.
\item
  G2: choose the two nodes other than s.
\end{itemize}

The exact exceptional node numbering and complete Gram matrices are
serialized. For E6/E7/E8 they are stars with arm lengths respectively
(2,2,2), (1,3,3), and (1,2,5), numbered consecutively from the center
along each arm. The rules do not depend on the subsequent contact rows,
their zero sets, labels, or heights.

\section{Unmodified classical cases}\label{unmodified-classical-cases}

The \href{fresh_nikulin_energy_charge_20261015_review.md}{reviewed
contact-cost lemma} already gives the stronger inequality

\begin{verbatim}
σ τ E/M + 2C ≥ 2r/9
\end{verbatim}

for the ordinary A/B/C/D choices. A-cycle rotation and D-fork switching
preserve those diagrams and estimates. Thus only the modified B and C
endpoint choices require new work. This includes the separately checked
A9 localization in the earlier review; no unstated large-rank threshold
is being applied to rank nine.

\section{Modified B and C choices}\label{modified-b-and-c-choices}

Consider B\_r when the right short node is forbidden, and C\_r when the
left end is forbidden. The other C case is obtained by reversing its
entire diagram. In the modified support the forbidden end becomes an
isolated A1. Its inverse diagonal is 1/2.

When C=0 the rows are point contacts at their omitted nodes. The
weighted point energy is (r−1)/4 for modified B\_r with r≥3, and (r−1)/2
for modified C\_r. Modified B2 instead has point energy 1. All these
values are at least 2(r−1)/9.

For ranks 2 through 5, every retained inverse diagonal is at least 1/2.
Consequently C\textgreater0 implies 2C≥1≥2(r−1)/9, proving (1) without
using energy.

For ranks 6 through 9, the isolated A1 is the only inverse diagonal
below one in either deletion support. If C≥(r−1)/9, its charge already
pays (1). Otherwise 0\textless C\textless(r−1)/9\textless1, and exactly
one retained entry can be nonzero across the two rows. It is the
isolated A1 entry, of magnitude b≥1 and cost b²/2. The other row is
supported only at its omitted node. With i the modified omission, l the
isolated node and j the opposite omission, write

\begin{verbatim}
p=a e_i+b e_l,   q=c e_j,   u=δ_l b/(δ_i a+δ_l b).
\end{verbatim}

Here a≥0, c≥1 and 0≤u≤1. The complete inverse-diagonal lists and the
following three resistances are checked exactly for all eight cases:

{\def\LTcaptype{none} % do not increment counter
\begin{longtable}[]{@{}lrrrr@{}}
\toprule\noalign{}
Type & R\_ij & R\_lj & R\_il & Resulting energy \\
\midrule\noalign{}
\endhead
\bottomrule\noalign{}
\endlastfoot
B\_r & (r−1)/4 & r/4 & 1/4 & (r−1+u²)/4 \\
C\_r & (r−1)/2 & r/2 & 1/2 & (r−1+u²)/2 \\
\end{longtable}
}

The energy formula is the squared-distance interpolation identity

\begin{verbatim}
E=(1−u)R_ij+uR_lj−u(1−u)R_il.
\end{verbatim}

Since min δ=1, every nonzero row has height at least one. Equation (2)
therefore bounds the weighted energy below by (r−1)/4 for B, or (r−1)/2
for C. Either is at least 2(r−1)/9, even without adding its positive
contact cost.

For every r≥10, the inherited fixed-choice localization gives weighted
energy at least (r−5)/4 in modified B and (r−5)/2 in modified C. The
closed finite B/D inverse formulas show that the isolated A1 still has
the smallest diagonal, 1/2; all other retained inverse diagonals are at
least one. Thus C\textgreater0 implies 2C≥1. At r=10+t, t≥0, the exact
margins are

\begin{verbatim}
(r−5)/4 +1−2(r−1)/9 = (t+9)/36 >0,
(r−5)/2 +1−2(r−1)/9 = (5t+27)/18 >0.
\end{verbatim}

The C=0 point-contact calculation already covers every rank. This proves
(1) for all modified classical cases, without enumerating contact
magnitudes or imposing a rank cutoff.

\section{Direct exceptional cases}\label{direct-exceptional-cases}

For A1,E6,E7,F4,G2 the prescribed pair has both point energy at least
the target 2(r−1)/9 and twice the minimum retained inverse diagonal at
least that target. The C=0 and C\textgreater0 cases are therefore
immediate. The records cover every forbidden node, not only
diagram-orbit representatives.

The E7 replacement is useful here: pair 4,7 has point energy 3/2 and
minimum inverse diagonal 3/2; pair 2,5 has the same point energy and
minimum diagonal 2/3. Both meet the new target 4/3. No cheap-contact
subcase is needed in E7.

For A1 the target is zero. Its two omissions coincide; two rows
supported at this common node have E=C=0. Hence the old target 2r/9
cannot hold uniformly under an avoid-node constraint, even at the level
of admissible local contact rows. The additive loss 2/9 in (1) is
therefore sharp for this uniform local accounting. This observation does
not preclude a different global argument from improving the eventual
dimension bound.

\section{E8 and its replacement
omissions}\label{e8-and-its-replacement-omissions}

Here the target is 14/9. If C≥7/9 the charge alone suffices. In the
remaining case 0\textless C\textless7/9, the exact inverse diagonals
force a single cheap retained contact.

For pair 3,7 this is node 8 after deleting 7, with cost b²/2. Its null
coefficients are δ\_i=δ\_j=2, δ\_l=1 and its resistances are
(1/2,1,1/2). This is the previously reviewed E8 argument: if a=0, σ τ
E/M≥1 and 2C≥1; if a≥1, both heights are at least two and
E=(1+u²)/2≥1/2, so σ τ E/M≥2. Both cases exceed 14/9.

When s is 3 or 7 the new omissions are 1,6. Their null coefficients both
equal three. The only inverse diagonals below 7/9 are nodes 7 and 8
after deleting 6, each equal to 2/3. Every other retained diagonal is at
least 8/9. Two nonzero retained contacts would cost at least 4/3, so
only one can occur. Its row is p=a e\_6+b e\_l, while the other is q=c
e\_1, with c≥1.

{\def\LTcaptype{none} % do not increment counter
\begin{longtable}[]{@{}lrrrrr@{}}
\toprule\noalign{}
Cheap node l & δ\_l & R\_61 & R\_l1 & R\_6l & E \\
\midrule\noalign{}
\endhead
\bottomrule\noalign{}
\endlastfoot
7 & 2 & 2/9 & 7/18 & 1/6 & (4+3u²)/18 \\
8 & 1 & 2/9 & 8/9 & 2/3 & 2(1+3u²)/9 \\
\end{longtable}
}

If a≥1, both heights are at least three and E≥2/9. Equation (2) gives σ
τ E/M≥2.

If a=0 and l=7, the heights are at least two and three. The weighted
energy is at least 4·7/18=14/9, as required. If a=0 and l=8, the energy
is at least 8/9 and the cost contributes 2C≥4/3, giving at least 20/9.
These are all cases. The only discreteness used is that a is either zero
or at least one.

\section{Consequence for the narrow-facet
dichotomy}\label{consequence-for-the-narrow-facet-dichotomy}

Use the unchanged point/contact-cost omissions in every non-narrow
factor and the above avoid-node choices in the single narrow factor. The
\href{fresh_nikulin_narrow_20261015_products.md}{frozen product
argument} then supplies actual terminating framing walls x,y. In
particular, both outgoing edges retain the narrow node; at an ideal
terminal point its positive-definite edge support omits one node per
affine component, and a suitable missing wall has a finite angle with
the narrow wall. The strict-center projection argument makes their
intersection an actual ridge. No merely ideal-point incidence is
substituted for Nikulin's framing condition.

Writing N=n−1, summing (1) and the stronger non-narrow estimate gives

\begin{verbatim}
Σ_a σ_a τ_a E_a ≥ M(2N/9−2Σ_a C_a−2/9)
                   ≥ M(2N/9−8−2/9).
\end{verbatim}

The two endpoint Schur budgets still give Σ\_a C\_a≤4, now including the
narrow factor's own cost. The common height ratio and the Lorentz
identity give

\begin{verbatim}
−(x,y) = (1/2)Σ_a σ_a τ_a E_a−q−1/q
        ≥ M(N−55)/9.
\end{verbatim}

For n≥182, N≥181 and this is at least 14, contradicting the strict
narrow-facet distance bound arccosh 7 for square-two normals. Thus the
ideal-vertex branch gives n≤181. If the narrow facet has no ideal
vertex, it is compact and the independently reviewed compact-facet bound
n≤143 applies. The resulting candidate bound is n≤181.

Only the avoid-node accounting is new. The published narrow-facet
theorem, affine classification, common-height identity, endpoint
existence and actual-ridge bridge, and compact-facet proof remain the
explicitly bound dependencies of the
\href{fresh_nikulin_dimension_189_candidate_20261015.md}{reviewed 189
checkpoint}. The new lemma requires its own independent review before
181 replaces that checkpoint.

\chapter{Independent review of the avoid-node
estimate}\label{independent-review-of-the-avoid-node-estimate}

The new local estimate and its dimension-181 consequence pass an
independent mathematical and exact arithmetic review. This is an
internal research review; external validation and novelty are not
established.

The \href{../scripts/fresh_nikulin_avoid_node_20261015_review.py}{review
checker} and
\href{fresh_nikulin_avoid_node_20261015_review.json}{certificate} import
no arithmetic from the \href{fresh_nikulin_avoid_node_20261015.md}{new
producer}. They reuse elementary Fraction elimination from the earlier
independent review and reconstruct rational congruences of each physical
Gram matrix. Energies come from grounded linear equations, with every
equation checked, rather than the producer's regularized inverse. Every
retained inverse diagonal is compared with the saved primary data.

All 34 exceptional forbidden-node choices pass. For E8, the full
cheap-contact list is rebuilt, the mixture's constant, linear and
quadratic coefficients are computed independently, and both zero and
positive omitted-contact cases meet the target. All 16 modified B/C
cases in ranks 2--9 pass; ranks 10--12 separately check the boundary
formulas. These finite checks supplement the all-rank argument, not
replace it.

The mathematical review checks the following quantifiers and boundaries:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  Omissions are prescribed before the terminating walls are selected.
  A-cycle rotation and D-fork interchange retain the earlier lemma; B/C
  end avoidance is precisely the modification treated in the frozen
  product proof's localization section.
\item
  At ranks 6--9, cost below the target's half allows only the isolated
  A1 entry. Nonnegative inverse entries prevent cancellation. The row's
  omitted entry is either zero or at least one; every nonzero row has
  height at least one after the stated kernel normalization.
\item
  For ranks at least ten, the inherited localization applies to the
  modified finite D or B component, including rank-nine D at the
  boundary. A positive retained cost contributes at least one after
  multiplication by two. The remaining margins are \texttt{(t+9)/36} for
  B and \texttt{(5t+27)/18} for C, with \texttt{t=r−10≥0}. The zero-cost
  case instead uses the point energy for all ranks.
\item
  In E8's replacement omission pair, either retained diagonal is 2/3 or
  at least 8/9. Thus cost below 7/9 leaves one cheap entry. The
  reconstructed positive omitted-contact energy is at least two. With
  that contact absent, the node-7 energy is at least 14/9; node 8 has
  energy at least 8/9 and charge at least 4/3.
\item
  Coincident omissions in A1 are permitted. They produce zero energy and
  zero cost, explaining the unavoidable 2/9 loss for this uniform local
  formulation. They do not invalidate the global argument: the other
  factors supply separation in the excluded dimension range.
\item
  The summed endpoint Schur budget includes the narrow factor and
  remains at most four. The common positive height ratio is unchanged.
  Retaining the narrow node, followed by the finite/ideal terminal-wall
  choice already reviewed, makes both selected walls actual ridge
  neighbors of the narrow facet.
\end{itemize}

Hence the total energy is at least \texttt{M(2N/9−8−2/9)}, where
\texttt{N=n−1} and \texttt{M≥1}. The Lorentz identity gives
\texttt{−(x,y)≥M(N−55)/9}; at \texttt{n=182} this reaches 14. The
separately reviewed compact-facet alternative still gives 143. The full
combined research candidate is therefore \textbf{n≤181}.

The inherited actual-ridge geometry, common-height scaling,
classification inputs and compact-facet argument remain bound through
the \href{fresh_nikulin_dimension_189_candidate_20261015.md}{189
package}. No arithmetic assumption, bound on finite labels, simple-cusp
assumption or fixed facet count was added.

\chapter{Coupling the contact charge to the common height
ratio}\label{coupling-the-contact-charge-to-the-common-height-ratio}

\textbf{Research proof candidate, pending independent review:} every
finite-sided finite-volume real hyperbolic Coxeter polytope has
dimension at most \textbf{166}. The new step is a local charge estimate
of \(7/6\) when the common affine height ratio is at most \(21/20\). For
larger ratios the frozen reviewed \(4/3\) estimate is already
sufficient. No arithmetic hypothesis is used.

The \href{../scripts/fresh_nikulin_coupled_charge_20261015.py}{checker}
and \href{fresh_nikulin_coupled_charge_20261015.json}{exact data} have
passed generation and saved replay. This is producer verification,
separate from independent proof review. All earlier
\href{fresh_nikulin_unit_charge_20261015_dimension169.md}{169 artifacts}
and the \href{fresh_nikulin_balanced_height_20261015.md}{balanced
unit-charge obstruction} remain unchanged. There is no claim of
publication priority, optimality, or formal proof-assistant
verification.

\section{Local statement and common
choices}\label{local-statement-and-common-choices}

Use the normalization and geometric hypotheses of the frozen
\href{fresh_nikulin_narrow_20261015_products.md}{product-cusp proof}.
Each affine factor has rank \(r\), Gram matrix \(G\) with root squares
two, and positive kernel \(\delta\) normalized by \(\min\delta_k=1\).
The prescribed omitted nodes are \(i,j\). The two nonnegative contact
rows \(p,q\) are nonzero, and every nonzero entry is at least one. Each
endpoint's total retained-support Schur cost is at most two. Set

\[
\sigma=\delta\cdot p,\quad \tau=\delta\cdot q,\quad
M=\max(\sigma/\tau,\tau/\sigma),\qquad
C=p_{S_i}^{T}G(S_i)^{-1}p_{S_i}
 +q_{S_j}^{T}G(S_j)^{-1}q_{S_j}.
\]

The normalized-row energy is \(E\ge0\), and

\[
W=\sigma\tau E/M=\min(\sigma,\tau)^2E.
\]

For the same preset omissions as in the
\href{fresh_nikulin_unit_charge_20261015_review.md}{reviewed 4/3 lemma},
we prove

\[
\boxed{M\le21/20\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
 W+\tfrac76 C\ge T},
\qquad
T=\begin{cases}2r/9,&\text{ordinary factor},\\
2(r-1)/9,&\text{factor containing the forbidden narrow-facet node}.
\end{cases}
\tag{1}
\]

The choices are made before the terminating rows or their common ratio
are known. In particular, ordinary E8 uses omissions \texttt{(1,6)}; the
avoid-node E8 rules still use \texttt{(3,7)} or \texttt{(1,6)} as
prescribed in the frozen proof. Both branches of the global argument use
these identical choices.

This is compatible with the balanced counterexamples: at \(M=1\), the E8
common unit row has \(C=14/9\) and \(W=0\). A unit charge fails, while
\((7/6)(14/9)=49/27>16/9\).

\section{The elementary height
improvement}\label{the-elementary-height-improvement}

If the two rows have lower height bounds \(\sigma\ge h_1>0\),
\(\tau\ge h_2>0\), then \(M\le B=21/20\) implies

\[
\min(\sigma,\tau)^2\ge
H(h_1,h_2):=
\max\!\left\{\min(h_1,h_2)^2,
\frac{\max(h_1,h_2)^2}{B^2}\right\}.
\tag{2}
\]

Indeed, the smaller height is at least the smaller individual lower
bound, and is also at least the larger actual height divided by \(B\).
No contact-label cutoff or approximation enters this estimate.

The case \(C\ge T/(7/6)\) proves (1) immediately. We therefore restrict
to the strict small-cost range

\[
C<6T/7.
\tag{3}
\]

Every inverse retained Gram is entrywise nonnegative. A retained nonzero
entry at node \(k\) costs at least its inverse diagonal \(c_{ik}\), and
two entries in the same row also contribute their nonnegative cross
term. These facts give the complete finite exceptional support
classification below.

\section{Exceptional factors, including every forbidden
node}\label{exceptional-factors-including-every-forbidden-node}

The checker reconstructs the literal Grams, positive kernels, principal
inverses and point resistances for A1, E6, E7, E8, F4 and G2. The six
ordinary records and all 34 forbidden-node records exactly match the
preset choices in the frozen proof.

For a single retained contact, orient the rows as

\[
p=a e_i+b e_l,\qquad q=c e_j,
\qquad b,c\ge1,\quad a=0\text{ or }a\ge1.
\]

Write \(R_{uv}\) for the energy of the normalized point-row difference
\(e_u/\delta_u-e_v/\delta_v\). If \(a=0\), then \(E=R_{lj}\), while
\(\sigma\ge\delta_l\), \(\tau\ge\delta_j\). Therefore

\[
W+\tfrac76C\ge
H(\delta_l,\delta_j)R_{lj}+\tfrac76c_{il}.
\tag{4}
\]

If \(a\ge1\), the heights are bounded below by \(\delta_i+\delta_l\) and
\(\delta_j\). With

\[
u=\frac{\delta_l b}{\delta_i a+\delta_l b}\in[0,1],
\qquad
E(u)=(1-u)R_{ij}+uR_{lj}-u(1-u)R_{il},
\]

we obtain

\[
W+\tfrac76C\ge
H(\delta_i+\delta_l,\delta_j)\min_{0\le u\le1}E(u)
+\tfrac76c_{il}.
\tag{5}
\]

The energy is a convex quadratic. Its minimum is checked exactly at both
endpoints and, if it lies in the interval, at its stationary point. All
\textbf{54 single-contact occurrences} in the full 40-record list
satisfy (4) and (5). The smallest recorded excess over the target is
\(2363/1764>0\). Repeated forbidden-node choices are retained
explicitly; the count is not a count of distinct diagrams.

The inverse-diagonal and cross-term census leaves exactly one
two-contact pattern in (3): ordinary E7 with omissions \texttt{(3,6)},
one isolated A1 contact at node 4 in the first row and one at node 7 in
the second. Its exact normalized energy is

\[
E(u,v)=\tfrac12(1+u^2+v^2)\ge\tfrac12.
\]

Both heights are at least one and the total cost is at least one, so

\[
W+\tfrac76C\ge\tfrac12+\tfrac76=\tfrac53>\tfrac{14}{9}.
\]

Every other two-contact support is excluded by its exact minimum cost,
and three retained contacts exceed the threshold in every record. Thus
this is complete support coverage with arbitrary real contact magnitudes
satisfying the zero-or-at-least-one gap, not a scan of selected labels
or unit rows. Zero retained contacts give the frozen point-row bound.
The coincident-omission A1 avoid-node case has target zero and is
immediate.

\section{Classical A: point surplus pays the excess linear
loss}\label{classical-a-point-surplus-pays-the-excess-linear-loss}

The following part is unconditional in \(M\). For affine A\_r put
\(m=r+1\), and choose opposite cycle nodes 0 and
\(h=\lfloor m/2\rfloor\). Let

\[
R(k)=\frac{k(m-k)}m\quad(0\le k<m),\qquad
R_{ij}=R(h).
\]

For a retained node \(k\), its inverse diagonal is \(c_k=R(k)\), and its
linear energy loss from the first omission is

\[
\ell_k=R_{ij}+R(k)-R(k-h),
\]

with arguments read modulo \(m\). Reflection of the cycle interchanges
the omissions, so the same complete list covers the other row.

The frozen linear-loss identity, with nonnegative inverse entries and
the contact gap, gives

\[
E\ge R_{ij}-\lambda C
\]

whenever \(\ell_k\le\lambda c_k\) at every possible retained contact.
Since both heights are at least one, \(W\ge E\). In the range (3), only
nodes with \(c_k<6T/7\) and \(c_k\le2\) can occur. Thus for
\(\lambda\ge7/6\),

\[
W+\tfrac76 C\ge
R_{ij}-(\lambda-7/6)\frac{6T}{7}.
\tag{6}
\]

For each of the 18 cycle sizes \(m=2,\ldots,19\), the checker enumerates
every node, takes the exact maximum of \(7/6\) and \(\ell_k/c_k\) over
the allowed nodes, and verifies that (6) is at least \(T=2r/9\). This
finite check covers all small ranks; it is not a cutoff on the theorem.

For larger ranks, the endpoint budget two implies that a retained
contact is at cyclic distance at most two from its omission: for
\(m\ge10\),

\[
\frac{3(m-3)}m>2,
\]

and the inverse diagonal increases up to the antipode. Write
\(\varepsilon=m\bmod2\). At distance \(d\le2\),

\[
c=\frac{d(m-d)}m,\qquad
\ell\le\frac{(m+\varepsilon)d}m,
\qquad
6m\bigl(\tfrac76c-\ell\bigr)
\ge d(m-7d-6\varepsilon).
\]

The last expression is nonnegative for every even \(m\ge20\) and odd
\(m\ge21\); all four distance/parity classes are checked symbolically.
Finally the point surplus is positive:

\[
R_{ij}-2r/9=
\begin{cases}(m+8)/36,&m\text{ even},\\
(m-1)(m+9)/(36m),&m\text{ odd}.
\end{cases}
\]

This proves the ordinary estimate in every rank. Rotating the same
omission pair to avoid a forbidden node preserves it and proves the
weaker avoid-node target. A1 with coincident omissions is already
handled separately.

\section{Classical B, C and D}\label{classical-b-c-and-d}

The complete prefix-coordinate identities and their index-class coverage
are inherited from the frozen
\href{fresh_nikulin_unit_charge_20261015_review.md}{independent 4/3
review}. The new checker explicitly re-evaluates all \textbf{24} classes
at threshold \(6T/7\).

For every non-distant contact the previously proved identity gives
\(\ell\le c\), which is stronger than needed. The only other classes
have costs \(r/4\), \(r/2\), \((r-1)/4\), or \((r-1)/2\), and remain
strictly above the new small-cost threshold. For example,

\[
\frac r4-\frac{6}{7}\frac{2r}{9}=\frac{5r}{84}>0,
\]

and the modified B case is the same expression with \(r-1\). Each
all-rank substitution is checked as an exact polynomial with nonnegative
coefficients in independent nonnegative rank/index parameters. This is
an inherited all-rank coordinate proof with new threshold comparisons,
not an inference from a finite rank sample.

The point resistances \(r/4,r/2,(r-1)/4,(r-1)/2\) exceed their
respective targets. Modified B2 is separate: its point energy is one,
while a positive contact costs at least \(1/2\), whose \(7/6\) charge
already exceeds the target \(2/9\). Consequently all B/C/D cases satisfy
(1), without using the height-ratio condition.

\section{The global split at a common
ratio}\label{the-global-split-at-a-common-ratio}

The frozen narrow-facet and actual-ridge arguments supply two
terminating walls with a \textbf{single common ratio} \(M\) across all
affine factors. The total endpoint costs satisfy \(\sum C_a\le4\). The
sole avoid-node penalty remains \(2/9\), and \(N=\sum r_a=n-1\).

If \(M\le21/20\), summing (1) and applying the unchanged Lorentz
identity gives

\[
-(x,y)\ge M\left(\frac N9-2\cdot\frac76-\frac19-2\right)
=M\frac{N-40}{9}.
\]

If \(M\ge21/20\), use the frozen 4/3 estimate with the same omissions:

\[
-(x,y)\ge M\frac{N-43}{9}.
\]

For \(N=166+t\), \(t\ge0\), the first lower bound is at least
\(14+t/9\). The second is at least

\[
\frac{21}{20}\frac{123+t}{9}
=\frac{287}{20}+\frac{7t}{60}>14.
\]

Both contradict the strict narrow-facet bound \(-(x,y)<14\) for its
norm-two framing normals. The ideal-vertex branch therefore excludes
\(n\ge167\). The separately reviewed compact-facet branch gives
\(n\le143\), so the combined candidate is \(n\le166\).

All geometric coverage conditions---finite-sided finite volume, cusp
products, endpoint existence, common height ratio, actual framing ridges
and the compact-facet alternative---are inherited from the reviewed 169
chain. The new proof is the smaller charge under a common-ratio
condition and the two-branch optimization. Independent scrutiny of this
new local step remains required.

\chapter{Reviewed research proof candidate: dimension at most
166}\label{reviewed-research-proof-candidate-dimension-at-most-166}

\textbf{Candidate theorem.} Every finite-sided, finite-volume real
hyperbolic Coxeter polytope has dimension \textbf{n≤166}, without an
arithmeticity, compactness, simple-cusp or facet-count assumption.

The \href{fresh_nikulin_coupled_charge_20261015.md}{common-height
estimate} and
\href{fresh_nikulin_coupled_charge_20261015_review.md}{independent
review} sharpen the frozen
\href{fresh_nikulin_unit_charge_20261015_dimension169.md}{169
candidate}. The
\href{../scripts/fresh_nikulin_coupled_charge_20261015_dimension166.py}{case
binder} and
\href{fresh_nikulin_coupled_charge_20261015_dimension166.json}{certificate}
bind both branches and recursively verify the cited source hashes. This
is an internally reviewed research proof candidate; external validation,
novelty and current-best literature status remain unestablished.

Nikulin's narrow-facet theorem supplies a facet F whose framing
hyperplanes have pairwise distance strictly below \texttt{arccosh\ 7}.
If F contains an ideal vertex, its Euclidean link is a product of affine
Coxeter simplices with total rank \texttt{N=n−1}. The reviewed endpoint
and actual-ridge arguments supply two framing walls x,y with total
retained-support cost at most four and one common height ratio
\texttt{M≥1}.
\href{https://www.mathunion.org/fileadmin/ICM/Proceedings/ICM1986.1/ICM1986.1.ocr.pdf}{Nikulin,
official ICM report, printed pp.654--655 and 657--659}.

For \texttt{M≤21/20}, the local charge improves to \texttt{7/6}, giving
\texttt{−(x,y)≥M(N−40)/9}. For \texttt{M≥21/20}, the earlier
\texttt{4/3} charge gives \texttt{−(x,y)≥M(N−43)/9}. Both use identical
preset omissions, including the node-avoidance rule for F. At
\texttt{N≥166}, the first lower bound is at least 14 and the second at
least \texttt{287/20\textgreater{}14}. Each contradicts narrowness. If F
has only finite vertices, it is compact, and the separately reviewed
\href{fresh_nikulin_narrow_20261015_compact_facet.md}{compact-facet
argument} gives \texttt{n≤143}. The complete split yields 166.

The new estimate covers every affine type and every rank, with arbitrary
contact magnitudes satisfying the Coxeter zero-or-at-least-one gap.
Exact exceptional support enumeration is combined with symbolic
classical-family inequalities. The published geometric and
classification inputs remain mathematical dependencies, not formally
certified software axioms.

For literature comparison, Prokhorov's published bound is 995 and
Nikulin's ICM report announces the stronger bound below 300. These are
distinct from the repository's candidate. The present improvement
concerns unrestricted finite-volume polytopes; the published arithmetic
ceiling 29 and noncompact arithmetic ceiling 21 are already much
smaller.
\href{https://www.mathnet.ru/php/getFT.phtml?jrnid=im&paperid=1484&what=fullteng}{Prokhorov,
printed p.402},
\href{https://www.mathunion.org/fileadmin/ICM/Proceedings/ICM1986.1/ICM1986.1.ocr.pdf}{Nikulin,
printed p.659}, \href{https://arxiv.org/pdf/1506.03111}{Belolipetsky's
survey}.
