\chapter{A coarse dimension bound from a compact
facet}\label{a-coarse-dimension-bound-from-a-compact-facet}

\textbf{Theorem.} Let P be a finite-sided, finite-volume hyperbolic
Coxeter polytope in H\^{}n.~If P has a compact facet, then
\textbf{n≤143}. The facet need not itself be a Coxeter polytope. No
narrowness assumption is required for this lemma.

The proof uses a coarser version of Vinberg's graph-distance weighting.
It allows parabolic subdiagrams in the ambient face stars. This report
establishes the compact-facet branch separately; any combination with
the \href{fresh_nikulin_narrow_20261015_products.md}{conditional
narrow-facet product-cusp bound} requires review of both proofs and
their common hypotheses.

The
\href{../scripts/fresh_nikulin_narrow_20261015_compact_facet.py}{small
exact checker} and
\href{fresh_nikulin_narrow_20261015_compact_facet.json}{certificate}
verify the final scalar inequalities, the h-vector coefficient minima,
classical distance-count examples, and an explicit counterexample to the
stronger localization premise discussed below. The geometric argument
and the stated classification inputs are not replaced by a numerical
test.

\section{Published inputs and the localization
issue}\label{published-inputs-and-the-localization-issue}

Prokhorov defines quasi-Lannér diagrams by minimal indefiniteness and
records both the maximal order ten and extraction from any hyperbolic
diagram in §2, Propositions 1--2, printed pp.407--408. These statements
supply the classification input here.
\href{https://www.mathnet.ru/php/getFT.phtml?jrnid=im&paperid=1484&what=fullteng}{Primary
paper}.

Vinberg's §4 Proposition 10, printed p.77, bounds the number of
unordered node pairs at graph distance at most c in a spherical diagram
of order r by cr. His §1, pp.70--71, provides the symmetric nonnegative
h-vector estimate for a simple polytope.
\href{https://www.mathnet.ru/php/getFT.phtml?jrnid=mmo&option_lang=rus&paperid=444&what=fullt}{Primary
paper}.

The finer compact-chamber weights cannot simply be imported: Vinberg's
§3.2 and Proposition 9 use absence of parabolic subdiagrams, and §6.4
invokes that fact. Compactness of one marked face does not imply this
absence. The Coxeter tetrahedron with path labels 3--3--6 has a compact
triangular facet at node 0 but an affine G2 subdiagram on nodes 1,2,3.
The checker verifies determinant −1/16, dual-ray squares (0,−4,−12,−8),
a strict timelike center, and all three spherical corners of facet 0.
This diagnoses a gap in the finer transplant; it does not contradict
Vinberg's compact theorem or the coarser proof below.

\section{Minimal indefinite diagrams}\label{minimal-indefinite-diagrams}

All Gram matrices below have diagonal one and nonpositive off-diagonal
entries. A minimal indefinite principal subdiagram L is connected:
otherwise its indefinite component is a smaller such subdiagram. Every
proper principal submatrix is positive semidefinite.

If every proper subdiagram is positive definite, L is Lannér. Otherwise
choose a connected affine component A of a proper positive-semidefinite
subdiagram. Its null vector has strictly positive coefficients.
Connectedness of L supplies an outside node v adjacent to A. The Gram of
A+v is already indefinite: evaluating on the positive null vector plus a
sufficiently small positive multiple of v gives a negative value.
Minimality therefore forces L=A+v. In particular the affine component
has codimension one; there can be no additional disconnected affine or
spherical part. Its nonzero coupling to the affine null vector makes L
nonsingular with inertia (\textbar L\textbar−1,1).

Consequently the general minimal-indefinite situation has exactly the
Lannér/quasi-Lannér scope of the cited classification. This also follows
directly from Prokhorov's Proposition 2. It gives \textbar L\textbar≤10;
the Lannér case has the stronger bound five, which is not needed. A
strict dotted edge, if present in a minimal indefinite subdiagram,
already constitutes a two-node indefinite diagram and causes no
exception to the size bound.

\section{Compact two-face stars}\label{compact-two-face-stars}

Let Q be a compact two-dimensional face of P. Let W be the n−2 facet
normals whose facets contain Q, and mark the other facets that cut its
polygonal sides black. All corners of Q are finite. Therefore W together
with each pair of consecutive black nodes is a positive-definite diagram
of order n.

The whole star has a negative direction. One way to see this is to
project its black normals off the positive subspace spanned by W: their
hyperplanes bound the compact polygon Q in a Lorentzian
three-dimensional space. The polygon side normals span that space. Every
star subdiagram consequently has negative index at most one, as does the
ambient Gram matrix.

Two elementary incidence facts will be used. A positive-definite set of
wall normals of an acute chamber has an actual common face: project a
strict interior timelike point orthogonally off their span. The inverse
of a positive-definite Z-matrix is entrywise nonnegative, so all other
wall inequalities remain strict and the projected vector stays timelike.
If instead a principal block is positive semidefinite and singular, one
connected affine component supplies a positive null combination c.~This
combination is nonzero since its pairing with a strict interior point is
negative. It is future null, orthogonal to every normal in that
positive-semidefinite block, and nonpositive against every other chamber
normal. It is therefore an ideal point of the chamber. These facts do
not require the entire chamber to be compact.

For a triangle, any indefinite subdiagram of the star must contain all
three black nodes: omitting a black node puts it inside a
positive-definite corner diagram. Choose a minimal indefinite subdiagram
L. It has at most ten nodes. In a connected graph with three marked
nodes, at least two marked nodes can each be deleted while the other two
remain joined by a path. For example, use the leaves of the minimal
subtree joining the marks in a spanning tree. The resulting two paths
lie in L with one black node removed, hence have length at most eight.
They lie in two actual corner diagrams of Q.

For a quadrilateral, split the black nodes into its two pairs U,V of
opposite sides. The full principal block W+U is indefinite. If it were
positive definite, the actual-face projection argument would make the
opposite sides intersect in Q. If it were singular positive
semidefinite, the null-vector argument would produce an ideal point on
every white wall, hence in Q, contradicting compactness. The same
reasoning applies to W+V. This is the required replacement for the
global no-parabolic assertion.

Choose minimal indefinite subdiagrams L⊆W+U and M⊆W+V. Each must contain
its two black nodes, since W plus either single black node is positive
definite. Both have at most ten nodes and at most eight white nodes.
They cannot be orthogonal: their two negative directions would give
ambient negative index at least two. Thus they overlap in a white node
or are joined by an edge. A shortest path between the black sets U and V
in this connected union has only white internal nodes. It has length at
most 8+1+8=17. Its two black endpoints are consecutive sides of Q, so
the path is contained in their actual corner diagram.

Assign a planar angle of a compact two-face weight one if its two marked
nodes have graph distance at most 17 in the full ambient finite-vertex
diagram, and zero otherwise. The triangle argument gives total weight at
least two; the quadrilateral argument gives at least one. Polygons with
k≥5 need only nonnegative total weight. In all cases the total is at
least 5−k.

\section{Counting on a compact facet}\label{counting-on-a-compact-facet}

Let F be a compact facet, d=n−1. It is a compact simple d-polytope
because all of its vertices are finite vertices of the acute chamber.
Its two-faces are also two-faces of P, so the preceding weights apply.
At each vertex of F these weights count a subset of the unordered pairs
in the full ambient spherical diagram, whose order is n.~The published
spherical distance bound therefore gives a vertex subtotal at most
17n=17(d+1). No reflection structure on F is being asserted.

Write f\_i for the face numbers of F. Summing the two-face lower bounds
gives

\begin{verbatim}
total weight ≥ 5 f_2 − binom(d,2) f_0.
\end{verbatim}

For a simple polytope its nonnegative h-vector is symmetric with
h\_0=h\_d=1. Pairing the coefficients binom(k,2) and binom(d−k,2) gives
the strict bounds

\begin{verbatim}
f_2/f_0 > d(d−2)/8          if d is even,
f_2/f_0 > (d−1)^2/8        if d is odd.
\end{verbatim}

Strictness follows from the nonzero endpoint coefficients, which exceed
the middle coefficient minimum. It follows that the average vertex
subtotal is strictly greater than d(d−6)/8 in even dimension, and
(d−1)(d−5)/8 in odd dimension. Comparing with 17(d+1) gives a
contradiction whenever d≥143. Explicitly, writing the odd dimensions as
d=143+2t and the even ones as d=144+2t, eight times the difference of
lower and upper bounds is respectively

\begin{verbatim}
4t²+288t+12 > 0,
4t²+292t+152 > 0.
\end{verbatim}

Thus d≤142 and n≤143, as claimed.

The proof is deliberately coarse and makes no current-best or novelty
claim. Its useful feature is that it permits the affine subdiagrams that
obstruct the direct use of the finer compact-chamber weighting. The
checker imports no earlier producer arithmetic. Generation and saved
replay are run with:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\ExtensionTok{python}\NormalTok{ scripts/fresh\_nikulin\_narrow\_20261015\_compact\_facet.py}
\ExtensionTok{python}\NormalTok{ scripts/fresh\_nikulin\_narrow\_20261015\_compact\_facet.py }\AttributeTok{{-}{-}verify}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\chapter{A product-cusp separation bound for a narrow
facet}\label{a-product-cusp-separation-bound-for-a-narrow-facet}

\textbf{Conditional theorem.} If a Nikulin narrow facet of a
finite-sided finite-volume real hyperbolic Coxeter polytope
(P\ensuremath{\subset}\texttt{\textbackslash{}mathbb\ }H\^{}n) contains
an ideal vertex, then (n\ensuremath{\le225}).

This treats products of affine cusp components, including arbitrarily
many factors of small rank. It is a further explicit step in
reconstructing the historical narrow-facet argument. It does
\textbf{not} yet give an unrestricted bound of 225: a chosen narrow
facet may have only finite vertices. The latter case, which Nikulin's
outline proposes treating combinatorially, is still open in this
reconstruction. No novelty or current-best claim is made.

The \href{../scripts/fresh_nikulin_narrow_20261015_products.py}{checker}
and \href{fresh_nikulin_narrow_20261015_products.json}{certificate}
verify the finite exceptional constants and the all-rank scalar
identities. The argument uses the inverse and coordinate formulas proved
in the separate \href{fresh_nikulin_narrow_20261015.md}{classical-cusp
package}, whose files remain frozen. The published narrow-facet input is
\href{https://www.mathunion.org/fileadmin/ICM/Proceedings/ICM1986.1/ICM1986.1.ocr.pdf}{Nikulin,
ICM 1986, printed p.655}.

\section{Setup and the common height
ratio}\label{setup-and-the-common-height-ratio}

Use outward normals of square 2 in Lorentz signature ((n,1)). At an
ideal vertex (v), a horospherical link is a compact Euclidean Coxeter
polytope, hence a product of affine Coxeter simplices. Let their ranks
be (r\_a\ensuremath{\ge1}), with

\[
N:=n-1=\sum_a r_a.
\]

Every factor has (r\_a+1) nodes. Deleting one node in each factor
specifies a vertex of the horospherical link, hence an outgoing edge of
(P). Its retained support (S) has (N) roots and positive-definite
block-diagonal Gram matrix. The standard Euclidean reflection
classification, including the parallel two-wall affine (A\_1) case, is
the only diagram classification imported here.

Choose two such deletion tuples as described below, and let (x,y) be
terminating walls at the other endpoints of their edges. The next
section ensures these can be chosen to meet the narrow facet in actual
ridges. Their contact rows against the initial cusp roots are
nonnegative after negating pairings. In a factor (a), write these rows
as (p\_a,q\_a), its positive null coefficients as
(\ensuremath{\delta}\_a), and

\[
c_a=\sum_j\delta_{a,j}\alpha_{a,j},\quad
\sigma_a=\delta_a\cdot p_a=-(x,c_a),\quad
\tau_a=\delta_a\cdot q_a=-(y,c_a).
\]

All (c\_a) are positive multiples of the same future null vector.
Therefore the ratio

\[
q:=\sigma_a/\tau_a>0
\]

is \textbf{the same in every factor}, although their individual scales
need not agree. Put
(M=\texttt{\textbackslash{}max}(q,1/q)\ensuremath{\ge1}).

The cusp quotient is an orthogonal direct sum of the Euclidean factor
spaces. Let (E\_a) be the squared norm of the factor component of
(x/\ensuremath{\sigma}\_a-y/\ensuremath{\tau}\_a). The Lorentz identity
from the classical package becomes

\[
\boxed{-(x,y)=\frac12\sum_a\sigma_a\tau_aE_a-q-1/q.}
\]

The relative null scales cancel in each summand. This is why the proof
does not require commensurable cusp scales, arithmeticity, or a
prescribed horosphere.

\section{Choosing terminating walls that really meet the narrow
facet}\label{choosing-terminating-walls-that-really-meet-the-narrow-facet}

Let the narrow facet have normal (\ensuremath{\alpha}\_s). In its affine
factor, both deletion tuples avoid (s), so both outgoing edges lie in
the narrow facet. At a finite second endpoint, every additional wall has
finite angle with (\ensuremath{\alpha}\_s).

At an ideal second endpoint, let (T\_b) be its affine components. Its
full rank is again (N). The retained edge support (S) is positive
definite with exactly (N) nodes, so it contains at most
(\ensuremath{\operatorname{rank}}T\_b) nodes from each component.
Equality of the total counts forces equality in every component. Thus
exactly one node in each (T\_b) is missing from (S), and these are
additional terminating walls.

If the component containing (\ensuremath{\alpha}\_s) has rank at least
2, choose its missing node. Every two nodes in such an irreducible
affine diagram have finite angle, so this wall meets
(\ensuremath{\alpha}\_s). If that component has rank 1, its missing node
is parallel to (\ensuremath{\alpha}\_s); instead choose a missing node
of another component. That wall is right to (\ensuremath{\alpha}\_s).
Another component exists for (n\ensuremath{\ge3}), the only range
relevant to the claimed contradiction.

In either case the chosen terminating wall and (\ensuremath{\alpha}\_s)
have positive-definite rank-two Gram. Projecting a strict interior point
of (P) onto their common orthogonal complement gives a timelike point
still strict against every other wall, because the inverse Gram is
nonnegative and all distinct wall pairings are nonpositive. Hence they
share an \textbf{actual ridge}, not merely a point at infinity. This
proves that (x,y) belong to the exact framing-wall set controlled by the
narrow-facet theorem.

\section{At most eight factors can carry retained nonright
contacts}\label{at-most-eight-factors-can-carry-retained-nonright-contacts}

At either second endpoint, the Gram matrix of (S\ensuremath{\cup}\{x\})
is positive semidefinite. Thus

\[
p_S^T G(S)^{-1}p_S\le2.
\]

A positive-definite matrix with diagonal 2 has inverse diagonal at least
(1/2), by its one-node Schur complement. A positive-definite Coxeter
Gram is a symmetric (Z)-matrix, so its inverse is entrywise nonnegative.
Every nonzero retained contact has magnitude at least 1. Consequently at
most four entries of (p\_S) can be nonzero. The same holds for (y).

Call a factor \textbf{spoiled} if either terminating wall has a nonright
contact with any retained node in that factor. There are at most eight
spoiled factors. Also mark the factor containing (s), regardless of its
contacts. Thus at most nine factors are marked. In all unmarked factors
each contact row is supported only on the deleted node. A terminating
wall cannot have zero contact with an entire factor, since its null sum
is a positive multiple of the cusp vector and its height is positive.

\section{Point-contact energy in every affine
type}\label{point-contact-energy-in-every-affine-type}

For a factor with Gram (G), null vector (\ensuremath{\delta}), and two
chosen omitted nodes (i,j), define

\[
R_{ij}=\left(e_i/\delta_i-e_j/\delta_j\right)^T
G^+\left(e_i/\delta_i-e_j/\delta_j\right),
\quad L_{ij}=\min(\delta_i^2,\delta_j^2)R_{ij}.
\]

The definition is unchanged by rescaling (\ensuremath{\delta}). In an
unspoiled factor the two contact magnitudes are at least 1. Since their
null-height ratio is (q),

\[
\sigma_a\tau_a\ge
\max(q\delta_j^2,\delta_i^2/q)
\ge M\min(\delta_i^2,\delta_j^2).
\]

The omitted nodes can be chosen so that (L\_\{ij\}\ensuremath{\ge}2r/9)
for \textbf{every} irreducible affine type of rank (r):

{\def\LTcaptype{none} % do not increment counter
\begin{longtable}[]{@{}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 4\tabcolsep) * \real{0.3000}}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 4\tabcolsep) * \real{0.3000}}
  >{\raggedleft\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 4\tabcolsep) * \real{0.4000}}@{}}
\toprule\noalign{}
\begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
Type
\end{minipage} & \begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
Chosen nodes
\end{minipage} & \begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedleft
Exact or lower point-contact energy (L\_\{ij\})
\end{minipage} \\
\midrule\noalign{}
\endhead
\bottomrule\noalign{}
\endlastfoot
(\texttt{\textbackslash{}widetilde\ }A\_r, r\ensuremath{\ge2}) &
opposite cycle nodes &
(\ensuremath{\lfloor}(r+1)\^{}2/4\ensuremath{\rfloor}/(r+1)\ensuremath{\ge }r/4) \\
(\texttt{\textbackslash{}widetilde\ }B\_r) & a fork leaf and the short
end & (r/4) \\
(\texttt{\textbackslash{}widetilde\ }C\_r) & the two short ends &
(r/2) \\
(\texttt{\textbackslash{}widetilde\ }D\_r) & fork leaves at opposite
ends & (r/4) \\
(\texttt{\textbackslash{}widetilde\ }A\_1) & its two nodes & (1/2) \\
(\texttt{\textbackslash{}widetilde\ }E\_6) & two outer leaves &
(4/3=2r/9) \\
(\texttt{\textbackslash{}widetilde\ }E\_7) & equal-weight nodes
specified in JSON & (2) \\
(\texttt{\textbackslash{}widetilde\ }E\_8) & equal-weight nodes
specified in JSON & (2) \\
(\texttt{\textbackslash{}widetilde\ }F\_4) & its two path ends & (1) \\
(\texttt{\textbackslash{}widetilde\ }G\_2) & its two path ends &
(2/3) \\
\end{longtable}
}

The classical values follow from the explicit coordinates in the first
package. For (B,D), the normalized point difference has (r) coordinates
of magnitude (1/2); for (C), it has (r) coordinates of magnitude 1 and
the minimum squared null coefficient is (1/2). The finite exceptional
calculation is exact: the checker uses
((G+\ensuremath{\delta}\ensuremath{\delta}\textsuperscript{T)}\{-1\}) on
the orthogonal complement of (\ensuremath{\delta}), where it agrees with
(G\^{}+). The certificate records each full matrix and node choice,
rather than referring only to diagram names.

For every unmarked factor we use these choices. They do not need to
avoid a narrow-facet node, since that factor was separately marked.

\section{Every marked factor loses at most
2}\label{every-marked-factor-loses-at-most-2}

We claim that in each marked factor of rank (r), the omission choices
can be made so that

\[
\sigma_a\tau_aE_a\ge M(2r/9-2).
\]

For (r\ensuremath{\le9}), simply use nonnegativity of energy. If it is
the narrow-facet factor, choose any node other than (s) for both
omissions; they may coincide. Since (2r/9-2\ensuremath{\le0}), this
proves the claim without a low-rank search.

For (r\ensuremath{\ge10}), only the classical families occur. Use the
following choices and Schur-localization estimates. Importantly, the
choices are made \textbf{before} seeing the terminating contact rows.

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  For (A\_r), take opposite cycle nodes, rotating both to avoid (s) when
  necessary. Deleting a node leaves (A\_r); the inverse-diagonal test
  localizes either row within two cyclic nodes of its deletion. The two
  long-arc energy estimate gives (E\_a\ensuremath{\ge}(r-8)/4). All null
  coefficients equal 1, so
  (\ensuremath{\sigma}\_a\ensuremath{\tau}\_a\ensuremath{\ge }M).
\item
  For (B\_r), take a left fork leaf and the right short end. Deletion
  leaves respectively (B\_r) and (D\_r). In the first row only nodes
  (0,1,2) can be contacted; the other row is supported within the last
  three nodes. If the short end is (s), delete the adjacent interior
  node instead; the retained diagram is (D\_\{r-1\}+A\_1), and the
  second row uses at most the last four nodes. If the chosen left leaf
  is (s), use the other left leaf. Thus at least (r-5) intervening
  spatial coordinates have normalized difference (1/2). Every allowed
  null coefficient is at least 1, giving
  (\ensuremath{\sigma}\_a\ensuremath{\tau}\_aE\_a\ensuremath{\ge }M(r-5)/4).
\item
  For (D\_r), take fork leaves at opposite ends, switching to the other
  leaf if one is (s). Each deletion leaves (D\_r); inverse-diagonal
  localization allows only the adjacent end cluster. At least (r-4)
  coordinates have normalized difference (1/2). The weaker bound
  (M(r-5)/4) suffices.
\item
  For (C\_r), take its two ends. If one is (s), move that deletion
  inward by one node; the retained diagram there is (A\_1+B\_\{r-1\}).
  Localization leaves at least (r-5) coordinates with normalized
  difference 1. The allowed null coefficients are at least
  (1/\ensuremath{\sqrt2}), giving
  (\ensuremath{\sigma}\_a\ensuremath{\tau}\_aE\_a\ensuremath{\ge }M(r-5)/2).
\end{itemize}

These are applications of the same closed (A,B,D) inverse formulas and
cumulative-coordinate calculations already proved in the first package.
In all cases (r\ensuremath{\ge10}) meets the needed rank thresholds,
including (D\_\{r-1\}) in the modified (B) choice. The elementary
identities

\[
\frac{r-8}{4}-(2r/9-2)=r/36,\qquad
\frac{r-5}{4}-(2r/9-2)=r/36+3/4,
\]

and

\[
\frac{r-5}{2}-(2r/9-2)=5r/18-1/2>0
\]

prove the claimed uniform loss bound. No assumption about the contacts'
maximum labels or magnitudes is used.

There is no circular choice here: in every non-narrow factor use the
point-contact omissions from the preceding table. If that factor
subsequently turns out spoiled, the same classical end choices satisfy
these localization estimates; the low-rank estimate needs no change.
Only the narrow factor uses the stated modified choices, and it is
already included in the loss allowance whether or not it is spoiled.

\section{Summing the energies}\label{summing-the-energies}

There are at most nine marked factors, so

\[
\sum_a\sigma_a\tau_aE_a\ge M\left(\frac{2N}{9}-18\right).
\]

Since (q+1/q\ensuremath{\le}2M), the Lorentz pairing identity yields

\[
-(x,y)\ge M\left(\frac N9-11\right).
\]

If (n\ensuremath{\ge226}), then (N\ensuremath{\ge225}) and the right
side is at least 14. But both (x,y) are actual framing walls of the
narrow facet, whose pairwise hyperplane distance is strictly below
(\ensuremath{\operatorname{arccosh}}7). For square-two normals this
contradicts (-(x,y)\ensuremath{\ge14}). Therefore (n\ensuremath{\le225})
under the stated ideal-vertex hypothesis.

The bound remains conditional. It proves that in dimension at least 226
a Nikulin narrow facet, if one existed in a finite-volume Coxeter
polytope, would have only finite vertices. Turning that remaining case
into an unconditional dimension bound requires a separate argument; it
cannot be obtained by silently declaring the facet itself a Coxeter
polytope.

\chapter{Ordered endpoint budgets: dimension-163
candidate}\label{ordered-endpoint-budgets-dimension-163-candidate}

\textbf{Internal research proof candidate, pending independent review:}
the frozen, independently reviewed
\href{fresh_nikulin_defect_frontier_20261015.md}{164 argument} sharpens
to dimension at most \textbf{163}. The two endpoint Schur budgets are
each at most two. Keeping their order, rather than replacing them by
their sum, gives the complete near-balanced energy-loss envelope \[
\boxed{\sum_a(T_a-W_a)\le4\quad\text{if }M\le21/20.}\tag{1}
\] The proof does not assert a uniform unit-charge estimate. Such
estimates have known balanced counterexamples. Nor does it extrapolate
from a finite rank or finite dihedral-label search.

The
\href{../scripts/fresh_nikulin_two_budget_frontier_20261015.py}{checker}
and \href{fresh_nikulin_two_budget_frontier_20261015.json}{certificate}
preserve all previous files. They use the frozen standalone Fraction
grounded-matrix
\href{../scripts/fresh_nikulin_height_charge_20261015_review.py}{review
helper} read-only. New support lists, convex minima, radical bounds,
tail inequalities, and ordered packing decisions are recomputed.
Published geometric inputs and the compact-facet branch remain the
explicitly inherited reviewed chain. No publication-priority,
current-best, or formal-verification claim is made.

\section{Framework and the residual
lemma}\label{framework-and-the-residual-lemma}

Use exactly the preset omissions of the reviewed 164/165/169 packages.
For a rank-r affine factor, let \[
T=2r/9,\qquad T=2(r-1)/9\text{ in the sole avoid-node factor}.
\] Its endpoint contact rows p,q have nonzero entries at least one. The
positive affine kernel \(\delta\) is normalized by \(\min\delta_i=1\).
Put \[
\sigma=\delta\cdot p,\quad \tau=\delta\cdot q,\quad
M=\max(\sigma/\tau,\tau/\sigma),\quad
W=\min(\sigma,\tau)^2E.
\] Here E is the squared distance of the normalized Euclidean
point-potential means. The same M applies to every factor. Write
\(C_0,C_1\) for its two retained-support quadratic costs. The actual
endpoint geometry gives \[
\sum_a C_{a,0}\le2,\qquad\sum_a C_{a,1}\le2.\tag{2}
\]

The new residual-product lemma is:

\((10/9,4/3)\) & \(20/9\) \\
\((1,3/2)\) & \(22/9\) \\
\((3/2,1)\) & \(22/9\) \\
\end{longtable}
}

It covers arbitrary numbers and ranks of prescribed factors, with at
most one avoid-node factor, for every \(M\le21/20\). All three maxima in
the relaxed local domain are attained by the exact table records below.
The proof first establishes a complete continuous envelope for every
factor with \(C_0,C_1\le3/2\), then performs finite exact ordered-budget
packing.

\section{Complete continuous domains at finite
ranks}\label{complete-continuous-domains-at-finite-ranks}

For an omitted node i and a retained node k, the inverse diagonal is
\(\delta_k^2R(i,k)\), where R is the squared distance of the normalized
point potentials. The retained inverse Gram is entrywise nonnegative.
Therefore every actual support lies among all subsets of nodes with
diagonal at most \(3/2\), and its cost is bounded below by evaluating
every nonzero coordinate at one, including all same-row cross terms. No
support-size cutoff is used.

For every pair of retained supports, the checker includes both
possibilities for each omitted entry: zero, or at least one. Empty full
rows are discarded because their positive affine height must be nonzero.
If both retained supports are empty, the previously reviewed
point-energy inequality gives \(W\ge T\), so they contribute no positive
loss.

For full supports U,V, the normalized means lie in the two finite convex
hulls. The checker constructs an exact rational closest-pair
certificate. For their signed Euclidean Gram K, barycentric vector x and
the two simplex constraints A, it verifies \[
x\ge0,\quad Ax=(1,1),\quad
Kx+A^t\lambda\ge0,\quad
x_i(Kx+A^t\lambda)_i=0.
\] The explicit Euclidean models make K positive semidefinite. These
identities prove the global minimum
\(E\ge e=x^tKx=-\lambda_0-\lambda_1\), including singular minimizer
sets. There is no floating-point optimization in the certificate.

The full supports also give height lower bounds
\(s=\sum_{k\in U}\delta_k\), \(t=\sum_{k\in V}\delta_k\). Thus \[
W\ge H_B(s,t)e,\qquad
H_B(s,t)=\max\{\min(s,t)^2,\max(s,t)^2/B^2\},\quad B=21/20.
\tag{3}
\] Square roots in s,t are either exact rational numbers or replaced by
certified 64-bit rational lower bounds. H is increasing in each
argument, so this is a valid downward energy bound. Surviving
support-cost floors are checked to be exactly rational; radical lower
bounds used while excluding other supports cannot discard a feasible
support.

The finite coverage is A cycles of sizes 2 through 17, B/C ranks 2
through 7, D ranks 4 through 17, all ordinary/avoid E6/E7/E8/F4/G2
records, and the separate modified B2. This gives \textbf{91 models,
1,116 retained-support pairs and 3,630 continuous full-support domains}.
Exactly 1,395 computed loss upper bounds are positive. Each is
dominated, with the same modified/ordinary flag, by one of the following
28 rational records: the dominating record has no larger cost floor in
either endpoint and no smaller loss upper bound.

\section{Dimension consequence and sharp local
accounting}\label{dimension-consequence-and-sharp-local-accounting}

The targets sum to \((2N-2)/9\), where N=n−1 and the subtraction is the
sole avoid-node penalty. Therefore (1) gives \[
\sum W\ge(2N-38)/9,\qquad -(x,y)\ge M(N-37)/9
\quad(M\le21/20).
\] For M≥21/20, the unchanged four-thirds estimate with the \textbf{same
preset omissions} gives \(-(x,y)\ge M(N-43)/9\). At N=163+t the two
lower bounds are respectively at least \[
14+t/9,\qquad14+7t/60.
\] They contradict the strict narrow-facet inequality \(-(x,y)<14\) for
every t≥0. The ideal-vertex branch therefore gives n≤163; the inherited
compact facet branch gives n≤143. Combined, the research candidate is
\(\boxed{n\le163}\), without arithmetic hypotheses.

The local loss constant four is sharp. Take two ordinary E7 factors with
both rows at node7, and two ordinary B2 factors with both rows at node0.
Their common M is one, W=0, the endpoint cost totals are exactly (2,2),
and the total target is four. Adding a zero-target modified A1 and 24
zero-cost E6 factors with W=T gives total rank163. This is a checked
configuration of the local charge domain, \textbf{not} an ambient
polytope. Further improvement may need rank-sensitive accounting or
additional geometric restrictions; no claim of an optimal dimension
bound follows from this local witness.

framing/terminating-wall existence, common height ratio, endpoint

\chapter{Reviewed research proof candidate: dimension at most
163}\label{reviewed-research-proof-candidate-dimension-at-most-163}

\textbf{Candidate theorem.} Every finite-sided, finite-volume real
hyperbolic Coxeter polytope has dimension \textbf{n≤163}, without
arithmeticity, compactness, a simple-cusp hypothesis, or a facet-count
restriction.

The new
\href{fresh_nikulin_two_budget_frontier_20261015.md}{ordered-budget
proof} and
\href{fresh_nikulin_two_budget_frontier_20261015_review.md}{independent
review} sharpen the frozen
\href{fresh_nikulin_defect_frontier_20261015_dimension164.md}{164
candidate}. This
\href{../scripts/fresh_nikulin_two_budget_frontier_20261015_dimension163.py}{case
binder} and its
\href{fresh_nikulin_two_budget_frontier_20261015_dimension163.json}{certificate}
check the local outputs, complete geometric case split and recursive
source hashes. They preserve every preceding artifact. Historical
pending-review wording in the frozen primary report is superseded by the
independent review bound here. External validation, novelty, and
current-best literature status remain unestablished.

If the chosen narrow facet has an ideal vertex, its affine factors have
total rank N=n−1. Use the inherited actual framing walls, common height
ratio M≥1, prescribed omissions, and separate Schur budgets C₀≤2 and
C₁≤2. For M≤21/20 the new all-rank continuous envelope proves total
target loss at most four. When unit charge fails, select any failing
factor. An ordinary E8 factor leaves endpoint budgets at most
(10/9,4/3), whose residual loss is at most20/9; its own target is16/9.
An E7-type factor leaves (1,3/2) or (3/2,1), whose residual loss is at
most22/9; its own target is14/9. Both sums are four, and additional
failures are included in the residual product. With no failing factor
the two total budgets already give four.

The independently checked envelope covers all 91 finite models and all
3,630 continuous support domains, plus analytic A/B/C/D tails at every
remaining rank. It uses no finite-angle cutoff. The two same-row E7
possibilities are excluded by separate exact convex certificates, and
the 28-record envelope is packed with both endpoint budgets in their
stated order. The review uses independently reconstructed physical
Grams, Fraction convex-certificate checks and a separate packing
algorithm.

\section{Independent arithmetic and domain
coverage}\label{independent-arithmetic-and-domain-coverage}

The checker builds literal norm-two affine Grams for all relevant types,
computes their positive kernels, and grounds the rational weighted
Laplacian \(\operatorname{diag}(\delta)G\operatorname{diag}(\delta)\). A
separate Fraction Gaussian elimination gives the Euclidean
point-potential Gram. For every omitted node in the finite census, its
inverse physical spherical Gram is independently checked against

\[
J_{kl}=\frac{\delta_k\delta_l}{2}
       \bigl(R(i,k)+R(i,l)-R(k,l)\bigr).
\]

All inverse entries are nonnegative and every diagonal is at least one
half. Since every nonzero contact is at least one, a support with
endpoint cost at most 3/2 must be a subset of the nodes whose inverse
diagonal is at most 3/2. The review enumerates every such subset and
tests its \textbf{exact physical} cost, including all cross terms. This
separately confirms the primary's radical lower-bound exclusion logic.
No feasible support is lost by an interval test, and the retained costs
are exactly rational.

The finite domain contains 91 models, 1,116 retained-support pairs, and
3,630 continuous full-support domains. Both omitted-entry alternatives,
zero and at least one, are included. Empty full rows are excluded only
because the inherited geometry gives positive affine height. The
zero-retained-cost cases satisfy the independently checked point-energy
bound W≥T.

For each continuous domain, the saved barycentric vector and equality
multipliers are checked against a separately reconstructed Gram. The
nonnegativity, simplex constraints, gradient slack and complementary
slackness prove the global convex minimum. This verifies all 3,630 exact
KKT certificates, including singular minimizer sets. It does not depend
on trusting a numerical optimizer or finding a new minimizer
independently.

If the full support forces heights at least s and t and the actual
common height ratio is at most B=21/20, then

\[
\min(\sigma,\tau)^2\ge
\max\{\min(s,t)^2,\max(s,t)^2/B^2\}.
\]

This bound is increasing in both support-height lower bounds. The exact
rational enclosures for their square roots therefore have the correct
direction. Multiplying by the nonnegative convex energy gives a valid
lower bound for W over the entire contact domain, not only at its
unit-contact point.

The review derives the 28-record Pareto frontier independently from all
1,395 positive-loss domains and verifies every saved domination map. A
separate forward reachability calculation, which permits all record
sequences rather than using the producer's ordered-multiset recursion,
proves:

Negative-loss factors can be dropped when seeking an upper bound.

\section{All-rank tails}\label{all-rank-tails}

The finite census is supplemented by an analytic, not sampled, tail
proof. The literal prefix coordinates give the following complete
inverse-diagonal reductions. Interior distances below mean integers at
least two.

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  For ordinary B, omission 0 leaves node1 of cost1; the other node
  classes have costs k≥2 or r/2. Omission r leaves r−1 of cost1; the
  other classes have costs r/4 or r−k≥2. For modified B, omission r−1
  leaves r−2 and r of costs1 and1/2, while its other classes have costs
  (r−1)/4 or r−1−k≥2. The opposite omission0 again leaves only node1.
\item
  For ordinary C the only nodes left at the two ends are1 and r−1, each
  of cost1. The other costs are at least two or r/2. Modified omission1
  leaves0 and2 with costs1/2 and1; the remaining end cost is (r−1)/2.
\item
  For D, omission0 leaves only1, and omission r leaves only r−1, each of

\end{itemize}

These exclusions hold for all B/C ranks r≥8 and D ranks r≥18. Inserting
the coordinate formulas shows that arbitrary convex means in the
surviving full supports differ in fixed coordinates. Their energies are
at least (r−2)/4, (r−3)/4, (r−2)/2, (r−3)/2 and (r−2)/4, respectively.
In both B cases one full support has all kernel coefficients at least
√2, so the height-square factor is at least 2/B². The resulting W−T
expressions are affine in r−8 or r−18 with nonnegative constant and
positive slope. The checker verifies these symbolic expressions and
separately checks their physical coordinate identities at the boundary
ranks.

For A cycles of size m≥18 even or m≥19 odd, the resistance is
\(R(d)=d(m-d)/m\). Its concavity shows that any retained distance at
least two exceeds the cost cap. Two distinct retained entries also
exceed the cap, so each full support is its omission plus at most one
adjacent node. Two singleton full supports have separation at least
floor(m/2)−2. If a full support has two nodes, its height is at least
two. Expanding the difference of the two means leaves a nonnegative
square and a linear loss at most \(2(m+(m\bmod2))/m\). The independent
symbolic calculation reproduces the primary's two positive parity
polynomials and proves W≥T at every remaining rank. Rotations and fork
swaps implement the stated avoid-node choices; avoid-A1 has target zero.
Thus no unexamined large rank or dihedral-label cutoff remains.

\section{Failing-factor split and dimension

For the affine-factor energy estimate, coefficient one is impossible

and the existing avoid-node choices. It is optimal for this local lemma
with slope 2/9 and omissions prescribed before the contact rows. This is
a statement about that particular accounting scheme, not an optimal
dimension bound.

The resulting \textbf{research proof candidate is n≤169} for
finite-sided finite-volume real hyperbolic Coxeter polytopes. The
\href{fresh_nikulin_dimension_181_candidate_20261015.md}{reviewed 181
candidate} remains frozen. The new argument requires independent review
before it becomes the reviewed baseline. No priority or current-best
claim is made.

The \href{../scripts/fresh_nikulin_unit_charge_20261015.py}{checker} and
\href{fresh_nikulin_unit_charge_20261015.json}{certificate} check all
exceptional cases, complete E6/E7/E8 omission-pair obstructions, and
symbolic all-rank classical formulas. They use no finite-label cutoff
and import no producer arithmetic.

\section{Precise local statement}\label{precise-local-statement}

Retain the notation and geometric hypotheses of the
\href{fresh_nikulin_narrow_20261015_products.md}{product proof} and
\href{fresh_nikulin_avoid_node_20261015.md}{avoid-node proof}. The
affine roots have square two; the positive kernel δ has minimum entry
one. For prescribed omissions i,j, contact rows p,q are nonnegative and
nonzero, and every nonzero entry is at least one. Each endpoint's full
Schur cost is at most two. Write

\begin{verbatim}
σ=δ·p,  τ=δ·q,  M=max(σ/τ,τ/σ),
C=p_SiᵀG(S_i)⁻¹p_Si + q_SjᵀG(S_j)⁻¹q_Sj,
W=σ τ E/M=min(σ,τ)² E.
\end{verbatim}

The new inequalities are

\begin{verbatim}
W+(4/3)C ≥ 2r/9                         (ordinary factor),
W+(4/3)C ≥ 2(r−1)/9                     (factor avoiding a fixed node).
\end{verbatim}

Use the frozen ordinary choices except that E8 now uses nodes
\textbf{1,6}. Use exactly the frozen avoid-node choices in the factor
containing the narrow-facet normal. Thus every choice remains
independent of the eventual contact rows. In particular, the new
ordinary E8 choice does not replace the separate rule needed when node 1
or 6 must be avoided.

\section{Exact obstruction to coefficient
one}\label{exact-obstruction-to-coefficient-one}

With the old ordinary E8 omissions 3,7, take the row at omission 7 to be
p=e8 and the other row q=e3. Their heights are 1,2, the total cost is
1/2, and W=1. Consequently W+C=3/2\textless16/9; this pair would require
a charge at least 14/9.

The certificate checks every unordered omission pair, not just the old
choice. A pair whose zero-cost point rows have energy below 2r/9 is
ineligible for every coefficient. Among the remaining pairs it tests all
unit point-contact rows whose two individual costs are at most two.
These are legal rows under the stated local hypotheses and use only
contact magnitudes zero and one.

\section{A linear loss identity}\label{a-linear-loss-identity}

Choose Euclidean point potentials v\_k for the normalized point rows
e\_k/δ\_k, defined up to a common translation. Put
R\_ab=\textbar v\_a−v\_b\textbar². The contact-row potentials are convex
combinations

\begin{verbatim}
z_p=Σ_k (δ_k p_k/σ)v_k,   z_q=Σ_k (δ_k q_k/τ)v_k.
\end{verbatim}

Set a=z\_p−v\_i, b=z\_q−v\_j and

\begin{verbatim}
ℓ_ik=R_ij+R_ik−R_kj.
\end{verbatim}

Direct expansion gives

\begin{verbatim}
E=R_ij−Σ_k (δ_k p_k/σ)ℓ_ik
       −Σ_k (δ_k q_k/τ)ℓ_jk+|a−b|².          (1)
\end{verbatim}

The inverse diagonal for a retained node k after omission i is

\begin{verbatim}
c_ik=δ_k² R_ik.
\end{verbatim}

All inverse entries are nonnegative, so the row cost is at least Σ\_k
c\_ik p\_k². Every convex weight δ\_k p\_k/σ is at most one; when it is
nonzero, p\_k²≥1. Therefore, if every possible retained contact
satisfies \texttt{ℓ\_ik≤α\ c\_ik} (and similarly for the other row),
each linear loss in (1) is paid by α times its diagonal cost. Negative ℓ
terms only improve the bound. It follows that

\begin{verbatim}
E+αC≥R_ij,  hence W+αC≥R_ij,                (2)
\end{verbatim}

because σ,τ≥1 and E≥0. This elementary identity uses the energy and cost
together, instead of discarding all energy when a contact occurs.

For each factor with target T, the case C≥T/α is immediate. In the
remaining case every retained contact has diagonal
\texttt{c\_ik\textless{}T/α} and \texttt{c\_ik≤2}. These restrictions
eliminate the exceptional distant contacts in the following coordinate
tables.

\section{All classical ranks}\label{all-classical-ranks}

For A\_r let m=r+1, take opposite cycle nodes, and let ε=m mod 2. A node
at cyclic distance d from an omission has

\begin{verbatim}
c=d(m−d)/m,    ℓ≤(m+ε)d/m.
\end{verbatim}

For r≤5 the minimum retained diagonal r/(r+1) is already at least the
small-cost threshold r/6, so a nonzero retained contact is impossible
below that threshold. For r=6,7,8, the threshold excludes distance two
and farther; only d=1 remains. For r≥9, the individual endpoint budget
two excludes d≥3, since \texttt{3(m−3)/m\textgreater{}2} for m≥10 and
the diagonal increases up to the antipode. Thus d≤2.

In all these remaining cases, multiplying \texttt{(4/3)c−ℓ} by 3m gives
the lower bound

\begin{verbatim}
d(m−4d−3ε)≥0.
\end{verbatim}

For odd m≥11 the smallest case is m=11,d=2, where equality holds. The
cases m=7,8,9,d=1 and even m≥10 are also nonnegative. Opposite-cycle
point energy is at least 2r/9. Equation (2) proves the ordinary and
rotated avoid-node estimates for every rank. A1 is handled separately
below.

For B,C,D use orthonormal coordinates e1,\ldots,er. The following point
potentials give all required resistances directly by squared distances;
their adjacent differences solve the corresponding normalized
affine-root equations.

\begin{itemize}

  B\_r: \texttt{v0=0}, \texttt{v1=e1}, and \texttt{vk=(e1+…+ek)/2} for
  2≤k≤r. Kernel entries are 1 at nodes 0,1; 2 at nodes 2,\ldots,r−1; and
  √2 at r.
\item
  C\_r: \texttt{v0=0}, \texttt{vk=(e1+…+ek)/√2} for 1≤k≤r. Kernel

\end{itemize}

The ordinary omissions are 0,r. The modified B omission pair is r−1,0;

\section{Exceptional factors and every forbidden
node}\label{exceptional-factors-and-every-forbidden-node}

The checker reconstructs the six ordinary exceptional cases and all 34
forbidden-node cases from their literal Gram matrices. Let T be the
target and discard the immediate case C≥3T/4. Nonnegative inverse
entries then restrict retained contacts to nodes with diagonal strictly
below 3T/4.

There are only 46 single-contact occurrences across these records, and
one possible two-contact pattern. Every other support is excluded by its
diagonal costs, including cross terms when two contacts lie in the same
row. There is no restriction on the magnitude of any remaining contact
beyond the endpoint cost and the gap between zero and one.

For one retained contact the rows are

\begin{verbatim}
p=a e_i+b e_l,  q=c e_j,
b,c≥1,  a=0 or a≥1.
\end{verbatim}

Writing \texttt{u=δ\_l\ b/(δ\_i\ a+δ\_l\ b)}, the normalized-row energy
is the quadratic

\begin{verbatim}
E(u)=(1−u)R_ij+uR_lj−u(1−u)R_il.

If a=0, a valid lower bound for W+(4/3)C is

\begin{verbatim}
min(δ_l,δ_j)² R_lj +(4/3)c_il.
\end{verbatim}

If a≥1, a valid lower bound is

\begin{verbatim}
min(δ_i,δ_j)² min_[0,1] E(u) +(4/3)c_il.
\end{verbatim}

Both bounds meet T in every serialized occurrence. The quadratic minima
are evaluated exactly at the two endpoints and, when applicable, the

The only surviving two-contact pattern is ordinary E7: one isolated A1
contact at node 4 after deleting 3 and one at node 7 after deleting 6.

one. Thus W+(4/3)C≥11/6\textgreater14/9. Three contacts already exceed

The avoid-node rules remain those of the frozen 181 proof, including E7

1/2 and positive cost at least 1/2; its avoid-node target is zero. It

\section{Global consequence and
scope}\label{global-consequence-and-scope}

The same geometric argument supplies actual terminating walls framing
the chosen narrow facet, with a common height ratio q and total cost
ΣC≤4. Only the single factor containing the facet normal uses the
avoid-node target. Consequently

\begin{verbatim}
Σ σ_a τ_a E_a ≥ M(2N/9−(4/3)·4−2/9),
−(x,y) ≥ M(N−43)/9,  N=n−1.

For clarity about constants, coefficient one with the same total cost

\chapter{Reviewed research proof candidate: dimension at most
169}\label{reviewed-research-proof-candidate-dimension-at-most-169}

\textbf{Candidate theorem.} Every finite-sided, finite-volume real
hyperbolic Coxeter polytope has dimension \textbf{n≤169}, without an
arithmeticity, compactness, simple-cusp or facet-count assumption.

The \href{fresh_nikulin_unit_charge_20261015.md}{four-thirds estimate}
and its \href{fresh_nikulin_unit_charge_20261015_review.md}{independent
review} sharpen the frozen
\href{fresh_nikulin_dimension_181_candidate_20261015.md}{181 proof
candidate}. The
\href{../scripts/fresh_nikulin_unit_charge_20261015_dimension169.py}{case
binder} and
\href{fresh_nikulin_unit_charge_20261015_dimension169.json}{certificate}
bind the complete dependency chain. This is an internally reviewed
research proof candidate; external validation, novelty and current-best
literature status remain unestablished.

Nikulin's narrow-facet theorem supplies a facet F whose framing
hyperplanes have pairwise distance strictly below \texttt{arccosh\ 7}.
If F contains an ideal vertex, its Euclidean link is a product of
irreducible affine Coxeter simplices of total rank \texttt{N=n−1}.
Preset omissions select two edges in F, and actual terminating walls x,y
can be chosen to meet F in ridges. Their two total Schur costs sum to at
most four.
\href{https://www.mathunion.org/fileadmin/ICM/Proceedings/ICM1986.1/ICM1986.1.ocr.pdf}{Nikulin,
official ICM report, printed pp.654--655 and 657--659}.

For each affine factor, the new estimate is

\begin{verbatim}
σ_a τ_a E_a / M + (4/3)C_a ≥ 2r_a/9,
\end{verbatim}

with target \texttt{2(r\_a−1)/9} in the single factor containing F's
normal. The height ratio is common across factors and
\texttt{M=max(q,1/q)≥1}. The proof covers every affine type and all
ranks, with no label cutoff. It combines a linear energy-loss identity
with exact exceptional-case analysis; the ordinary E8 omission changes
to nodes 1 and 6.

Summation and the Lorentz identity yield

\begin{verbatim}
−(x,y) = (1/2)Σ σ_a τ_a E_a − q − 1/q
       ≥ M(N−43)/9.
\end{verbatim}

At \texttt{n≥170}, this is at least 14, contradicting narrowness for
square-two normals. If F has only finite vertices, it is compact; the
separately reviewed
\href{fresh_nikulin_narrow_20261015_compact_facet.md}{compact-facet
argument} gives \texttt{n≤143} without assuming that F itself is
Coxeter. The two cases establish the candidate 169 bound.

For comparison, Prokhorov's published Theorem C gives 995, and Nikulin's
ICM report already announces the stronger unrestricted bound below 300.
The repository's candidate is separate from those literature statements
and is not presented as an externally validated theorem.
\href{https://www.mathnet.ru/php/getFT.phtml?jrnid=im&paperid=1484&what=fullteng}{Prokhorov,
printed p.402},
\href{https://www.mathunion.org/fileadmin/ICM/Proceedings/ICM1986.1/ICM1986.1.ocr.pdf}{Nikulin,
printed p.659}.

The compact and arithmetic dimension ceilings remain 29; the noncompact
arithmetic range remains \texttt{n≤19} or \texttt{n=21}. The 169
candidate addresses the general finite-volume class and does not improve
those stronger restricted bounds.

The primary report's pending-review sentence records its earlier frozen
state. This binder records the completed independent review without
rewriting that artifact. Arithmetic and source integrity checks do not
replace the stated mathematical and published dependencies.

\chapter{Independent review of the four-thirds contact-cost
estimate}\label{independent-review-of-the-four-thirds-contact-cost-estimate}

The new local estimate and its dimension-169 consequence pass
independent arithmetic and mathematical review. This is an internal
research review. External validation, publication priority and
current-best status remain unestablished.

The
\href{../scripts/fresh_nikulin_unit_charge_20261015_review.py}{review
checker} and
\href{fresh_nikulin_unit_charge_20261015_review.json}{certificate}
import no arithmetic from the
\href{fresh_nikulin_unit_charge_20261015.md}{primary proof}. They reuse
only elementary Fraction matrix operations from an earlier independent
checker. Exceptional energies are recovered from grounded rational
linear systems, with every equation checked, rather than the producer's
regularized inverse. The nonsimply-laced matrices are treated by
rational diagonal congruences; the literal physical Gram entries and the
normalized kernel squares are compared with the primary data.

\section{Coverage of the local lemma}\label{coverage-of-the-local-lemma}

For each of the 40 ordinary and forbidden-node exceptional cases, the
review rebuilds every retained inverse diagonal. It enumerates
\textbf{every subset} of contacts whose diagonal costs are below the
trivial-charge threshold, adding the inverse cross terms for contacts in
the same row. All inverse entries are nonnegative, so setting every
nonzero magnitude to one gives a valid support-cost lower bound. This
establishes support coverage for arbitrary real contact magnitudes at
least one, with no finite-label cutoff.

There are 46 single-contact occurrences and one remaining two-contact
support. In the single-contact case, the energy is a convex quadratic in
the normalized mixture weight. The review computes its three
coefficients and exact minimum separately, then checks both
possibilities for the omitted-node contact: zero, or at least one. The
latter distinction supplies the correct lower bound on the two null
heights. The sole two-contact support is ordinary E7; polarization of
the independently reconstructed resistance matrix gives
\texttt{(1+u²+v²)/2}. Its cost is at least one. Both cases meet their
stated targets.

The complete E6/E7/E8 omission-pair census is independently
reconstructed. Zero-cost rows eliminate the ineligible pairs; all unit
point-contact rows satisfying each endpoint budget at most two give the
remaining necessary coefficients. Their best values are 1, 10/9 and 4/3.
In E8, the omissions \texttt{(1,6)} and contact rows at nodes 1 and 8
attain the 4/3 obstruction. This proves optimality for the
\textbf{specified local lemma}, whose slope is fixed at 2/9 and whose
omissions must precede the contact rows. These local rows need not be
realizable together in a whole hyperbolic chamber, and no global
optimality follows.

\section{The all-rank step}\label{the-all-rank-step}

The linear identity used by the producer has the correct sign. For point
potentials \texttt{v\_i}, write \texttt{z\_p=v\_i+a} and
\texttt{z\_q=v\_j+b}. Expanding their squared distance gives

\begin{verbatim}
E=R_ij−Σw_k(R_ij+R_ik−R_kj)
       −Σz_k(R_ij+R_jk−R_ki)+|a−b|².
\end{verbatim}

Each coefficient is a convex weight. When its contact is nonzero, that
weight is at most one and the squared contact magnitude is at least one.
Since the retained inverse has nonnegative entries, its cost dominates
the sum of diagonal contributions. Thus a linear loss bounded by
\texttt{(4/3)c\_ik} is paid by the corresponding cost. Nonpositive
losses require no payment. Finally \texttt{W=min(σ,τ)²E≥E}, since the
normalized affine kernel has minimum entry one and both rows are
nonzero. These steps use neither arithmeticity nor a bound on the
contact labels.

The classical point potentials have an independent direct verification.
For B and D use roots \texttt{α0=−e1−e2}, \texttt{αk=e\_k−e\_(k+1)},
with final root \texttt{√2\ e\_r} in B and final two roots
\texttt{e\_(r−1)−e\_r}, \texttt{e\_(r−1)+e\_r} in D. In C use
\texttt{α0=−√2\ e1}, the same difference roots, and
\texttt{αr=√2\ e\_r}. The prefix vectors in the primary proof satisfy,
for every index,

\begin{verbatim}
α_l·v_k = 1_(l=k)/δ_k − 1_(l=0)/δ_0.
\end{verbatim}

This follows by subtracting adjacent coordinates; the two fork/end
equations check the boundary cases. It identifies the potentials with
normalized point contacts, proves their squared-distance formula, and
gives \texttt{c\_ik=δ\_k²R\_ik} by deleting node i. It is an all-rank
identity, not an extrapolation from small diagrams.

The reviewer computes distances from these coordinate vectors by
symbolic interval intersections. It checks 24 index classes partitioning
the required B/C/D rows, with independent nonnegative parameters for the
node index and excess rank. Every class either satisfies the four-thirds
loss inequality or has cost strictly above the trivial-charge threshold.
Path reversal and fork automorphisms cover the stated symmetric rows and
forbidden-node choices. The exceptional modified B2 pair is checked
directly. No producer resistance table is imported.

For A, direct substitution in \texttt{R(d)=d(m−d)/m} gives linear losses
\texttt{d(m±ε)/m} for the two directions from an opposite omission,
where \texttt{m=r+1} and \texttt{ε=m\ mod\ 2}. Below the trivial-charge
threshold, ranks 2--5 allow no retained contact, and ranks 6--8 allow
only distance one. For \texttt{m≥10}, the endpoint budget excludes
distances at least three because \texttt{3(m−3)/m\textgreater{}2};
monotonicity up to the antipode completes this restriction. For the
remaining distances, the cleared margin is \texttt{d(m−4d−3ε)},
nonnegative in both parity classes. A1 and its coincident avoid-node
omissions are included among the exact exceptional cases. Cycle rotation
avoids any prescribed node in all other ranks.

\section{Global hypothesis and threshold
check}\label{global-hypothesis-and-threshold-check}

The \href{fresh_nikulin_dimension_181_candidate_20261015.md}{frozen 181
binder} supplies the geometric dependencies: actual ridge neighbors of
the narrow facet, terminating walls at finite or ideal endpoints, a
common null-height ratio across affine factors, the Lorentz pairing
identity, and the compact-facet branch. The new omission in ordinary E8
is chosen before the contact rows and does not alter the separate
avoid-node rule. Thus the framing argument still applies.

There are two endpoint budgets, each at most two. Exactly one affine
factor contains the narrow-facet normal and incurs the avoid-node
deficit 2/9. With \texttt{N=n−1}, the new local estimate therefore gives

\begin{verbatim}
Σ σ_a τ_a E_a ≥ M(2N/9−16/3−2/9),
−(x,y) ≥ M(N−43)/9,    M≥1.
\end{verbatim}

At \texttt{n=170}, this is at least 14. It contradicts the strict
narrow-facet distance bound \texttt{arccosh\ 7} for square-two normals.
At \texttt{n=169}, the scalar lower bound alone is smaller than 14, so
no further one-unit improvement has been silently inferred. The
ideal-vertex branch gives 169; the inherited compact-facet branch gives
143. These two alternatives exhaust the chosen narrow facet.

The checker certifies the exact arithmetic and finite coverage
supporting these arguments. The coordinate identities, geometric bridge
and published classifications remain mathematical proof dependencies,
not a formal proof-assistant development.

\chapter{Nonincident cusp carriers: exact multiplicity
obstructions}\label{nonincident-cusp-carriers-exact-multiplicity-obstructions}

The known finite-volume H17 pyramid has \textbf{1,048 unpaid
quadrilateral faces} under the fine corner rule, of which987 are
compact. Every one has the two affine E8 factors of the same nonincident
cusp in its original face star. This disproves two natural proposed
bounds: charging at most one unpaid face per edge of the carrier cusp
link, or at most six per link vertex per small factor. It does not
disprove a stronger bound with a larger constant, or one that uses
additional geometry.

Separately, an explicit family of finite-volume H3 Coxeter chambers has
arbitrarily many compact quadrilateral faces carried by a
fixed-combinatorial-type cusp. Those faces are fully paid. Thus a useful
global estimate must depend on the \textbf{payment deficit}, not merely
on the presence of a nonincident carrier.

The
\href{../scripts/fresh_nonincident_carrier_incidence_20261017.py}{checker}
and \href{fresh_nonincident_carrier_incidence_20261017.json}{data}
preserve the distinction. No dimension bound is asserted.

\section{Exact chamber and complete two-face
ledger}\label{exact-chamber-and-complete-two-face-ledger}

Use the19-root shared-L25 Gram from the frozen
\href{fresh_selective_distance13_dimension146_20261017.md}{selective-distance13
proof} and its
\href{fresh_selective_distance13_dimension146_20261017_review.md}{independent
reconstruction}. Its nodes split into

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist

  L=\{0,\ldots,8\};
\item
  R=\{10,\ldots,18\};
\item
  the shared node9.
\end{itemize}

The Gram radical is

\texttt{(-6,-3,-4,-2,-5,-4,-3,-2,-1,0,6,3,4,2,5,4,3,2,1)}.

In covector coordinates p\_i=x·n\_i the chamber cone is p\_i\textless=0
with z·p=0. Its complete extreme rays are the single-coordinate ray
supported on9 and the81 two-coordinate rays supported on one node of L
and one of R. A rational18-by18 inverse rechecks all squares and the
strict common timelike center. There are80 finite vertices and two ideal
vertices: the apex supported on9, and the base vertex supported
on\{3,13\}. The frozen chamber proof supplies the proper cusp links and
actual-facet checks; the new calculation independently recovers all82
rays and their signs.

The projective combinatorics is a pyramid over Delta8×Delta8. A two-face
allows four covector coordinates, at least one from each of L,R; its
supporting whites are the other15 roots. This is exhaustive: the
restricted cone has dimension3 exactly in these cases, since its
positive and negative z coordinates impose one independent relation. The

edge, not every allowed coordinate. The checker also recognizes

\section{Literal quadrilateral
payments}\label{literal-quadrilateral-payments}

At a finite corner the checker uses Vinberg's actual rule: weight2 in a
connected component of order at most4; weight1 in orders5 through7; in a
larger classical component, weight1 for adjacency or membership in a
connected end segment of order at most6 invariant under interchange of
fork leaves. Otherwise the weight is0. The definition is the one in
\href{https://www.mathnet.ru/php/getFT.phtml?jrnid=mmo&option_lang=rus&paperid=444&what=fullt}{Vinberg,
§6.1--2, printed pp.80--81}, also bound in the
\href{fresh_compact_dimension_bound_20261015.md}{frozen finite-component
checker}. It is not replaced by a short-distance finite rule.

or D. Thus no literal E8 excluded-pair list is needed. At the other

frozen
\href{fresh_cusp_spectator_role_payments_20261017.md}{distance-three and
invariant-end-segment rule}. The small-factor weight2 modification from

cusp is not on these faces.

\section{What the unpaid example rules
out}\label{what-the-unpaid-example-rules-out}

Write Q\_bad for the number of unpaid quadrilaterals and sum only over
cusps which carry a small factor. This chamber gives

\texttt{Q\_bad=1048\ \textgreater{}\ 648\ =\ sum\ f1(link\_v)}.

Also, with s\_small(v) the number of small factors and V\_v the
link-vertex count,

\texttt{Q\_bad=1048\ \textgreater{}\ 6·2·81=972},

and even the compact unpaid count987 exceeds972. Consequently an
inequality

\texttt{Q\_bad\ \textless{}=\ c\ sum\ s\_small(v)V\_v}

would require c\textgreater=524/81 in general, and c\textgreater=329/54
if restricted to compact unpaid quadrilaterals. This remains true if
each defective face is assigned to just one of its carriers: all
available small carriers lie at the same cusp, and the right side
already includes both factors. These are necessary tests on a proposed
multiplicity theorem, not an upper bound established by this example.

\section{Unbounded carrier incidence with all faces
paid}\label{unbounded-carrier-incidence-with-all-faces-paid}

For every integer N\textgreater=1, take the upper-halfspace region

\texttt{−1/2\ \textless{}=\ x\ \textless{}=\ 1/2},

\texttt{−1/sqrt2\ \textless{}=\ y\ \textless{}=\ (2N−1)/sqrt2},

outside the N unit hemispheres centered at(0,sqrt2·k), k=0,\ldots,N−1.
In the Lorentz metric diag(−1,1,1,1), norm-one outward normals are

\texttt{X±=(1/2,±1,0,1/2)},

\texttt{Y−=(1/sqrt2,0,−1,1/sqrt2)},

\texttt{Y+=((2N−1)/sqrt2,0,1,(2N−1)/sqrt2)},

\texttt{B\_k=(k²,0,sqrt2·k,k²−1)}.

The pairings give:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  X±·B\_k=−1/2, hence angle pi/3;
\item
  B\_j·B\_k=1−(j−k)², hence adjacent caps meet at pi/2 and all others
  are dotted;
\item
  the end cap meets its end y-wall at pi/4; other cap/end-wall pairs are
  dotted;
\item
  the vertical x/y pairs are right, and each opposite vertical pair is
  parallel.
\end{itemize}

Every cap is an actual facet. Its visible patch lies over the rectangle
x∈{[}−1/2,1/2{]}, y∈{[}(2k−1)/sqrt2,(2k+1)/sqrt2{]}, clipped only by the
two global end walls when appropriate. It is a compact quadrilateral.
The bottom is the upper envelope of these hemispheres. The nearest
center has horizontal squared distance at most1/4+1/2=3/4, so the bottom
height is at least1/2 everywhere. The finite horizontal rectangle and
the integral of z\^{}(−3) from this positive lower height to infinity
prove finite volume. Only the point at infinity is ideal; its link is a
bounded rectangle.

All finite vertices are

\texttt{(x,y,z)=(±1/2,(2j−1)/sqrt2,1/2)}, j=0,\ldots,N.

Thus there are2N+2 finite vertices and one proper ideal vertex. Endpoint
finite corners are B3, interior finite corners A3. Each cap's four
planar angles therefore has fine weight2, total8. The x-wall pair is the
same affine A1 factor in every cap's star and its cusp is not on any
cap. The other cusp factor is also A1, independent of N, and the link
has four vertices.

This is an all-N symbolic argument; the six exact samples
N=1,2,3,7,16,64 only check the displayed identities. It proves that no
bound on \textbf{all} such carrier incidences can depend solely on cusp
factor ranks or the combinatorics of its link. It does not refute a
bound on unpaid incidences: these N faces are fully paid.

\section{Verification and scope}\label{verification-and-scope-6}

Generation and a fresh saved replay pass:82 exact rays,3,456 two-face
incidences, all1,296 quadrilateral payments, and six exact strip checks.
Syntax, ten direct source hashes and all local report links pass. A
separate internal symbolic-geometry review of the strip confirms its
angles, complete vertex description, positive bottom height and sole
proper rectangular cusp; it does not duplicate the H17 payment census.
The known H17 chamber is not a new construction, and the strip family is
used only as an elementary multiplicity obstruction; no novelty claim is
made. The earlier dimension proofs and their frozen files are unchanged.
Source, data and report are final/frozen.

\section{Complete native cost bounds}\label{complete-native-cost-bounds}

For an end define g=2l/h+c0/h², with the corresponding far variables.
After the two immediate near alternatives have been handled, every near
profile has g\textless=5, with a unique extreme type: a simple contact
to one of the old outer leaves10,11, no opposite contact, height1/2 and
g=5. Every other near profile has g\textless=3. Here is a complete
argument.

For the outer-only profile, A3+c is a principal subdiagram of the strict
actual edge. Thus e\textless2. Any two nonzero contacts give
e\textgreater=Kii+Kjj+2Kij\textgreater=2, so at most one A3 contact is
possible. With none, positive height implies t\textgreater=1 and
g\textless=2. A contact at the middle0 is simple and gives g\textless=1.
A single leaf contact q with t=0 gives g=8/q²-3: this is5 for q=1 and at
most1 for q\textgreater=sqrt2. If t\textgreater=1 instead,
c0\textless=5/4 and h\textgreater=3/2, giving g\textless=5/9. These
bounds include all allowed native opposite products, not just simple
ones. For the simple-at2 profile, positive semidefiniteness of D10+c
plus A3 gives0\textless=c0\textless=1 and h\textgreater=1, hence
g\textless=3. Additional spectators only strengthen these restrictions.

At the far end the isolated profile with t=1 and the simple-at13 profile
with t=0 both have k=1/2 and g=8. Every other far profile has
g\textless=4: the isolated nonunit case has t\textgreater=sqrt2;
simple-at13 with t\textgreater=1 has g\textless=3; and the doubled-at13
or simple-at9 cases have g\textless=4 for every t\textgreater=0. Thus
these are the complete two far extreme types.

Eliminating Z, with J=G\_Z\^{}(-1), gives the exact determinant identity

\begin{verbatim}
0 = 1-(g_c+g_d)/10 + E/10,
E=(x/h-y/k)^T J (x/h-y/k) >= 0.

g\_c+g\_d\textless=5+4=9, giving a strict positive gap at least1/10.
Hence the far end is extreme.

\section{Actual face setup}\label{actual-face-setup-1}

For an actual quadrilateral, write W for its supporting white roots and
U,V for the two opposite pairs of black side roots. Normalize every root
to square 2. W and W together with any one black root are positive
definite; W with an adjacent black pair is positive semidefinite. The
opposite sides do not meet, even in the closed quadrilateral, so W+U and
W+V are indefinite. Choose minimal indefinite cores L and M. Each
contains its two black roots, and deleting either black root gives a
positive-definite diagram.

Assume there is no path of length at most 10 from U to V with white
internal nodes. The complete order-6 through order-10 catalogue has 384
marked contexts, with maximum marked radius 7. Cores of order at most 4
have radius at most 2. Order-5 cores have radius at most 3 and require a
separate treatment in the disjoint case below.

An external supporting white contacting node i of a black-deletion Gram
A has squared projection at least (A inverse)ii. This uses the entrywise
nonnegative spherical inverse, nonpositive contacts, and minimum nonzero
Coxeter magnitude 1. If either black-deletion inverse diagonal is at
least 2, positive definiteness of W plus the remaining black root is
impossible. Equality 2 is excluded, since this is an edge-support test.
Of the 527 high-order ports at marked distance at least 3, exactly 161
pass.

Whenever a required positive-definite diagram fails, the producer
records a nonnegative nonzero vector with nonpositive square. Symmetric
elimination of a Z-matrix yields such a vector at its first nonpositive
pivot; the saved vector and square are checked exactly. Its sign makes
the obstruction valid after arbitrary additional nonpositive contacts or
larger bond magnitudes are restored. Label-4 diagrams are rationalized
by a positive diagonal congruence with squared scales 1 or 2. Inverse
diagonals are returned to the norm-two gauge before comparison with 2.

\section{Disjoint high-order cores, including multiple cross
edges}\label{disjoint-high-order-cores-including-multiple-cross-edges}

Disjoint indefinite cores cannot be orthogonal in an ambient Lorentzian
space. Each cross bond joins white ports with marked distances summing
to at least 10. Each distance is therefore at least 3.

The 161 allowed high-order ports give 1,478 ordered candidate joins. In
363, the simple cross bond already gives a nonnegative vector of
nonpositive square in W. The other 1,115 possible edges occur in 1,007
ordered marked-context pairs: 905 admit one edge, 96 admit two, and six
admit three. Thus one cannot assume uniqueness of the cross bond at this
distance threshold.

Every possible cross bond is nevertheless simple. Each endpoint has a
three-node white path. Coefficients (1,2/3,1/3) on that path have square
at most 4/3, since native bond magnitudes are at least 1. The two paths
together have square at most 8/3-2 beta for cross magnitude beta;
additional acute contacts only decrease this value. Positive
definiteness forces beta\textless4/3, leaving only the simple Coxeter
magnitude 1. This excludes all larger finite labels, parallel contacts,
and dotted contacts without a label cutoff.

All 35 underlying single-edge Grams have exactly two negative
directions. For the context pairs admitting multiple edges, the source
tests every subset of size at least two. All 120 such choices have a
nonnegative nonpositive-square witness in W plus one black root. Thus
every nonempty subset is impossible, and no unspecified cross bond can
repair the single-edge inertia obstruction.

\section{Complete small-order
supplement}\label{complete-small-order-supplement}

The radius inequality alone does not exclude an order-5 core here:
radius 3 plus radius 7 permits a connecting edge at distance 11. This
supplement is essential. Orders at most 4 are excluded because
2+7+1\textless=10, and two small cores are also excluded.

Number the black roots 0,1 and a white root at marked distance 3 by 4.
The other whites must form the path 4-3-2. Neither black can contact 3
or 4. Connectivity leaves exactly three tree attachments:

\begin{verbatim}
0-1-2-3-4;
1-0-2-3-4;
0-2, 1-2, 2-3, 3-4.
\end{verbatim}

The only additional possibility would contain the triangle 0,1,2. Three
nonright Coxeter contacts give a nonpositive square on the positive
all-ones vector, with equality only for the affine simple triangle. In
the equality case its attached white 3 makes the proper four-node
diagram indefinite. Thus the triangle is impossible.

All edges in these five-node trees have finite labels at most 5. Indeed,
each edge belongs to a connected proper four-node principal diagram,
which must be positive semidefinite. An edge of magnitude at least
sqrt(3), together with an adjacent nonright edge, has a three-node Gram

kernel. Its connected fourth-node extension again contradicts

argument. Hence enumerating labels 3,4,5 is exhaustive, rather than a
search cutoff.

\section{Preferred corners and actual radical
relations}\label{preferred-corners-and-actual-radical-relations}

For each surviving context, the certificate checks all four adjacent
corners and chooses one whose marked roots lie in a connected component
of order at most 17. Every corner is decomposed into finite or affine
components. A new white can contact a finite component only at
normalized inverse-diagonal entries at most 2; it is orthogonal to an
affine component by the positive kernel. The two omitted black roots are
included separately in the possible contact domain.

In the radical cases the Gram has one negative direction and one null
direction. The radical gives an actual root relation: its linear
combination is orthogonal to a timelike vector in the core span and has
square zero, so it vanishes in the positive-definite perpendicular
space. For rationalized Grams, the positive diagonal scaling changes
coefficients but not their signs or zeros.

The selected contact domains contain no zero-radical coordinate. The
certificate assigns the two radical signs to the two marked pairs and
checks that any pair of opposite-sign contacts gives a marked path of
length at most 10 through the new root. Acuteness and the actual
relation force both signs whenever there is any contact. Hence every
additional supporting white is orthogonal to these cores. Their marked
components are isolated with order at most 17.

\section{Nonsingular cores and the residual norm
budget}\label{nonsingular-cores-and-the-residual-norm-budget}

All other surviving cores are nonsingular Lorentzian. In each preferred
corner, the allowed contact domain splits into two end sets, each within
distance 4 of its own marked pair. A root contacting both ends gives a
path of length at most 10. Within either end, the full inverse-Gram
block is strictly positive.

For a norm-two new root with core contact vector b, write its orthogonal
decomposition as e=e\_core+w. The perpendicular space is positive
definite, so

\begin{verbatim}
b^T G^{-1} b <= 2,     w^2 = 2-b^T G^{-1}b.
\end{verbatim}

Exact inverse entries show that two nonzero contacts at one end exceed
the budget. Every permitted diagonal is greater than 1, so the next
Coxeter magnitude sqrt(2) also exceeds the budget. Consequently a
nonorthogonal supporting white must have a sole contact -1 at a listed
node i. Its projection square h\_i=(G inverse)ii is one of

\begin{verbatim}
2, 3/2, 4/3,
\end{verbatim}

with residual square rho\_i=0,1/2,2/3, respectively.

There is at most one such core-contacting white in total. For each pair
of candidate nodes i,j, the exact certificate checks

\begin{verbatim}
((G inverse)ij)^2 > rho_i rho_j.
\end{verbatim}

If the inverse entry is positive, Cauchy's inequality makes the actual
product positive, violating acuteness. If negative, the actual product
is strictly negative and therefore creates an edge between the two new
whites. The certificate checks that this edge gives a marked path of
length at most 10. The same test with i=j excludes two distinct roots at
a single candidate node. In the zero-residual case the root is uniquely
determined in the core span as well.

It remains to control whites attached indirectly through that one root.
All other supporting whites are core-orthogonal. Their Gram E is a
positive-definite principal submatrix of W. If c is the extra root's
contact vector with these whites, projection gives

\begin{verbatim}
c^T E^{-1} c <= rho.
\end{verbatim}

Each contacted connected component costs at least 1/2. A connected
component of order at least two costs at least 2/3, and one of order at
least three costs at least 3/4. These bounds follow by projecting onto a
connected two- or three-node principal subdiagram through a contacted
node; the explicit inverse inequalities are proved in the
\href{fresh_distance10_extension_20261017.md}{supporting-extension
lemma}. Larger diagrams and additional contacts cannot lower projection
cost.

Thus rho=0 permits no attachment, rho=1/2 permits only one A1, and
rho=2/3 permits only one A1 or A2. This bounds the entire connected
attachment, with no ambient-rank cutoff. The core-contacting root plus
this tail adds at most one, two, or three nodes, respectively. Every
selected marked component still has order at most 17, as checked context
by context. This explicitly handles supporting extensions with positive
Euclidean residual; unchanged isolation is not assumed.

At an ideal corner, the inherited factor-fiber theorem places the entire
varying affine factor inside W plus the two side roots. The bounded
marked component is therefore the actual component relevant to payment.
Omitted spectator cusp walls cannot enlarge it. The argument includes
nonsimple cusps.

\section{Face payments and dimension
inequalities}\label{face-payments-and-dimension-inequalities}

Pay 1 on a corner pair if its distance is at most 10 or its connected
component has order at most 17, and 0 otherwise. The classification
above pays every quadrilateral at least 1. The inherited triangle
argument gives two paths of length at most 8, so every triangle receives

The inherited all-rank graph counts give finite vertex cost at most 10n.
At an ideal vertex with affine factor ranks r\_i and link vertex count
V=product(r\_i+1), factor-fiber multiplicity gives

C(v)/V <= sum min(10,r_i/2).

The shape inequality has normalized ideal curvature

kappa/V = 3d/4 - (5/2) E|sum X_i|,    d=n-1,

At ambient dimension 116, the profile (20,20,20,20,20,15) has margin

For a compact facet of dimension d=n-1, finite payments give

Every finite-sided, finite-volume real hyperbolic Coxeter polytope has
dimension at most136. The argument has no arithmeticity, compactness,
simple-cusp, factor-rank or facet-count restriction. For a chamber
having a compact facet, the ambient dimension is at most103.

proof} by replacing distance13 with distance12. As before, pairs in the
same connected corner component of order at most17 are also paid. The
new exception consists of two minimal cores sharing a terminal edge. A
Lorentzian Schur-complement argument isolates that core, replacing the
radical argument used for the previously known shared-vertex exception.

\section{Actual-face setup and complete core
domain}\label{actual-face-setup-and-complete-core-domain}

For an actual quadrilateral, let W be its supporting white roots and U,V
its opposite black pairs. Normalize roots to square two. W and W plus
any one black root are positive definite; W plus an adjacent black pair
is positive semidefinite. Each opposite pair gives an indefinite
diagram. Choose minimal indefinite cores L in W+U and M in W+V. Each
contains both its black roots; deleting either black root is positive
definite. Their proper principal subdiagrams are positive semidefinite.
