The complete high-order catalogue, of orders six through ten, has 384
marked contexts and maximum marked radius seven. Orders at most three
cannot participate in a disjoint unpaid join or overlap. Two cores of
order at most five cannot do so either. The remaining small/high cases
require a separate classification; they are not discarded by the old
distance-ten radius argument.

The small-core lemma proves that all order-four labels are at most six,
and all order-five labels at most five. It exhausts all weighted graphs,
obtaining 32 and 14 canonical minimal-indefinite types, respectively.
Black-deletion and port tests leave 104 low-first joining-label cases.
Eleven fail white positive definiteness; the other 93 have two negative
directions. Six multiple-edge choices have a white affine cycle. Of 30
low-first overlaps, 24 fail the inverse test and six have an isolated
marked corner of order at most 12. Reversing the cores covers the other
orientation. Both fork/radical and label-five/nonsingular overlap cores
are handled over all further supporting whites.

\section{High-order disjoint cores}\label{high-order-disjoint-cores}

An external supporting white contacting a node of a positive-definite
black deletion has squared projection at least that normalized inverse
diagonal. Thus a simple contact requires both deletion inverse diagonals
strictly below two. Among 1,262 high-order ports at marked distance at
least two, exactly 378 pass. Each distant cross edge has endpoint
distances summing to at least nine, giving 4,442 ordered possibilities.

For a simple edge between white ports x,y, eliminating the two white
blocks gives the necessary condition

\begin{verbatim}
(G_WL inverse)xx (G_WM inverse)yy < 1.
\end{verbatim}

It excludes 1,103 joins. For every remaining join, either one endpoint
black-deletion inverse diagonal is at least one, or twice the displayed
product is at least one. Therefore every magnitude at least sqrt(2)
violates an actual-edge or white positive-definiteness condition. All
labels at least four, parallel contacts and dotted contacts are
excluded. Every remaining cross edge is simple, without a label cutoff
assumption.

The 3,339 remaining joins have 85 underlying single-edge Gram types,
each with exactly two negative directions. Some context pairs admit
several candidate edges: 2,007 admit one, 348 admit two, 180 admit three
and 24 admit four. All 1,332 subsets with at least two edges have an
explicit nonnegative nonpositive-square witness in W plus one black.
Extra negative bonds only strengthen these witnesses. Every nonempty
cross-edge set is therefore impossible.

The producer rationalizes each required positive-definite principal
diagram separately. A full joined indefinite graph may have an odd
label-four cycle even though such a principal diagram is a forest. If a
principal graph itself has no rational sqrt(2) gauge, replacing its
nonright bonds by simple bonds gives an entrywise larger Z-matrix; a
nonnegative obstruction for that relaxation remains valid for the native
Gram. The certificate records the gauge or relaxation used for each
witness. No irrational Gram is silently treated as rational.

\section{High-order overlaps and fixed core
Grams}\label{high-order-overlaps-and-fixed-core-grams}

Every shared white has marked-distance sum at least ten. Both distances
are at least three. The source exhausts all injective partial
identifications of eligible nodes, checking every contact on shared
nodes. Of 312,316 candidates, 20,718 are consistent; inverse tests
exclude 18,721 and actual-edge witnesses exclude 1,048 more.

The remaining 949 marked contexts have 54 oriented literal core types.
All four adjacent corner decompositions are checked as finite/affine. An
extra bond between exclusive core parts either creates a path of length
at most nine (60,831 tests), or contradicts actual-edge positive
definiteness (888 tests). Thus the full Gram of each surviving core is
fixed before the extension argument is used.

At a selected corner, a further supporting white is orthogonal to every
affine component by its positive kernel. On each finite component, a
contact is possible only at normalized inverse diagonal at most two.
Omitted black roots are also retained in the possible contact domain.
This accounts for contacts anywhere in the core.

The ordinary argument handles 880 contexts. In a singular indefinite
core, its radical is an actual root relation in a Lorentzian
realization. The chosen contact domain avoids zero radical coordinates;
balancing its two signs forces a forbidden short path. In nonsingular
cores, projection onto the core leaves a positive-definite residual
space. Positive inverse end blocks and short-path tests force a single
simple contact. Pairwise residual Cauchy tests allow at most one
core-contacting white; the entire indirect tail is bounded by the lemma
below.

\section{A rank bound for all indirectly attached
roots}\label{a-rank-bound-for-all-indirectly-attached-roots}

Let E be a connected positive-definite Coxeter Gram of order m,
normalized to diagonal two. Every diagonal entry of E inverse is at
least m/(m+1). To prove this, write E=2I-A with A entrywise nonnegative.
Positive definiteness implies spectral radius(A)\textless2. Removing
bonds to a spanning tree and replacing its bond magnitudes by one
decreases A and therefore decreases the inverse entrywise, by the
convergent Neumann series.

At a chosen root of that unit tree, let its branches have orders m\_i.
Induction and Schur complementation give

\begin{verbatim}
(E inverse)root,root >= 1 / (2 - sum m_i/(m_i+1)).
\end{verbatim}

Since sum m\_i=m-1 and sum m\_i/(m\_i+1)\textgreater=(m-1)/m, the
required lower bound follows. The base case is the one-node Gram
{[}2{]}.

If a root of residual square rho contacts several orthogonal supporting
components, with total order m, its projection cost is at least the sum
of their order/(order+1) bounds, hence at least m/(m+1). Nonpositive
multiple contacts cannot decrease this cost because inverse entries are
nonnegative. Therefore, for rho\textless1,

\begin{verbatim}
m <= floor(rho/(1-rho)).
\end{verbatim}

This bounds the entire contacted components, including every indirect
tail. It is not a fixed-rank enumeration. Equality can occur for a
simple A\_m path contacted at an endpoint; rho=1 must be treated
separately.

\section{The new relevant-component
argument}\label{the-new-relevant-component-argument}

The remaining 69 contexts have a preferred marked component of order at
most 16 after all extensions. Some roots outside that component can have
residual square one, so bounding every external root by the preceding
lemma would be invalid. Only attachments that can enlarge the marked
component need to be controlled.

The exact inverse tests split each contact domain into two positive
inverse end blocks. Any contact at both ends gives a short marked path;
two contacts at one end already have projection square greater than two.
Thus each external core-contacting white has one contact. All candidate
projection squares are at least one. A projection-one node can have a
simple or label-four contact; every larger label exceeds the norm
budget. Every node that can directly enlarge the selected marked
component has projection square strictly greater than one, hence only a
simple contact.

If there is no such relevant contact, the marked component is isolated,
regardless of external attachments elsewhere. Otherwise call its new
white G, with residual vector g of square rho\textless1. Cauchy
inequalities and the Coxeter gap between -1 and zero exclude every other
relevant root. They also exclude all label-four external contacts in the
presence of G. At most one possible outside simple-contact node remains.
Call its root C and residual vector c.~It lies outside the marked
component and must be orthogonal to G: the allowed inner-product
interval has lower endpoint greater than -1, while acuteness requires a
nonpositive Coxeter product.

Write P for the positive product of the two core projections. Then
g.c=-P. If c has square less than one, two roots of its type cannot
coexist by the same positive-product test. If c has square one, two such
roots would have to be orthogonal with opposite unit residuals. Their
common product -P with g makes this impossible. Thus at most one C
coexists with G.

The exact surviving residual cases are:

Here S is the Gram of g,c, with negative off-diagonal entry -P. If C is
absent, every remaining white is core-orthogonal and the rank lemma
bounds G's entire tail. If det S=0, g and c have a positive linear
relation; nonpositive products force every core-orthogonal white to be
orthogonal to both, so no tail can join them.

If det S\textgreater0, its inverse is entrywise positive. A
core-orthogonal norm-two white contacting G has projection cost at least
(S inverse)GG. The value four excludes it. At the value two, equality
forces contacts (-1,0) to G,C and puts that white entirely in their
residual span, with negative coefficients. Its product with every other
core-orthogonal supporting white is then nonnegative; acuteness forces
zero. It is also orthogonal to C. Thus this one possible tail root
cannot lead to a longer tail or to C's other attachments. This
explicitly excludes an indirect bridge through an otherwise unbounded
projection-one attachment.

All preferred marked components in the 949 high-order cases have order
at most 17, and the small-core lemma gives at most 12. At ideal corners,
the inherited factor-fiber theorem places the entire varying affine
factor inside W plus the two marked sides. Omitted spectator cusp walls
cannot enlarge this component. No simple-cusp assumption is made.

\section{Payments and the dimension
conclusion}\label{payments-and-the-dimension-conclusion}

Pay one on a corner pair when its distance is at most nine, or when both
marks lie in a connected component of order at most 17. The complete
classification pays every quadrilateral at least one. The inherited
triangle argument supplies two paths of length at most eight, hence pays
each triangle at least two. Nonnegative weights suffice for larger
polygons, giving total payment at least 5-k on a k-gonal two-face.

The inherited all-rank finite/affine path, cycle and fork counts give
finite cost at most 9n. Small components of order at most 17 have total
pair cost at most eight times their order, so the extra payment does not
break that bound. At a cusp with affine ranks r\_i and link vertex count
V=product(r\_i+1), cost divided by V is at most sum min(9,r\_i/2).

The shape inequality and convex-order transfer apply with cap 18. For
link dimensions d=108 through 115, the reduced profiles consist of
copies of 18, at most one smaller positive part and at most one larger
part. All 756 profiles have positive curvature-minus-cost, with minimum
45873/2476099 at six copies of 18. The finite slack is also positive in
ambient dimensions 109 through 116. The completed 116 theorem excludes
the higher tail, giving dimension at most 108.

At ambient 108, the profile (18,18,18,18,18,17) has margin -4659/260642.
The same scalar weights do not prove 107; that profile is not a
finite-volume realization.

For a compact facet of dimension d=n-1, finite payments imply
beta\_d\textless9(d+1). At d=79+2t and 80+2t, eight times the opposite
difference has coefficient lists (12,160,4) and (88,164,4),
respectively. Both are positive for all t\textgreater=0. Therefore
d\textless=78 and ambient dimension is at most 79.

The finite classifications and numerical inequalities are exact. The
written geometric and all-rank arguments remain explicit mathematical
inputs. This package makes no construction, external-refereeing,
proof-assistant or publication-priority claim.

\section{Mathematical review}\label{mathematical-review}

No gap was found in the stated geometric composition. An actual edge
supplies the strict positive-definiteness needed in the port tests,
including when its endpoints are ideal. A nonnegative nonpositive-square
witness remains an obstruction after adding or strengthening acute
bonds. Disjoint cores with no cross bond already have two negative

A singular indefinite core has an actual linear root relation: its Gram
radical represents a null vector orthogonal to a timelike vector, and

so the norm projection and Cauchy inequalities apply. Every nonzero

positive inverse blocks and the short-path alternatives consequently
control all contacts, rather than just chosen one-node recipes.

The general inverse-diagonal bound m/(m+1) for a connected
positive-definite Coxeter Gram is valid by inverse monotonicity to a

indirectly attached component, including nodes not directly contacting
the new wall. At residual square one it does not give a finite rank

component instead. The separate69-context review closes the possible
bridge through an outside projection-one root: positive residual
relations force orthogonality, and the inverse-diagonal-two equality

tail-rank bound at residual one would be invalid.

At an ideal corner the actual factor-fiber lemma places the entire
varying affine factor in the supporting whites plus the marked pair.

The inherited triangle payment, all-rank finite/affine graph counts,

scalar contradiction applies in ambient109 through116; the previously
completed116 theorem covers the higher tail. The compact-facet

\chapter{An affine-A corner of a quadrilateral is paid in every
rank}\label{an-affine-a-corner-of-a-quadrilateral-is-paid-in-every-rank}

Let P be a finite-volume hyperbolic Coxeter n-polytope, with every
vertex simple and n\textgreater=14. If an actual quadrilateral has a
corner whose full n-node diagram is affine A\_(n-1), then the
\href{fresh_simple_cusp_vinberg_weight_frontier_20261017.md}{proposed
mixed weight} pays that quadrilateral: either the two marked roots at
this corner have cycle distance at most3, or the marked roots at the
opposite corner are adjacent. This resolves the complete affine-A-cycle
branch, with no bound on labels or arc lengths. Other affine corner
types remain outside this result; \textbf{no new ambient dimension bound
is asserted}.

The
\href{../scripts/fresh_simple_cusp_affine_a_quadrilateral_20261017.py}{checker}
and \href{fresh_simple_cusp_affine_a_quadrilateral_20261017.json}{data}
use exact Fraction arithmetic in Q(sqrt(2)), a formal determinant
expansion, and256 rectangle-corner checks. The argument below explains
why these finite checks certify all ranks rather than a bounded search.

\section{Geometry and complete replacement
profiles}\label{geometry-and-complete-replacement-profiles}

Use roots of norm2. Write a,b for the two marked roots of the affine
corner, c opposite a, and d opposite b in the quadrilateral. If a,b have
cycle distance\textless=3, the ideal weight already pays. Otherwise the
two cycle arcs have edge lengths P,Q\textgreater=4, P+Q=n.~Deleting a,b
leaves the white diagram W=A\_(P-1)+A\_(Q-1). The roots a,b attach to
the first and last ends, respectively, of both paths. In particular
a.b=0.

The actual adjacent corner W+b+c is either spherical or, if ideal, a
connected affine diagram on n nodes. The old diagram W+b is the single
long path A\_(n-1). Consequently its complete one-root extension list
is:

\endhead
\bottomrule\noalign{}
\endlastfoot
none & A\_(n-1)+A1 \\

one bond4 at either endpoint & B\_n \\
one bond3 at either next-to-end node & D\_n \\
bonds3 at both endpoints & affine A\_(n-1) \\
\end{longtable}
}

This is a classification argument in every n\textgreater=14. A new root
touching the connected old path produces an irreducible diagram of order
n. Exceptional finite and affine types are too small. Among the
classical finite and affine diagrams, deleting one node to leave the
entire path A\_(n-1) gives precisely the displayed possibilities. In
particular the other three large affine types do not have such a
deletion. The finite and affine classification is the standard primary
input recalled in
\href{https://www.mathnet.ru/php/getFT.phtml?jrnid=mmo&option_lang=rus&paperid=444&what=fullt}{Vinberg,
section2}.

Here the endpoints and next-to-end nodes lie near a, not b, because both

list for d uses the last ends near b and gives d.a=0. The isolated A1
profile is explicitly retained; its height comes from its omitted-root
contact with a or b.

If c.d\textless0, the opposite corner has adjacent marked roots, so it
is paid by either the finite or ideal rule. It remains to contradict
c.d=0. Write x=-c.a\textgreater=0 and y=-d.b\textgreater=0. Each is an
arbitrary Coxeter contact: zero, 2cos(pi/m) for m\textgreater=3,
parallel2, or dotted\textgreater2. No arithmetic field restriction is
imposed on x,y.

\section{Small affine diagrams force uniform height

Let w be c's vector of nonnegative contact magnitudes with W, and put
h=x+sum(w). The complete low-contact exclusions are:

\section{Exact Schur identity}\label{exact-schur-identity}

Set a0=1/P, b0=1/Q, alpha=a0+b0. The norm2 A\_(P-1) inverse is

\begin{verbatim}
J_ij=min(i,j)*(P-max(i,j))/P,  1<=i,j<=P-1.
\end{verbatim}

After eliminating W, the residual a,b Gram is
alpha{[}{[}1,-1{]},{[}-1,1{]}{]}. For c define

\begin{verbatim}
B=v_b^t J w,  C=2-w^t Jw,
\end{verbatim}

and for d define A=v\_a\^{}t Jz, D=2-z\^{}t Jz. Finally E=w\^{}t Jz.
Here v\_a,v\_b are the nonnegative old endpoint contact vectors and J is
the inverse Gram of all W. Since the first and last inverse rows sum
entrywise to1, the residual a.c product is B-h and the residual b.d
product is A-k. Under the remaining assumption c.d=0, the full residual
matrix in order a,b,c,d is

\begin{verbatim}
S = [[ alpha, -alpha, B-h,   -A  ],
     [-alpha,  alpha, -B,    A-k ],
     [ B-h,    -B,     C,    -E  ],
     [-A,      A-k,   -E,     D  ]].
\end{verbatim}

The actual quadrilateral star has n+2 roots in Lorentz dimension n+1,
rank n+1, negative index1 and corank1. In particular det S=0. The formal
24-permutation determinant check gives

\begin{verbatim}
det S=(hk-kB-hA)^2-alpha*(C*k^2+D*h^2+2E*h*k).             (1)
\end{verbatim}

Only this necessary determinant condition will be needed. No Gram matrix
with the wrong rank or signature is promoted to an actual face.

For each profile introduce its two endpoint moments l=(l1,l2) and c0:

{\def\LTcaptype{none} % do not increment counter
\begin{longtable}[]{@{}llr@{}}
\toprule\noalign{}
Profile & l & c0 \\
\midrule\noalign{}

isolated & (0,0) & 2 \\
endpoint3 on arc i & unit vector e\_i & 1 \\
endpoint4 on arc i & sqrt(2)e\_i & 0 \\

both endpoints3 & (1,1) & 0 \\

}

Then B=a0\emph{l1+b0}l2 and C=c0+a0\emph{l1\textsuperscript{2+b0*l2}2.
For the d-profile write m,d0; then A=a0}m1+b0\emph{m2,
D=d0+a0}m1\textsuperscript{2+b0*m2}2 and E=a0\emph{l1}m1+b0\emph{l2}m2.
The latter formula includes the boundary P=4: the two next-to-end
positions can coincide, and the same inverse formula still gives4/P.

Put u=1/h\textgreater0, v=1/k\textgreater0 and L=u\emph{l+v}m.
Dividing(1) by h\textsuperscript{2*k}2 and substituting the displayed
expressions yields

\begin{verbatim}
F=1-2(a0*L1+b0*L2)
    -(a0+b0)*(c0*u^2+d0*v^2)-a0*b0*(L1-L2)^2 = 0.      (2)
\end{verbatim}

\section{The all-rank strict
inequality}\label{the-all-rank-strict-inequality}

Use the conservative closed bounds

\begin{verbatim}
u<=1/sqrt(2)                    for isolated,
u<=sqrt(2)-1                    for endpoint3/4 or next-to-end3,
u<=1-sqrt(2)/2                  for both endpoints3,
\end{verbatim}

and likewise for v. For fixed a0,b0\textgreater0, F is jointly concave
in(u,v): its quadratic part is the sum of a negative diagonal quadratic
and a negative square. Therefore its minimum on each closed height
rectangle is attained at a rectangle corner.

At the enlarged reciprocal-arc values a0=b0=1/4, the exact checker tests
all8\emph{8}4=256 corners in Q(sqrt(2)). Every value is nonnegative.
Exactly three values are zero: both isolated profiles at their upper
bounds, and the two choices of both next-to-end3 profiles on the same
arc at their upper bounds. These are the only finite algebraic checks
needed; concavity covers every real height in every rectangle.

Finally, for u,v\textgreater0 both partial derivatives with respect to
a0,b0 are strictly negative. For example

\begin{verbatim}
dF/da0=-2*L1-(c0*u^2+d0*v^2)-b0*(L1-L2)^2 < 0.
\end{verbatim}

All terms are nonpositive. If L1=0 and the middle term vanishes, some
nonzero moment remains in L2 and the last term is negative; if both
moments vanish, both profiles are isolated and the middle term is
negative. The other derivative is identical with the two arcs exchanged.

Actual P,Q\textgreater=4 and P+Q\textgreater=14 give a0,b0\textless=1/4
with at least one strict. Hence F(actual
a0,b0;u,v)\textgreater F(1/4,1/4;u,v)\textgreater=0, contradicting(2).
Thus c.d cannot vanish. Its negative native product makes the opposite
marked pair adjacent, proving the asserted quadrilateral payment.

\chapter{Global affine exclusion and the all-simple dimension
bound61}\label{global-affine-exclusion-and-the-all-simple-dimension-bound61}

Let P be a finite-sided finite-volume hyperbolic Coxeter polytope in
H\^{}n. If every ideal vertex of P is simple, then
\textbf{n\textless=61}. Finite vertices of an acute-angled polytope are
automatically simple. The statement permits both finite and ideal
vertices and requires no arithmetic hypothesis.

The key structural fact is stronger than a restriction on black
deletions: \textbf{every connected affine subdiagram of an all-simple P
has exactly n nodes}. Consequently, when n\textgreater=10, every minimal
indefinite subdiagram of order at most10 is Lanner, and every actual
simplex face has dimension at most4. Supporting white roots, including
affine subdiagrams containing every black root, are covered by this
global argument.

The
\href{../scripts/fresh_simple_cusp_affine_exclusion_20261017.py}{checker}
and \href{fresh_simple_cusp_affine_exclusion_20261017.json}{saved
certificate} give the small exact radius, graph-cost, and threshold
checks. This is a fresh successor to the frozen
\href{fresh_simple_cusp_distance_bound_20261017.md}{distance15 proof}.
Its compact-facet conclusion n\textless=127 remains unchanged. The
unrestricted finite-volume bound163 remains unchanged: arbitrary ideal
vertices need not be simple. No novelty or current-best published-bound
claim is made.

\section{An affine diagram must be a whole simple
cusp}\label{an-affine-diagram-must-be-a-whole-simple-cusp}

Use outward spacelike normals e\_i and a future timelike strict interior
point H, so H.e\_i\textless0. Distinct normals have nonpositive
products. Let C be a connected affine principal subdiagram. Its Gram
matrix has a strictly positive kernel vector (c\_i). Define

\begin{verbatim}
z = sum_{i in C} c_i e_i.
\end{verbatim}

Then z\^{}2=0, z.e\_i=0 for i in C, and z.e\_j\textless=0 for every
other wall j. Moreover H.z\textless0, so z is nonzero and lies on the
future null sheet. Thus {[}z{]} is a feasible point at infinity of P.

The projective closure of a finite-volume polytope is a finite convex
polytope contained in the closed Klein ball. Every point of this closure
on the boundary sphere is extreme: strict convexity of the ball forbids
expressing it as a nontrivial convex combination of two distinct points
of the closed ball. Hence {[}z{]} is an actual ideal vertex, not merely
a feasible direction unrelated to the vertex set. Every wall of C
contains this vertex.

At an ideal vertex the Euclidean link is a product of simplices. A
simple vertex has exactly n incident walls, so its (n-1)-dimensional
link is one simplex; its entire Coxeter diagram is connected affine of
order n. Every proper principal subdiagram of this connected affine
diagram is positive definite. Since it contains C, which is singular, C
must be the whole diagram. In particular,

\begin{verbatim}
order(C) = n.                                      (1)
\end{verbatim}

The primary
\href{https://ems.press/content/serial-article-files/43032}{Potyagailo--Vinberg
paper, printed pp.64 and69} states the finite/ideal local face structure
and the finite-volume projective convex-hull convention used here. The
positive-kernel and strict-convexity argument above supplies the
particular global conclusion. There is also direct primary confirmation
in \href{https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/0502413}{Felikson--Tumarkin,
Section1, PDF pp.3--4}: every parabolic subdiagram lies in an
ideal-vertex diagram, and a simple ideal vertex has a connected
parabolic diagram. Their displayed condition(iii), that parabolic
diagrams have order n, uses these simplicity facts; it does not use the
all-ideal assumption needed for their separate condition(ii) excluding
elliptic diagrams of order n.~We use only the former implication in the
mixed-vertex class.

\section{Consequences for small indefinite
stars}\label{consequences-for-small-indefinite-stars}

An inclusion-minimal indefinite principal diagram L is Lanner or
quasi-Lanner: if a proper principal subdiagram is affine, take one
connected affine component C. Any outside node coupled to its positive
kernel makes C plus that node indefinite. Minimality forces L to be
exactly C plus that node. Thus a quasi-Lanner diagram of order at most10
contains a connected affine diagram of order at most9.

For n\textgreater=10 this contradicts (1). Therefore every minimal
indefinite diagram of order at most10 is Lanner and has order at most5.
These classification inputs are the same ones used in the frozen
\href{fresh_multi_ideal_triangle_scope_20261017.md}{original-star
simplex proof}. The checker additionally reads all26 high-rank
quasi-Lanner diagrams and confirms that their listed affine deletions
are connected and of order at most9; it does not repeat their
classification.

In an actual k-simplex face, the original star has n-k supporting white
roots and k+1 black roots. Every indefinite principal subdiagram
contains all black roots, because deleting any black leaves normals at
an actual finite or ideal vertex. The original-star proof gives a
minimal L of order at most10. Hence for n\textgreater=10,

\begin{verbatim}
k+1 <= order(L) <= 5,  so k<=4.                    (2)
\end{verbatim}

In particular actual simplex faces of dimensions7,8,9 are all excluded,
not just the dimension9 case. No assumption that an induced face is a
Coxeter simplex is made. Equation (1) also handles the formerly delicate
white affine deletion containing every black node; that affine diagram
produces its own actual cusp elsewhere in P and is too small.

\section{Triangle and quadrilateral payments at
distance7}\label{triangle-and-quadrilateral-payments-at-distance7}

Retain the original-wall-star and graph-distance conventions of the
distance15 proof. Put weight1 at a polygon corner when its two side
normals are joined by a path of length at most7 within that corner's
incident diagram, and weight0 otherwise.

For a triangle, a minimal indefinite star contains its three black
nodes. It is now Lanner of order at most5. The tree joining the three
marked nodes has at least two marked-to-marked paths whose interiors
avoid the third black node. Each has length at most
order(L)-2\textless=3. These paths lie in actual corner diagrams, so
every triangle receives at least2.

For a quadrilateral, each opposite pair together with its white support
is indefinite. Otherwise the positive-definite common-face argument or
the nonzero feasible affine-kernel argument would put a finite or ideal
point in two disjoint CLOSED opposite edges. This remains impossible for
quadrilaterals with ideal vertices. Each resulting minimal indefinite
diagram L or M contains both opposite black nodes and has order at
most5.

In a connected N-node graph with two marked nodes, the distance of any
node to the nearer mark is at most N-2: a shortest path to their set has
no marked interior nodes. Hence this radius is at most3 for L and M. The
two indefinite diagrams cannot be disjoint and orthogonal, because that
would give two negative directions in a Lorentz space. They either
overlap or have a joining edge. Joining their paths and taking a
shortest path between their two black sets gives length at most

\begin{verbatim}
3+1+3 = 7.                                        (3)
\end{verbatim}

Its interior has only white nodes; its endpoints are consecutive sides,
so it lies in an actual corner diagram. Every quadrilateral receives at
least1. The checker confirms the radius bound for every connected simple
graph of orders2 through5 and every marked pair, rather than assuming a
particular list of low-order Coxeter diagrams.

\section{The vertex cost is at most7n, in every
rank}\label{the-vertex-cost-is-at-most7n-in-every-rank}

At a finite vertex the n incident normals form a finite Coxeter forest.
At a simple ideal vertex they form a connected affine diagram on n
nodes. For paths, cycles, single forks and double forks, the all-rank
formulas proved in the preceding distance15 report give at most N
unordered pairs at each positive fixed graph distance. Therefore the
total number at distance at most7 is at most7N. Summing over finite
components gives7n.

The exceptional connected finite/affine diagrams have at most9 nodes, so
even all their unordered pairs number at most4N\textless=7N. This
includes the affine D4 four-leaf star, separated from the double-fork
formula. No finite rank cutoff is used. The checker reconfirms the new
cost for all245 independently counted classical graphs and the seven
saved exceptional graphs; the inherited analytic formulas establish all
ranks.

Thus the total polygon-corner weight is at most7n f\_0(P), while the
triangle/quadrilateral payments give at
least2f\_2\textsuperscript{\{(3)\}+f\_2}\{(4)\}.

\section{Strict h-vector threshold}\label{strict-h-vector-threshold}

The projective closure of P is simple. The same strict simple-polytope
h-vector inequality used in the frozen distance proof gives

\begin{verbatim}
2 f_2^{(3)} + f_2^{(4)} > b_n f_0(P),
b_n = n(n-6)/8                 if n is even,
      (n-1)(n-5)/8             if n is odd.
\end{verbatim}

Consequently b\_n\textless7n. For n=62+2t and n=63+2t, respectively,

\begin{verbatim}
8(b_n-7n) = 4t^2+124t,
             4t^2+128t+68.
\end{verbatim}

Both are nonnegative for every integer t\textgreater=0. Equality at n=62
still contradicts the STRICT lower inequality. Therefore n\textless=61.
Dimensions n\textless=9, where the preceding Lanner reduction was not
invoked, already satisfy this conclusion.

\section{Verification and limits}\label{verification-and-limits-8}

Generation and a fresh saved replay pass: 7,521 marked low-order graph
checks, all26 high-rank affine-deletion checks, and245 inherited
classical graph-cost checks. Syntax, nine direct source hashes, and
report links pass. The
\href{fresh_simple_cusp_affine_exclusion_20261017_review.md}{independent
mathematical/source review} finds no gap and explicitly does not claim a
duplicate arithmetic replay. The checker uses exact integers/Fractions
and frozen source manifests. The polynomial identities and graph
formulas, not the finite confirmation ranges, justify the unbounded
dimension and rank claims. No optimizer, arithmetic field restriction,
or induced-face Coxeter assumption enters the proof.

This lemma supplies neither an unrestricted bound61 nor a construction.
The mixed-vertex all-simple class differs from the simple ALL-IDEAL
class, for which
\href{https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/0502413}{Felikson--Tumarkin} prove the
stronger dimension bound8. No transfer of that all-ideal result to the
mixed case is used here.

This review read the
\href{../scripts/fresh_simple_cusp_affine_exclusion_20261017.py}{successor
source}, its
\href{fresh_simple_cusp_affine_exclusion_20261017.json}{saved data}, the

\section{Affine subdiagrams and actual ideal
vertices}\label{affine-subdiagrams-and-actual-ideal-vertices}

For a connected affine principal diagram, its positive kernel gives a
normal combination \(z\) with \(z^2=0\). It is not the zero vector: its
product with a common strict future timelike interior point is strictly
negative. This also fixes its future orientation. Its products with all
other outward wall normals are nonpositive by acuteness, so it is a
feasible null ray.

Finite volume matters at the next step. The projective closure is a
finite convex polytope contained in the closed Klein ball. Strict
convexity of that ball makes every feasible boundary-sphere point
extreme; therefore this ray is an actual ideal vertex. It cannot be
merely an unattained direction or an interior point of a larger
projective face. All roots in the affine diagram belong to its
incident-wall diagram.

At a simple ideal vertex the Euclidean link is one simplex. Its full
incident diagram is irreducible affine of order \(n\); every proper
principal subdiagram is positive definite. The original singular affine
diagram must consequently be the whole incident diagram. This argument
includes affine subdiagrams consisting of white roots or containing all
marked black roots.

The primary
\href{https://ems.press/content/serial-article-files/43032}{Potyagailo--Vinberg
paper, printed pp.64 and69} supplies the local link structure and
finite-volume convex-hull convention. There is also direct support in
\href{https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/0502413}{Felikson--Tumarkin, Section1,
PDF pp.3--4}: parabolic subdiagrams extend into ideal-vertex diagrams,
and a simple ideal vertex has connected parabolic diagram. Their
condition(iii) follows from simplicity; their different condition(ii),
excluding elliptic diagrams of order \(n\), uses the all-ideal
hypothesis. The present mixed-vertex argument does not import
condition(ii).

\section{Minimal cores and payments}\label{minimal-cores-and-payments}

The inherited classification of inclusion-minimal indefinite diagrams
gives Lanner or quasi-Lanner order at most10. A non-Lanner minimal core
has a connected affine proper subdiagram of order at most9. This
contradicts the affine order \(n\) result when \(n\ge10\). Thus every
minimal indefinite core used in the argument is Lanner of order at
most5. Smaller ambient dimensions already satisfy the final bound.

For an actual simplex face, deleting any black side root leaves roots at
a finite or ideal vertex, hence a positive-semidefinite block. Every
indefinite subdiagram therefore contains all black roots. The usual
minimal-core argument then gives simplex dimension at most4, without
assuming the induced simplex has Coxeter angles.

For a triangle, a spanning tree of its minimal core has two paths
joining pairs of black nodes without the third in their interiors; each
has length at most \(5-2=3\). For a quadrilateral, opposite-side blocks
are indefinite: a positive-definite block would produce a finite common
point, and an affine block a feasible ideal common point, contradicting
disjointness of the \textbf{closed} opposite polygon edges. Each
opposite minimal core contains both marked roots and has radius at most3
from that pair. The two cores must overlap or have a joining edge, since
two disjoint orthogonal indefinite blocks would give two negative
directions. A shortest path between their black sets has only white
interior nodes and length at most7. It belongs to an actual corner
diagram.

Consequently distance7 corner weights pay at least2 on triangles and at
least1 on quadrilaterals, including ideal corners. This does not assume
all polygon vertices are finite.

\section{All ranks and strict
threshold}\label{all-ranks-and-strict-threshold}

The inherited path, cycle, single-fork and double-fork formulas give at
most \(N\) unordered pairs at each fixed positive graph distance. In
particular the affine double-fork family is included in every rank. The
small exceptional finite/affine diagrams have order at most9, so all
their pairs total at most \(4N\le7N\). The affine D4 four-leaf star is
treated as an exception. Thus every finite rank-\(n\) forest and every
simple affine order-\(n\) vertex costs at most \(7n\). Finite sampled
ranks merely confirm these explicit formulas; they do not stand in for a
tail proof.

The strict simple-polytope lower bound is

\texttt{
b\_n=\textbackslash{}begin\{cases\}n(n-6)/8\&n\textbackslash{}text\{\ even\},\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}(n-1)(n-5)/8\&n\textbackslash{}text\{\ odd\}.\textbackslash{}end\{cases\}
}

Independent substitution gives

\[
8(b_{62+2t}-7(62+2t))=4t^2+124t,
\qquad
8(b_{63+2t}-7(63+2t))=4t^2+128t+68.
\]

Both are nonnegative for every integer \(t\ge0\). Equality at62 is
excluded because the lower payment inequality is strict. Hence
\(n\le61\).

The checker uses exact arithmetic, preserves source manifests and
implements the stated checks. Its finite threshold loop confirms
polynomial identities whose displayed algebra supplies the unbounded
tail. This is an internal proof/source review, not external refereeing
or formal proof-assistant verification. No novelty or
best-published-bound assertion is supported or needed. The published
simple \textbf{all-ideal} bound8 has a different hypothesis.

\chapter{All classical affine-tree quadrilateral corners: proposed
completion}\label{all-classical-affine-tree-quadrilateral-corners-proposed-completion}

\textbf{Final internally reviewed lemma: generation and fresh saved
replay PASS.} Scope: an all-simple finite-volume hyperbolic Coxeter
polytope of dimension n\textgreater=18, with the weights in the
\href{fresh_simple_cusp_vinberg_weight_frontier_20261017.md}{frozen
interface}. The theorem proved below is that every quadrilateral having
an affine B/C/D corner receives its required payment. The
all-finite-corner transfer is a separate obligation; no dimension bound
is asserted here.

Normalize every root to square2. Denote the old ideal corner by W+a+b,
and the other corners by W+b+c, W+a+d, W+c+d.~Assume the old corner is
unpaid. Then a,b have graph distance at least4 and are not together in
either prescribed six-node end segment. If any of b.c, a.d, c.d is
nonzero, the corresponding corner is paid immediately. We therefore
impose all three products zero. All one-root extensions below must be
spherical, or must be the entire connected affine diagram of order n: a
smaller affine component is forbidden by the
\href{fresh_simple_cusp_affine_exclusion_20261017.md}{global simple-cusp
lemma}.

\section{Cusp normalization and the common Schur
identity}\label{cusp-normalization-and-the-common-schur-identity}

In an affine tree give cusp coefficient1 to every main-path node and
fork center, coefficient1/sqrt(2) to a terminal node on a bond4, and
coefficient1/2 to a fork leaf. Write the null vector as nu=sum nu\_i
n\_i. Replace the marked roots in the Schur calculation by nu\_a\emph{a
and nu\_b}b, leaving c,d at norm2. The scaled old Gram is a graph
Laplacian: conductance1 on a main-path or terminal bond4 edge, and
conductance1/2 on a fork edge. Its effective resistance between a,b is
R. Eliminating W gives the marked block
R\^{}-1{[}{[}1,-1{]},{[}-1,1{]}{]}.

For c write h=-c.nu\textgreater0, and similarly k for d.~Positivity
follows directly: all old contacts are nonpositive and every cusp
coefficient is positive; equality would make c orthogonal to all n cusp
normals, hence proportional to their nonzero null direction, contrary to
c\^{}2=2. If its contacts are localized at the a end, its residual
square and cross contact to the scaled b have the form C=c0+l\^{}2/R and
B=l/R. For d use D=d0+m\^{}2/R and A=m/R. Provided the contact supports
do not cross along the surviving path, the projection cross term is
E=lm/R. Consequently the
\href{fresh_simple_cusp_affine_a_quadrilateral_20261017.md}{formal
four-root determinant identity} gives

\texttt{det\ Schur/(h\^{}2\ k\^{}2)\ =\ 1-(g\_c+g\_d)/R}, where
\texttt{g\_c=2l/h+c0/h\^{}2}.

After eliminating the n−2 independent white roots, all four residual
normals lie in a three-dimensional Lorentz space. The residual a,b,c
determinant is −R\^{}-1 h\^{}2\textless0, so their span has rank3 and
the four-root Schur matrix has exactly corank1. In particular its
determinant is zero. A strict positive lower bound is a contradiction.
Here is an explicit all-rank derivation. In the scaled white coordinates
the Dirichlet inverse is the Green matrix of the weighted tree grounded
at a,b. Put resistance coordinate z along their unique path. For two
separated contact supports, with left coordinate z and right coordinate
z', the Green entry is z(R-z')/R. Multiplying by the cusp coefficients
in the native contact vectors gives E=lm/R. A left diagonal entry equals
its one-ended tree value minus z\^{}2/R. A branch off the path adds its
common branch resistance to that one-ended value. Thus ordinary first
and second path nodes give (c0,l)=(1,1),(0,2); a bond4 to the first
gives (0,sqrt(2)). At a fork-leaf mark, its mate lies on a resistance2
branch attached at z=2 and has cusp coefficient1/2, yielding (1,1), or
(0,sqrt(2)) for a bond4. These identities give every displayed terminal
row. Outer components grounded directly at a have z=0, yielding the
arbitrary outer cost q and zero cross moment. The two exceptional E8
supports overlap these local regions and are computed separately. No
finite-rank cutoff is used.

There are three exhaustive positions for a marked root: a main-path
node, including a fork center; a terminal bond4 node; or a fork leaf.
Two terminal marks at the same fork are already paid. The cases below
exhaust the remaining possibilities, up to exchanging a,b.

\section{Main-path marks, including fork
centers}\label{main-path-marks-including-fork-centers}

Let P be their graph distance. The outer components beyond a have type
B\_r, r\textgreater=1, or D\_r, r\textgreater=2; D2 here means two
orthogonal A1 leaves, with a their common fork center. There are P-1
intervening white path nodes and an analogous outer end beyond b. The
total order is n=r+s+P+1 and R=P.

The
\href{fresh_simple_cusp_affine_tree_short_ends_20261017.md}{short-end
proof} applies to B\_r and D\_r, r\textgreater=3. Its outer inverse
formulas and arbitrary-contact argument do not require an upper bound on
r. Add D2 with J=I/2, old attachment v=(1,1), and t=Jv=(1/2,1/2). For a
nonnegative outer contact vector w let q=w\^{}T Jw\textless2 and
t0=v\^{}T Jw. The strict inequality follows because W+c supports an
actual edge and is positive definite, so its subdiagram consisting of
the outer block and c is positive definite. If the opposite native
magnitude x=-a.c is at least1, q\textgreater=t0\^{}2 and
t0\textgreater=1/2 give \texttt{(2-q)/(x+t0)\^{}2\textless{}=1}. If x=0
and at least two outer contacts are nonzero, t0\textgreater=1 gives
q+t0\^{}2\textgreater=2. A single outer contact of magnitude1 creates a
proper affine E8 with arms1,2,5; magnitude sqrt(2) creates a proper
affine B4 (one doubled terminal arm at a fork). Thus any remaining
single contact has magnitude d\textgreater=phi\textgreater3/2, and its
contribution is \texttt{8/d\^{}2-2\textless{}14/9}.

When c joins the inner component to D2, classification gives either one
leaf by a bond3 (the other A1 remains separate), or both leaves by
bonds3. The inner contact is always a bond3 at its long endpoint. The
respective outer data (q,t0) are (1/2,1/2) and (1,1), with
h\textgreater=1+t0. Their contributions \texttt{2/h+(1-q)/h\^{}2} are at
most14/9 and1. A doubled bond to a single leaf would create a proper
affine component beside the unused A1; a bond5 cannot occur in a large
finite classical component. All other B/D joins are the complete
short-end list and contribute at most13/9. Isolated and inner-only
profiles contribute at most1 by the same proper affine B/D, A2 and
small-star exclusions as in that proof. Hence every ordinary main-path
profile has g\textless=14/9.

The only additional finite one-root extensions when an inner component
is small are D6 to E7 and D7 to E8. B\_j with j\textgreater=5 and D\_j
with j\textgreater=8 only admit the long-end bond3 finite extension.
Here a small inner rank is r+P\textless=8; since P\textgreater=4 and
n\textgreater=18 the opposite outer component has rank\textgreater=9. D6
to E7 is directly paid, since every pair in a finite component of
order\textless=7 is paid. D7 means either r=2,P=5 or r=3,P=4. In the
first case the marked a is the E8 branching vertex, so Vinberg's finite
special-vertex lemma pays it
(\href{https://www.mathnet.ru/php/getFT.phtml?jrnid=mmo&option_lang=rus&paperid=444&what=fullt}{original
paper, §6.3, printed p81}). The second case is treated below. Thus in
every nonexceptional case

\texttt{det\ Schur/(h\^{}2\ k\^{}2)\textgreater{}=1-28/(9P)\textgreater{}=2/9\textgreater{}0}.

\subsection{The main-path D3/P4 to E8
exception}\label{the-main-path-d3p4-to-e8-exception}

Use an old D-type end whose fork center is0, fork leaves are L,L', and a
is the next main-path node1. Let b be main-path node5. The new d has its
single bond3 to L', so W+a+d has an E8 component. The arbitrary opposite
contact is y=-b.d and k=y+1/2. At y=0 the old affine tree plus d
contains a proper affine E8, so y\textgreater=1 and v=1/k\textless=2/3.
Exact elimination gives alpha=1/4, A=1/2, D=5/4.

An outer-only c makes c,d belong to the same spherical component of
W+c+d of order at most5; that corner is paid. The remaining c profiles
and normalized determinant bounds are:

{\def\LTcaptype{none} % do not increment counter
\begin{longtable}[]{@{}llll@{}}
\toprule\noalign{}
c profile & reciprocal bound & normalized determinant & lower bound \\
\midrule\noalign{}
\endhead
\bottomrule\noalign{}
\endlastfoot
isolated & u\^{}2\textless=1/2 & 1-v-v\textsuperscript{2/16-u}2/2 &
1/18 \\
inner-only bond3 & u\textless=1/2 & 1-u/2-v-(2u-v)\^{}2/16 & 11/144 \\
join through fork center & u\textless=1/2 & 1-u/2-v-v\^{}2/16 & 1/18 \\
join through one fork leaf & u\textless=2/5 & 1-u/2-v-(u+v)\^{}2/16 &
14/225 \\
\end{longtable}
}

For the leaf join, x=0 creates an affine A4 cycle, so
h=x+3/2\textgreater=5/2. The displayed expression uses the larger cross
projection E=3/4 when c,d use the same leaf; the other leaf has E=1/4
and improves it. The inner-only and leaf-join quadratics are concave, so
their minima on the stated rectangles occur at corners. Every bound is
strictly positive.

\section{A terminal bond4 mark}\label{a-terminal-bond4-mark}

Let a be that terminal node. An unpaid old pair has graph distance
P\textgreater=6 from a to a main-path b; R=P and nu\_a=1/sqrt(2).
Deleting a leaves a large finite B or D diagram. Its complete
finite-or-connected-affine one-node extensions are: isolated; bond3 to
its long endpoint; bond4 to that endpoint; or bond3 to its next node.
The last two are full affine extensions. This list follows by deleting
the new node in the classical finite/affine diagrams: finite B/D permits
only an added long-end bond3 at rank\textgreater=9; affine C/B adds a
long-end bond4, and affine B/D adds a second-node bond3. No exceptional
finite or affine diagram has the required large order. The corresponding
(c0,l,h) are

\texttt{(2,0,x/sqrt(2))}, \texttt{(1,1,1+x/sqrt(2))},
\texttt{(0,sqrt(2),(x+2)/sqrt(2))}, \texttt{(0,2,1+x/sqrt(2))}.

In the first case x=0 is impossible by orthogonality to the full cusp,
x=1 induces affine F4, and x=sqrt(2) induces affine C2. The conservative
bound x\textgreater=sqrt(2) gives g\textless=2. In the second case x=0
induces the affine star(4,3,3), so x\textgreater=1 and again
g\textless2. The third gives g=4/(x+2)\textless=2. In the fourth, x=0
gives a proper affine B4 with the doubled terminal at the end of its
length-two arm. Thus x\textgreater=1 and
g\textless=8-4sqrt(2)\textless5/2. The uniform bound is therefore5/2.
The opposite main-path profile has g\textless=14/9: its near-terminal
inner component is B\_P of rank\textgreater=6, with no exceptional
finite extension. Hence the determinant is at least
\texttt{1-(5/2+14/9)/P\textgreater{}=35/108\textgreater{}0}.

\section{A fork-leaf mark}\label{a-fork-leaf-mark}

Let a be one leaf, with mate L and center0. An unpaid pair with a
main-path b has graph distance P\textgreater=5; R=P+1 and nu\_a=1/2.
Deleting a leaves a large finite B or D diagram. Complete
finite-or-connected-affine one-node extensions are: isolated; a bond3 to
L (finite); a bond4 to L (full affine); or a bond3 to0 (full affine).
The same complete large B/D deletion list applies. Their (c0,l,h) are

\texttt{(2,0,x/2)}, \texttt{(1,1,(x+1)/2)},
\texttt{(0,sqrt(2),(x+sqrt(2))/2)}, \texttt{(0,2,1+x/2)}.

For an isolated c, x=1 gives affine E8, x=sqrt(2) affine B4, and x=0 is
impossible. Hence x\textgreater=phi\textgreater sqrt(2), giving
g\textless=4. For the mate-leaf profile, x=0 gives affine E8 and x=1
gives affine A3; thus h\textgreater=(1+sqrt(2))/2 and
g\textless=8-4sqrt(2)\textless4. The mate-leaf bond4 profile gives
g=4sqrt(2)/(x+sqrt(2))\textless=4 even without excluding x=0. The center
profile gives g\textless=4 for all x\textgreater=0. The opposite inner
component is D\_(P+1). Its D6 to E7 extension is paid. Apart from D7 to
E8 below, the opposite profile has g\textless=14/9. Thus
\texttt{1-(4+14/9)/R\textgreater{}=2/27\textgreater{}0}.

\subsection{The fork-leaf P6 to E8
exception}\label{the-fork-leaf-p6-to-e8-exception}

Here b is main-path node5, P=6, and d has a bond3 to the other fork leaf
L. The same affine E8 exclusion gives k=y+1/2\textgreater=3/2. Literal
elimination gives alpha=1/7,A=5/14,D=8/7. If c attaches by a bond3 to L,
the opposite corner has a finite D8 component with c,d as its two fork
leaves (the far outer end is separated by the deleted b). They lie in
the same fork-invariant end segment, so the finite weight rule pays it.
If c attaches by a bond4 to L, the opposite corner contains the proper
affine star(4,3,3), impossible. For the center profile c→0, the opposite
component is finite E8 with arms1,2,4; it must not be called affine.
Here x=0 supplies a proper affine D4 centered0 with leaves a,c,L and
main node1, and x=1 supplies affine A2(a,0,c). Therefore
u=1/(1+x/2)\textless=2-sqrt(2). Its exact normalized determinant is
\texttt{1-4u/7-5v/7-v\^{}2/28}, at least
\texttt{(36sqrt(2)-40)/63\textgreater{}0}. For isolated c put
u=2/x\textless4/3 using x\textgreater=phi\textgreater3/2, and
v=1/k\textless=2/3. Then

\texttt{det\ Schur/(h\^{}2\ k\^{}2)=1-5v/7-v\^{}2/28-2u\^{}2/7\textgreater{}0},

because the expression is zero at u=4/3,v=2/3 and strictly decreases in
both positive variables.

\section{Two terminal marks}\label{two-terminal-marks}

They must be at opposite ends. The effective resistance is R=n-1, for a
pair of doubled terminals, a doubled terminal and a fork leaf, or two
fork leaves. Their respective total g bounds are5,13/2,8. Since
n\textgreater=18, all are strictly smaller than R. The local supports
are separated, so the same factorized Schur formula applies without an
E8 overlap.

\section{Status}\label{status}

The
\href{../scripts/fresh_simple_cusp_affine_tree_completion_20261017.py}{exact
checker} and
\href{fresh_simple_cusp_affine_tree_completion_20261017.json}{saved

\chapter{Long central corridors at affine tree
corners}\label{long-central-corridors-at-affine-tree-corners}

There is an all-rank paid branch for quadrilaterals with an affine B/C/D
corner. It is narrower than the full tree case. Suppose its two marked
roots a,b lie on the central simple-bond path, at distance
P\textgreater=4, and the two end diagrams beyond a,b are finite B or D
diagrams of ranks r,s\textgreater=9, attached at their long endpoints.
Then the opposite corner has adjacent marked roots and pays the
quadrilateral. Here n=r+s+P+1\textgreater=23. Marked roots in the
bounded decorated-end regions remain open. This lemma gives \textbf{no
new ambient dimension bound}.

The
\href{../scripts/fresh_simple_cusp_affine_tree_corridor_20261017.py}{checker}
and \href{fresh_simple_cusp_affine_tree_corridor_20261017.json}{data}
bind the
\href{fresh_simple_cusp_affine_a_quadrilateral_20261017.md}{affine-A
proof} and its
\href{review_simple_cusp_affine_a_quadrilateral_20261017.md}{independent
review}. The ambient assumptions are again finite volume and simplicity
of all vertices. Thus the
\href{fresh_simple_cusp_affine_exclusion_20261017.md}{global exclusion}
forbids every affine subdiagram of order below n.

\section{The complete four-profile
list}\label{the-complete-four-profile-list}

Deleting a from the old affine corner gives two finite components, each
of type B or D and rank\textgreater=9. The same holds after deleting b.
A new root c replacing a can therefore have only these contacts with the
remaining old diagram:

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  no contacts;
\item
  one bond3 at the exposed long endpoint of the outer component;
\item
  one bond3 at the exposed long endpoint of the inner component;
\item
  bonds3 at both of those long endpoints.
\end{enumerate}

To see completeness, every old component remains whole in any connected
new component. A connected finite extension of one B\_r or D\_r,
r\textgreater=9, can only be B\_(r+1) or D\_(r+1), extending its long
endpoint by a simple bond: exceptional types are too small, and the
retained double bond or fork rules out the other classical finite types.
A connected affine extension of only one old component would leave the
other component disconnected. This is neither a spherical corner nor the
irreducible affine diagram of a simple ideal corner, so it is forbidden.

If c touches both old components, the new connected diagram has all n
nodes. Two double-bond ends, a double-bond end and a fork, or two forks
can occur only in the corresponding affine C, B, or D diagram. In each
case the joining root has simple bonds to exactly the two long
endpoints. An extra attachment would produce a cycle or additional
branch absent from those diagrams. This proves the four-profile list
using the full finite/affine classification, in every rank. It does not
extrapolate a finite enumeration. In particular there are no free
unbounded-label contacts to old white roots in this list.

For c the outer component lies beyond a, and the inner component
contains b. The nearest contact of c on that inner component is the
first white node after a. Since P\textgreater=4, c.b=0. Analogously
d.a=0 for the root d opposite b. If c.d\textless0 the opposite marked
pair is adjacent and already paid; assume c.d=0 for a contradiction.

\section{Explicit low-contact
exclusions}\label{explicit-low-contact-exclusions}

Normalize all roots to norm2. Put x=-a.c. For the isolated profile, x=0
would make c orthogonal to the entire simple cusp, hence null. The value
x=sqrt(2) creates the four-node affine B3 star centered at a. The value
x=1 makes c a simple leaf on the central corridor.

Every such simple leaf creates a proper affine E8 with arms(1,2,5). For
a leaf at a, take the length5 arm towards the long outer block and the
length2 arm towards b. For a leaf at the exposed outer port, take five
steps into that block and two through a. For a leaf at the first inner
white node, take two steps towards a and the outer port, and five
towards b and, if necessary, into the other long block. Ranks
r,s\textgreater=9 and P\textgreater=4 provide these simple-bond arms;
the long port of D9 still has six simple steps before its fork, and B9
has seven before its double bond. The original diagram is a tree, so no
extra edge closes these arms. The new leaf has no other old contacts in
each case.

Thus isolated x=1 is excluded. A single-bond profile with x=0 is the
same forbidden leaf construction; with x=1 it creates an affine A2
triangle. For the both-ends profile, x=0 creates an affine A3
four-cycle, and x=1 creates an affine A2 triangle. All these affine
diagrams have order\textless=9\textless n.~The literal positive kernels
are checked in the inherited affine-A package.

The normalized cusp kernel has coefficient1 at a,b and their neighboring
long ports. Consequently the height h=-c.nu equals x, x+1, or x+2 for
the isolated, single, or both profiles. The same complete Coxeter
alphabet argument as before gives conservative reciprocal bounds

\begin{verbatim}
u=1/h <= 1/sqrt(2), sqrt(2)-1, or 1-sqrt(2)/2,
\end{verbatim}

respectively. All heights are positive. The identical bounds hold for
v=1/k of d.

\section{Schur reduction and uniform
gap}\label{schur-reduction-and-uniform-gap}

The inverse Gram at the long port of either finite B\_r or D\_r equals1.
This holds in every rank: its inverse column is1 along the main path,
with the last B-node coefficient1/sqrt(2), or the two D-fork leaves
each1/2. Direct multiplication gives the unit vector at the port. The
checker confirms these literal columns in184 examples of ranks9..100;
the displayed multiplication identity proves every rank.

Eliminating W leaves the residual a,b block
alpha{[}{[}1,-1{]},{[}-1,1{]}{]}, now with alpha=1/P. The intervening
A\_(P-1) path supplies the only cross term between c and d.~Introduce
moment l and constant c0 for c:

{\def\LTcaptype{none} % do not increment counter
\begin{longtable}[]{@{}lrrl@{}}
\toprule\noalign{}
Profile & l & c0 & upper bound on 2\emph{l}u+c0*u\^{}2 \\
\midrule\noalign{}
\endhead
\bottomrule\noalign{}
\endlastfoot
isolated & 0 & 2 & 1 \\
outer single3 & 0 & 1 & 3-2sqrt(2) \\
inner single3 & 1 & 1 & 1 \\
both3 & 1 & 0 & 2-sqrt(2) \\
\end{longtable}
}

Then B=l/P and C=c0+l\^{}2/P in the notation of the affine-A Schur
identity. For d use m,d0, giving A=m/P, D=d0+m\^{}2/P and E=l*m/P.
Substituting into that formally checked determinant identity cancels the
quadratic cross term and gives

\begin{verbatim}
detS/(h^2*k^2)
  =1-[2*(l*u+m*v)+c0*u^2+d0*v^2]/P.
\end{verbatim}

Each single-root expression is increasing on its permitted reciprocal
height interval and is at most1 by the exact table. Therefore the right
side is at least 1-2/P\textgreater=1/2. The actual quadrilateral star
has corank1, so detS=0, a contradiction. Hence c.d\textless0, as
claimed.

\section{Status}\label{status-1}

The four exact profile costs and184 inverse-column checks are generated
and freshly replayed by the checker. Syntax, all ten direct source
hashes and all five local links pass. A separate internal
mathematical/source read confirms the full B/D extension list, the three
leaf-E8 embeddings including P=4, the all-rank port columns and the
scalar Schur cancellation. That read does not claim a duplicate184-case
arithmetic replay. The completeness arguments above are classification
and all-rank identities, not finite cutoff claims. Only this long
central-corridor branch is closed. The full affine-tree quadrilateral
obligation, including all decorated-end positions, remains open. The
mixed rule and earlier dimension bounds are unchanged.

\chapter{Source 313}\label{source-313}

\chapter{Affine-tree quadrilaterals with short outer end
blocks}\label{affine-tree-quadrilaterals-with-short-outer-end-blocks}

There is a further all-rank paid branch for the proposed mixed
finite/ideal 3n rule. In an all-simple finite-volume Coxeter polytope of
dimension n\textgreater=14, let an affine B/C/D corner have central-path
marked roots a,b at distance P\textgreater=4. Write the diagram as

\texttt{F\_r\ —\ a\ —\ (P−1\ white\ path\ nodes)\ —\ b\ —\ F\_s},

where each end is B\_r (r\textgreater=1) or D\_r (r\textgreater=3). Here
B1 means A1 joined to a by a bond4; D3 means A3 joined at its middle
node. If \textbf{r+P\textgreater=9 and s+P\textgreater=9}, the opposite
marked roots c,d are adjacent. The quadrilateral is therefore paid.

This removes the large-outer-end restriction from the
\href{fresh_simple_cusp_affine_tree_corridor_20261017.md}{earlier
corridor lemma}. It leaves only 13 central-position types, up to
exchanging the two ends, together with fork-leaf and fork-center
positions. It is not a full quadrilateral theorem or a dimension bound.

The
\href{../scripts/fresh_simple_cusp_affine_tree_short_ends_20261017.py}{checker}
and \href{fresh_simple_cusp_affine_tree_short_ends_20261017.json}{data}
check the closed inverse formulas, the five distinct join costs, and
literal positive kernels for the two exceptional affine exclusions.
All-rank completeness comes from the arguments below, rather than the
range of the confirming matrix calculations.

\section{Complete extension classes}\label{complete-extension-classes}

Deleting a leaves the short outer F\_r and an inner B/D component of
rank s+P\textgreater=9. Every new connected component contains whole old
components. An extension touching only the outer component must be
finite: an affine component plus the untouched inner component cannot be
the connected affine diagram of a simple ideal vertex. Its contact
vector may otherwise be arbitrary, including unbounded labels for an A1
outer component. An extension touching only the inner component is its
unique finite long-end extension by a bond3. Extending it affinely would
again leave a disconnected corner. The isolated case is also allowed.

If c touches both components, its connected diagram has all n nodes. The
complete finite/affine classification now gives a classical diagram:
exceptional diagrams have order at most9. The large retained B/D
component determines its long port. At the outer end the possibilities
are precisely:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  B1: bond3 for a finite classical extension or bond4 for an affine
  extension;
\item
  B2: bond3 at either endpoint;
\item
  B\_r, r\textgreater=3: bond3 at its long port;
\item
  D3: bond3 at either path endpoint for a finite extension, or at the
  middle for an affine extension;
\item
  D4: bond3 at any of its three leaves;
\item
  D\_r, r\textgreater=5: bond3 at its long port.
\end{itemize}

The contact to the inner component is always bond3 at its long port.
This list follows by deleting a node from classical paths and
single/double forks; there is no remaining exceptional or cycle case
with the large B/D component. A proposed type incompatible with the
other end may be retained in the table as a harmless relaxation. In
particular c.b=0 because P\textgreater=4. The same reasoning gives
d.a=0. It suffices to contradict c.d=0, since a nonzero nonpositive
product is an adjacent pair under the rule.

\section{Exact end identities and arbitrary outer-only
contacts}\label{exact-end-identities-and-arbitrary-outer-only-contacts}

Normalize roots to norm2. Let J=G(F\_r)\^{}−1 and let v be the positive
contact vector from a to F\_r. Except for B1 it is the unit long-port
vector; for B1 it is sqrt(2) times that vector. In every case v\^{}T J
v=1. The cusp coefficients on F\_r are t\_j=(Jv)\_j.

For B\_r, r\textgreater=2, the diagonal of J is 1,2,\ldots,r−1,r/2, and
the t\_j are 1,\ldots,1,1/sqrt(2). For B1 the diagonal is1/2 and
t\_1=1/sqrt(2). For D\_r the diagonal is 1,\ldots,r−2,r/4,r/4, and t\_j
are 1,\ldots,1,1/2,1/2. The checker displays and multiplies the full
closed inverse matrices in 78 examples; sparse multiplication of the
same formulas proves them for every rank.

For an outer-only contact vector w\textgreater=0 put q=w\^{}T Jw and
t=v\^{}T Jw. Its finite corner requires q\textless2. Every nonzero
coordinate of w is at least1, and all t\_j\textgreater=1/2, so
t\textgreater=1/2. Cauchy--Schwarz in J gives q\textgreater=t\^{}2. If
x=−a.c\textgreater=1, then

\texttt{(2−q)/(x+t)\^{}2\ \textless{}=\ (2−t\^{}2)/(1+t)\^{}2\ \textless{}=\ 1}.

If x=0, the same bound follows from q+t\^{}2\textgreater=2. With two or
more contacts, t\textgreater=1 and Cauchy--Schwarz already proves this.
With one contact of magnitude at least sqrt(2), the displayed diagonals
prove it as well. The only remaining possibilities are one bond3 at B1,
the non-port endpoint of B2, or a fork leaf of D3,D4,D5,D6.

For B1/B2 that extra leaf and the first old path nodes give the
five-node affine F4 path with bonds(3,4,3,3). For D3..D6 the added leaf
extends one fork arm to length2; the other fork arm has length1, and the
old long direction supplies length5. This is the nine-node affine E8
with arms(1,2,5). The full dimension n\textgreater=14 supplies the five
simple steps before the other decoration. These are induced diagrams:
the new root has precisely its one outer contact and x=0. Both are
proper affine subdiagrams, forbidden by the
\href{fresh_simple_cusp_affine_exclusion_20261017.md}{all-simple affine
exclusion}. The checker verifies their positive kernels and positive
definite one-deletions. Thus every outer-only profile contributes at
most1, without an angle or rank cutoff.

\section{Heights of isolated and inner-only
roots}\label{heights-of-isolated-and-inner-only-roots}

Give the old cusp kernel coefficient1 at a,b and on the intervening
path. For an isolated c its height is h=−c.nu=x. The value x=0 would
make c orthogonal to the full simple cusp, hence proportional to its
null vector. The value x=1 supplies a proper affine B/D diagram: retain
the whole outer end, a, and the two simple leaves c and the first inner
path node. This diagram has order r+3\textless n.~The value x=sqrt(2)
gives the four-node affine star with bonds(4,3,3), unless the outer bond
itself is4, when the two bond4 contacts give the three-node affine C2.
Hence the conservative bound h\textgreater=sqrt(2) is valid and
2/h\^{}2\textless=1.

For the inner-only bond3 profile, h=x+1. At x=0 the same affine B/D
construction uses the outer end extended by a, with the first inner node
as its branch point, and c and the second inner node as its leaves. Its
order is r+4\textless n.~At x=1, a, the first inner node and c form an
affine A2. Therefore h\textgreater=1+sqrt(2), giving
\texttt{2/h+1/h\^{}2\textless{}=1}. These exclusions work with the
entire outer block and do not require it to have large rank.

\section{Join costs and the corank
contradiction}\label{join-costs-and-the-corank-contradiction}

For a join, write q=w\^{}T Jw and t=v\^{}T Jw for its outer contact. Its

Outer profile & q & t & bound on 2/h+(1−q)/h\^{}2 \\

Eliminate all white roots W. The a,b block is

\texttt{det(S)/(h\^{}2\ k\^{}2)\ =\ 1\ −\ {[}g\_c+g\_d{]}/P},

\texttt{det(S)/(h\^{}2\ k\^{}2)\ \textgreater{}=\ 1−26/(9P)\ \textgreater{}=\ 5/18\ \textgreater{}\ 0}.

The actual quadrilateral star has corank1, so det(S)=0. This

Failure of an inner-rank condition means, after exchanging ends,

\chapter{Source 314}\label{source-314}

\chapter{Distance15 bounds for simple cusps and compact
facets}\label{distance15-bounds-for-simple-cusps-and-compact-facets}

Let P be a finite-sided, finite-volume hyperbolic Coxeter polytope in
H\^{}n. The following restricted conclusions hold:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  If every ideal vertex is simple, then \textbf{n\textless=125}.
\item
  If P has a compact facet, then \textbf{n\textless=127}, with no
  simplicity assumption on its other ideal vertices.
\end{itemize}

Finite vertices are automatically simple. Neither hypothesis is asserted
for every finite-volume chamber; the full unrestricted bound163 is
unchanged. No novelty or current-best claim is made. The first assertion
uses a simple projective polytope, not an assumption that the chamber is
compact in hyperbolic space. The compact facet in the second assertion
need not itself have Coxeter angles.

The \href{../scripts/fresh_simple_cusp_distance_bound_20261017.py}{exact
checker} and
\href{fresh_simple_cusp_distance_bound_20261017.json}{certificate}
refine the earlier
\href{fresh_nikulin_narrow_20261015_compact_facet.md}{compact-facet
distance17 argument}. They use the frozen complete high-rank
quasi-Lannér catalogue to reduce the quadrilateral distance from17 to15.
The all-rank finite/affine graph bound and the passage to ideal polygon
corners are proved below.

\section{Local face stars, including ideal
corners}\label{local-face-stars-including-ideal-corners}

Every positive-dimensional k-face belongs to exactly n−k facets. The
facet normals of its supporting walls have positive-definite Gram,
because the relative interior contains a hyperbolic point. These
incidence facts, and the product-of-simplices description of an ideal
link, are stated for acute chambers in
\href{https://ems.press/content/serial-article-files/43032}{Potyagailo--Vinberg,
printed p.64}.

Let Q be an actual triangular or quadrilateral two-face. Write W for its
n−2 supporting facet normals and mark its side facets black. Each side
has exactly one original ambient facet beyond W. Its edge interior gives
W plus that black node positive definite. At a finite polygon corner, W
plus the two adjacent black nodes is positive definite. At an ideal
corner it is positive semidefinite. Under the simple-cusp hypothesis
these n normals are precisely the complete incident affine vertex
diagram. The compact-facet application has only finite corners.

The full face star is indefinite: after projecting the side normals off
the positive span W, they bound a nondegenerate finite-area polygon in a
Lorentzian three-space, which they span. Every principal block has
negative index at most one, since it is a block of the ambient Gram.

We use two acute-incidence facts from the inherited compact-facet proof.
A positive-definite set of original wall normals has an actual common
face, obtained by projecting a strict timelike interior point; the
inverse of a positive-definite matrix with nonpositive offdiagonals is
entrywise nonnegative. A singular positive-semidefinite set contains a
connected affine component whose positive null combination is a nonzero
future null vector. It is orthogonal to the whole PSD block and pairs
nonpositively with all other walls, hence gives an actual ideal point.
Nonzeroness and orientation follow from its strictly negative pairing
with the common interior point.

In a quadrilateral, the two \textbf{closed opposite sides are disjoint}.
This remains true when some or all four vertices are ideal: the four
vertices are distinct, and only consecutive sides have a common
endpoint. Consequently, for either opposite black pair U, the block W+U
is indefinite. Positive definiteness would give a finite common point of
those opposite sides; singular PSD would give an ideal common point.
Both contradict the actual closed polygon incidence. Compactness of Q is
not used in this step.

\section{Minimal diagrams and the radius7
certificate}\label{minimal-diagrams-and-the-radius7-certificate}

Every inclusion-minimal indefinite principal diagram L is connected and
has all proper principal blocks PSD. If a proper connected affine block
C occurs, its positive kernel pairs nontrivially with an adjacent
outside node; C plus that node is already indefinite. Minimality forces
that to be all of L. Thus L has the Lannér/quasi-Lannér classification
scope, with order at most10. Strict dotted pairs give only an order-two
case. The classification input and primary references are recorded in
the \href{fresh_high_rank_quasilanner_census_20261017.md}{frozen
high-rank census} and the inherited compact-facet proof; this package
does not repeat the large classification enumeration.

Choose minimal indefinite diagrams L in W+U and M in W+V, where U,V are
the opposite black pairs. Each contains both its black nodes. On
deleting either black node the remaining subdiagram lies in W plus one
side facet, so that deletion is \textbf{positive definite}, not merely
PSD. Therefore both marked nodes are in the catalogue's
\texttt{finite\_deletions}.

For every such marked pair in all26 high-rank types, the checker
performs a multi-source breadth-first search from the pair. There are384
pairs:

{\def\LTcaptype{none} % do not increment counter
\begin{longtable}[]{@{}lr@{}}
\toprule\noalign{}
Maximum distance to the marked pair & Number of pairs \\
\midrule\noalign{}
\endhead
\bottomrule\noalign{}
\endlastfoot
1 & 10 \\
2 & 123 \\
3 & 143 \\
4 & 61 \\
5 & 31 \\
6 & 12 \\
7 & 4 \\
\end{longtable}
}

The four radius7 cases are L23 with blacks \{0,1\}, farthest node8; and
L25 with blacks \{1,2\}, \{1,3\}, or \{2,3\}, farthest node9. Every
literal distance is saved. A connected diagram of order at most5 has
radius at most3 from a two-node set: a shortest path cannot pass the
other marked node before reaching the set. This treats all smaller types
without a label cutoff. Hence the radius7 bound is complete for every
possible L and M.

The two minimal indefinite diagrams cannot be disjoint and orthogonal,
as that would give two negative directions. They share a white vertex or
have an edge between them. In the overlap case the marked sets are
joined by a path of length at most14. In the joined case it is at most
7+1+7=15. Taking a shortest path from U to V ensures that all internal
vertices are white. Its endpoints are consecutive sides of Q, so this
path lies in their actual corner diagram.

For a triangle, every indefinite subdiagram contains all three black
nodes, since any black deletion lies in a PSD corner. A minimal one has
at most10 nodes. In a spanning tree, take the minimal subtree joining
the three marks. At least two marked leaves can be deleted separately
while the other two marks stay joined. Each resulting path has length at
most8 and belongs to one actual corner diagram. This argument uses PSD
corner blocks and is therefore valid at ideal corners as well.

Give a polygon corner weight1 when its two black nodes are at graph
distance at most15 in the full incident vertex diagram; otherwise give
weight0. Triangles receive at least2 and quadrilaterals at least1.
Larger polygons need only nonnegative payment. Thus every two-face with
k sides receives at least5−k.

\section{All-rank finite and affine vertex
costs}\label{all-rank-finite-and-affine-vertex-costs}

For a connected graph with N vertices let p\_k be the number of
unordered pairs at graph distance k. The unweighted underlying graphs of
the classical finite and affine Coxeter diagrams are paths, cycles, or
the single- and double-fork trees below. Edge multiplicities do not
change graph distance.

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  A path has p\_k=max(N−k,0).
\item
  A cycle has p\_k=N for 2k\textless N, p\_k=N/2 for 2k=N, and zero
  otherwise.
\item
  A path on m\textgreater=2 vertices with two extra leaves at one end
  has N=m+2 and
  p\_k=max(m−k,0)+2{[}1\textless=k\textless=m{]}+{[}k=2{]}.
\item
  A path on m\textgreater=2 vertices with two extra leaves at each end
  has N=m+4 and
  p\_k=max(m−k,0)+4{[}1\textless=k\textless=m{]}+2{[}k=2{]}+4{[}k=m+1{]}.
\end{itemize}

Each formula follows by separating path--path, leaf--path, and
leaf--leaf pairs. In every displayed case p\_k\textless=N. The affine D4
four-leaf star is the m=1 exception and is treated separately. Every
remaining exceptional finite/affine diagram has N\textless=9, so even
its total number of pairs is at most4N. The finite dihedral diagrams and
affine A1 are paths of order2; the other small F/G/H types are paths or
included exceptions. These classification alternatives cover all
connected finite and affine diagrams.

It follows in every case that the number of pairs at distance at most15
is at most15N. The same holds for a spherical forest by adding component
orders; pairs in different components have infinite distance. The
checker independently counts245 classical graphs and seven exceptional
graphs by BFS and compares the formulas. The explicit formulas and the
finite exceptional classification, not the tested rank range, prove the
all-rank statement.

At a finite vertex the full spherical forest has order n.~At a simple
ideal vertex the Euclidean link is one simplex, so its full incident
diagram is connected affine of order n.~In both cases all planar-angle
weights sum to at most15n. No such order-n assertion is made for a
nonsimple ideal vertex.

\section{Strict h-vector thresholds}\label{strict-h-vector-thresholds}

The projective closure of P is a bounded simple n-polytope when all its
ideal vertices are simple. The inherited nonnegative symmetric h-vector
argument gives the strict average corner-payment lower bound

\[
 b_d=\begin{cases}d(d-6)/8,&d\text{ even},\\
 (d-1)(d-5)/8,&d\text{ odd}.\end{cases}
\]

Its strictness follows from the positive endpoint h-coefficients.
Applied to the whole chamber, the payment bound gives b\_n\textless15n.
For n=126+2t and n=127+2t respectively, eight times b\_n−15n is

\[
 4t^2+252t,\qquad 4t^2+256t+132.
\]

Both are nonnegative for t\textgreater=0. Equality in the first at t=0
still contradicts the strict lower bound. Thus n\textless=125. Without
the new radius certificate, distance17 would similarly give the weaker
n\textless=141.

If P instead has a compact facet F, put d=n−1. F is a simple d-polytope
whose vertices are finite ambient vertices. Its two-faces are actual
two-faces of P, and their weights count only a subset of the pairs in
the ambient rank-n spherical vertex forest. Hence b\_d\textless15(d+1).
At d=127+2t and d=128+2t, eight times the difference is

\[
 4t^2+256t+12,\qquad 4t^2+260t+136,
\]

strictly positive. Therefore d\textless=126 and n\textless=127. This
replaces the older distance17 compact-facet bound143 in this restricted
branch only; the other unrestricted finite-volume branches are not
changed here.

\section{Comparison, verification, and
scope}\label{comparison-verification-and-scope}

Felikson--Tumarkin prove the much stronger n\textless=8 result for
\textbf{simple all-ideal} Coxeter polytopes. Their
\href{https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/0502413}{primary paper, §§1--3} uses
the absence of elliptic order-n diagrams, together with restrictions on
ideal triangles and quadrilaterals. That absence fails when finite
vertices are allowed, so their proof is not imported to the mixed case
here. This report makes no survey-based claim that125 is a best
published bound for the restricted class.

Generation and a fresh saved replay pass. Syntax, all nine direct source
hashes, and report links pass. Two internal mathematical/source reviews
found no gap; the
\href{fresh_simple_cusp_distance_bound_20261017_review.md}{separate
independent review} records its scope and does not claim a duplicate
arithmetic replay. The checker binds the frozen complete catalogue and
the preceding geometric proofs; its new arithmetic is the384 exact
distance calculations, independent classical graph counts, and rational
threshold identities. No coefficient field, arithmeticity, optimizer,
finite-tail cutoff, or induced-face Coxeter assumption is introduced.
