\section{Ideal quadrilaterals and the finite-black radius
condition}\label{ideal-quadrilaterals-and-the-finite-black-radius-condition}

The crucial extension from compact to ideal polygons is sound. The
relative interior of an actual edge contains a hyperbolic point even if
its endpoints are ideal. Its supporting normals therefore have a
positive-definite Gram. Thus, for a quadrilateral with white support W,
W plus any one black side is positive definite.

For two opposite sides, positive definiteness of their combined block
would give an actual finite common point by acute projection. A singular
PSD block gives a positive affine-kernel combination. Its pairing with a
strict timelike center is strictly negative, so this null vector is
nonzero and future directed. It is orthogonal to the PSD block and
nonpositive against all other walls by acuteness. Hence it gives a
feasible ideal point in both closed opposite sides. Closed opposite
edges of a genuine quadrilateral are disjoint, including when endpoints
are ideal. Both alternatives are impossible, so each opposite block is
indefinite.

A minimal indefinite subdiagram in that block contains both black nodes.
Deleting either one leaves a principal subdiagram of W plus a single
side, hence is \textbf{positive definite}. The catalogue test must
therefore use pairs of finite deletions, as the source does, rather than
arbitrary pairs of affine-or-finite deletions.

The frozen complete order6--10 catalogue covers those cases. Any
connected diagram of order at most5 has distance at most3 to a two-node
set: a shortest path to the set avoids the other marked node. The
low-order argument also covers arbitrary small labels, and a dotted
order-two core has radius zero. There is no unexamined rank or label
tail in the radius7 conclusion.

Two opposite minimal indefinite cores cannot be disjoint and orthogonal
in an index-one ambient space. An overlap gives a path of length at
most14 between the two black sets; an inter-core edge gives at
most7+1+7=15. A shortest such path has no black internal vertex. Its
endpoints are consecutive sides of the quadrilateral, so it is contained
in their actual finite or simple-ideal corner diagram.

For triangles, every black deletion lies in a PSD corner. A minimal
indefinite core contains all three marks and has at most10 nodes. Its
minimal connecting subtree yields at least two mark-to-mark paths
avoiding the third mark, each of length at most8. This is valid for
ideal corners as well.

\section{All-rank graph costs}\label{all-rank-graph-costs}

The path, cycle, single-fork and double-fork formulas correctly separate
path--path, leaf--path and leaf--leaf pairs. In particular, the affine-D
double fork with path order m\textgreater=2 has

\texttt{p\_k=max(m−k,0)+4{[}k\textless{}=m{]}+2{[}k=2{]}+4{[}k=m+1{]}},

with total order N=m+4. At k=2 the count is exactly N; the other cases
are at most N as well. The exceptional m=1 affine-D4 star is handled
separately. The remaining exceptional finite/affine graphs have order at
most9 and at most4N pairs in total. Finite dihedral diagrams, affine A1,
and the small path-shaped F/G/H diagrams are covered.

These explicit formulas and the finite classification, rather than the
checked rank interval, establish the uniform distance15 cost at most15N.
Spherical components add. A simple ideal vertex has a simplex Euclidean
link, hence one connected affine diagram of order n; a finite vertex has
a spherical forest of order n.~No order-n assertion is made for a
nonsimple cusp.

\section{Strict thresholds and scope}\label{strict-thresholds-and-scope}

For an all-simple chamber, the projective closure is a bounded simple
polytope, so the inherited strict h-vector inequality applies even when
the hyperbolic chamber has ideal vertices. At n=126 the scalar lower
bound equals15n, but the actual lower inequality is strict. This
excludes126, giving at most125. The two displayed parity polynomials are
nonnegative for every t\textgreater=0, not merely for the sampled t
values in the checker.

For a compact facet of dimension d=n−1, its vertices are finite and its
two-faces are actual ambient two-faces. Their angle weights form a
subset of ambient rank-n pair weights, so the upper budget is15(d+1).
The two parity differences become strictly positive starting at d=127
and128, giving d\textless=126 and ambient n\textless=127. The proof does
not assume that the induced facet is itself a Coxeter polytope.

The comparison with the stronger published simple \textbf{all-ideal}
bound is correctly separated from the mixed finite/ideal hypothesis
here. No novelty, current-best literature status, arithmeticity, or
external refereeing claim is made by this review.

\chapter{Vinberg's compact scope and a 3n affine weight
interface}\label{vinbergs-compact-scope-and-a-3n-affine-weight-interface}

The checked primary literature does \textbf{not} supply a mixed-simple
finite-volume dimension bound29 by direct citation. There is a concrete
extension candidate with the correct vertex budget: retain Vinberg's
finite-vertex weights and use the rule below at simple ideal vertices.
Its total vertex cost is at most3n, and the triangle payment transfers.
\textbf{Quadrilateral payment remains unproved.} Thus this package gives
no new ambient dimension bound; the frozen all-simple bound61 is
unchanged.

The
\href{../scripts/fresh_simple_cusp_vinberg_weight_frontier_20261017.py}{checker}
and \href{fresh_simple_cusp_vinberg_weight_frontier_20261017.json}{data}
verify the graph counts exactly. Their finite ranges are confirmations
of the all-rank formulas below, not cutoff-based proofs.

\section{What the primary theorem
says}\label{what-the-primary-theorem-says}

Vinberg's original Theorem1 on printed p.69 explicitly concerns compact
type. Its §6.1 begins with a bounded fundamental polytope, and §6.2
calculates costs for elliptic vertex diagrams. The original §4 is the
coarse distance7 argument; §§5--6 provide the much finer weights giving
the compact bound29. These are distinct proof steps.
\href{https://www.mathnet.ru/php/getFT.phtml?jrnid=mmo&option_lang=rus&paperid=444&what=fullt}{Original
paper}.

One modern wording that could suggest a broader scope occurs at the
opening of Burcroff's §9. But its following Proposition9.2 assumes a
compact Coxeter polytope, and Theorem10.2 again states the bound for the
compact class. That introductory wording does not provide a proof for
mixed finite/simple-ideal vertices.
\href{https://arxiv.org/pdf/2201.03437}{Primary preprint, §§9--10}.

The primary Felikson--Tumarkin introduction likewise attributes29 to the
compact theorem and separately proves8 for the simple all-ideal class.
\href{https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/0502413}{Primary paper}. This is a
bounded source check, not a claim to have established the best published
bound for the mixed-simple class.

\section{The proposed ideal-vertex rule has cost
exactly3n}\label{the-proposed-ideal-vertex-rule-has-cost-exactly3n}

Assume n\textgreater=14. A simple ideal vertex has a connected affine
diagram on n nodes. Exceptional affine types have at most9 nodes, so
only the four classical underlying shapes occur: a cycle, a path, a
single fork, or a double fork. Normalize every ideal corner weight to0
or1 as follows:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  weight1 if the two marked roots have graph distance at most3;
\item
  also weight1 if they belong to an end segment of order at most6;
\item
  otherwise weight0.
\end{itemize}

On a fork an end segment must contain both interchangeable fork leaves
or neither. The maximal allowed fork-end segment contains the two leaves
and the first four vertices of the central path. A cycle has no end
segments. Distances ignore bond multiplicity, just as in the preceding
\href{fresh_simple_cusp_affine_exclusion_20261017.md}{distance proofs}.

The exact costs are:

{\def\LTcaptype{none} % do not increment counter
\begin{longtable}[]{@{}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 6\tabcolsep) * \real{0.2000}}
  >{\raggedleft\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 6\tabcolsep) * \real{0.2667}}
  >{\raggedleft\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 6\tabcolsep) * \real{0.2667}}
  >{\raggedleft\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 6\tabcolsep) * \real{0.2667}}@{}}
\toprule\noalign{}
\begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
Underlying affine graph
\end{minipage} & \begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedleft
Pairs at distance\textless=3
\end{minipage} & \begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedleft
Additional end pairs
\end{minipage} & \begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedleft
Total
\end{minipage} \\
\midrule\noalign{}
\endhead
\bottomrule\noalign{}
\endlastfoot
cycle & 3n & 0 & 3n \\
path & 3n-6 & 6 & 3n \\
single fork & 3n-5 & 5 & 3n \\
double fork & 3n-4 & 4 & 3n \\
\end{longtable}
}

For a path, each end contributes two extra distance4 pairs and one
distance5 pair. A fork end contributes two distance4 pairs and no
distance5 pair. These extra pairs are disjoint for n\textgreater=14. The
short-pair counts follow directly from the all-rank path/cycle/fork
formulas already proved in the frozen distance package. This proves the
table in every rank. The checker reconstructs all348 graphs of orders14
through100 and counts their literal pair sets independently.

At finite vertices use Vinberg's published weights, including the four
E8 exceptions. Their total is at most3n by the
\href{fresh_compact_dimension_bound_20261015.md}{frozen finite-component
check} and its inherited all-rank proof. The new affine rule only
concerns ideal vertices; it does not reassign weights to finite forests.

\section{Triangle payment does
transfer}\label{triangle-payment-does-transfer}

By the \href{fresh_simple_cusp_affine_exclusion_20261017.md}{global
affine exclusion}, each triangle star in the all-simple class,
n\textgreater=14, contains a Lanner diagram L of order at most5
containing its three black roots. Follow the literal cases in Vinberg
§6.4, rather than importing the whole compact face theorem.

If L has order3 or is a4-cycle, there are two adjacent black pairs, so
two corners receive weight1. If L contains a bond5, the proof chooses a
corner whose connected diagram contains that bond; such a corner cannot
be a classical affine n-node diagram. It is finite of type H3 or H4 and
receives weight2 under the unchanged compact rule.

The remaining case is a5-cycle. Vinberg's two displayed marked patterns
give two corner contributions of weight1 by adjacency and his local
endpoint/special-edge lemmas. If either contributing corner is ideal,
the required marked pair is connected within L minus the omitted black
root, on at most4 vertices, so its distance is at most3. Our ideal rule
therefore gives at least the same unit payment. The finite corners
retain the original local lemma. Hence every triangle receives at
least2.

The classification and local finite-corner lemmas here are explicit
published inputs. The graph checker does not claim to reclassify Lanner
diagrams or independently replay their angle arithmetic.

\section{The precise remaining quadrilateral
obligation}\label{the-precise-remaining-quadrilateral-obligation}

The absence of affine diagrams of order below n does not make the whole
corner diagram elliptic. A quadrilateral can have a connected affine
n-node corner. In particular an affine A cycle has two marked-to- marked
arcs. Vinberg's §6.5 description of W\_ij as a tree with the two marked
roots at its ends does not apply verbatim to that corner. His later
classification of each T\_ij as a finite classical diagram or E8 also
needs new cases. Thus the compact quadrilateral theorem has not been
transferred by the cost calculation above.

The exact target is now clear: prove that every actual quadrilateral in
the all-simple class has at least one corner paid by this mixed rule, or
give a literal realizable counterexample. Any proof must retain the full
original star, all finite/affine vertex conditions, negative index1,
corank1, and the global exclusion of affine subdiagrams of order below
n. No label cutoff or bounded white-tail scan suffices.

Two tempting shortcuts have specific defects:

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  Taking the maximum compact weight over all single-root deletions of an
  affine A cycle marks exactly every pair at cyclic distance at most5.
  Its cost is5n for n\textgreater=14, not3n. The checker verifies all27
  sizes14..40; the proof is that a pair lies in a6-node end segment of a
  deleted cycle precisely when one of its cyclic connecting arcs has
  length at most5.
\item
  Deleting a supporting white root does not preserve a quadrilateral
  star's corank1. For a symmetric N-by-N Gram matrix of rank N-1 with
  kernel vector k, its adjugate is a nonzero scalar multiple of kk\^{}t.
  Deleting a node w with k\_w!=0 therefore leaves a nonsingular
  principal matrix. Vinberg §6.10 explicitly uses det H=0; a spherical
  deletion cannot silently be substituted for a full quadrilateral star.
\end{enumerate}

These are obstructions to particular transfer arguments, not
counterexamples to the proposed mixed rule or to a possible bound29.

\section{Status}\label{status-2}

Generation and a fresh saved replay pass, covering348 affine graph
checks and27 cycle-deletion envelopes. Syntax, all nine direct source
hashes, and report links pass. An internal mathematical/source read
independently confirms the triangle transfer, including the
original5-cycle case. The certificate status explicitly leaves
quadrilateral payment open and assigns no new ambient dimension bound.
The older61/127/163 theorems and all frozen predecessors are untouched.

\chapter{Vinberg payment for quadrilaterals with four finite
corners}\label{vinberg-payment-for-quadrilaterals-with-four-finite-corners}

\textbf{Claim.} Let \(P\subset\mathbb H^n\) be a finite-sided,
finite-volume Coxeter polytope which is simple at every finite and ideal
vertex, with \(n\ge18\). If a quadrilateral two-face \(F\) has four
finite vertices, then at least one of its corners has positive weight
under Vinberg's original finite-vertex rule. In particular its total
corner payment is at least one.

This is a transfer of the published diagram argument, not a new
classification of its finite cases. The audit below retains Vinberg's
finite Coxeter diagram classifications and local determinant
calculations as published inputs and checks precisely the hypotheses
that used compactness. It does not apply the compact theorem directly to
a noncompact polytope.

The primary source is Vinberg, \emph{Trudy Moskovskogo Matematicheskogo
Obshchestva} \textbf{47} (1984), 68--102, especially §3 Proposition 8,
§6.3, and §6.5--11, printed pp.82--91.
\href{https://www.mathnet.ru/php/getFT.phtml?jrnid=mmo&option_lang=rus&paperid=444&what=fullt}{Original
paper}, \href{https://www.mathnet.ru/eng/mmo444}{bibliographic record}.

The \href{fresh_simple_cusp_affine_exclusion_20261017.md}{simple-cusp
affine exclusion} is the other geometric input: every connected affine
subdiagram of \(P\) has exactly \(n\) nodes. In particular every
subdiagram on fewer than \(n\) nodes is affine-free. An order-\(n\)
affine diagram omitting a supporting white wall is \textbf{not} excluded
by this fact. No step below assumes otherwise.

\section{Geometric properties of the actual compact face
star}\label{geometric-properties-of-the-actual-compact-face-star}

Write \(W\) for the \(n-2\) supporting white walls of \(F\), and write
the four black walls as opposite pairs \(\{u_1,u_2\}\), \(\{v_1,v_2\}\).
The full star has \(n+2\) roots. Every \(W+u_i+v_j\) is positive
definite, since it is the wall diagram at an actual finite vertex. Also
\(W\) is positive definite. These assertions do not require compactness
of the ambient \(P\).

Both \(W+u_1+u_2\) and \(W+v_1+v_2\) are indefinite. Here is a direct
argument that deals with the potential ideal case. If the first Gram
matrix were positive definite, its inverse would be entrywise
nonnegative. Project a strict timelike interior point \(h\) onto the
common orthogonal complement of its normals. The projection adds a
nonnegative combination of those normals; its norm becomes more negative
and its products with all other walls remain strictly negative. This
produces an actual point of \(F\) on both opposite sides, which is
impossible.

If instead that Gram matrix were positive semidefinite and singular,
eliminate \(W\). Each of the two residual diagonals is positive, and the
residual off-diagonal is nonpositive. Singularity gives a kernel vector
with both black coordinates strictly positive. Lifting it through the
entrywise nonnegative inverse of \(W\) gives nonnegative white
coordinates. The resulting combination \(z\) of actual normals is null
and nonzero: \((z,h)<0\) for a strict center \(h\). It is orthogonal to
\(W\) and both opposite roots, and has nonpositive product with every
other wall. Thus it gives an ideal point of \(F\), contradicting
compactness of this four-finite-vertex face. Negative index at most one
leaves the asserted indefinite alternative.

Every indefinite subdiagram of the star contains an opposite black pair,
since otherwise it lies in one of the four positive-definite corner
diagrams. Hence all four black roots belong to the unique indefinite
connected component \(H\).

The projected side normals of a nondegenerate compact quadrilateral span
the three-dimensional Lorentz space \(W^\perp\). Consequently the full
star has rank \(n+1\) and corank one. The component \(H\) has corank one
as well; its other components are positive definite by the orthogonality
lemma below. In particular \(\det H=0\), just as required in §6.10.

The unique dependence has nonzero black coefficients, with the two
opposite \(u\)-coefficients of one sign and the two opposite
\(v\)-coefficients of the other. One way to see this is to normalize the
projected side normals against an interior point of \(F\). Their spatial
parts are the vertices of the polar convex quadrilateral. Its unique
affine dependence has alternating signs around the quadrilateral. This
also proves that no black coefficient vanishes.

\section{Two replacements for blanket affine
exclusion}\label{two-replacements-for-blanket-affine-exclusion}

First, if an actual subdiagram \(A\) is orthogonal to an indefinite
subdiagram \(B\), then \(A\) is positive definite. The span of \(B\)
contains a timelike vector, whose orthogonal complement is positive
definite. Thus the Gram matrix of \(A\) is positive semidefinite. If it
were singular, a connected singular Coxeter component would have a
positive kernel vector. The associated combination of its normals cannot
vanish because it pairs strictly negatively with an interior point. This
is impossible in the positive-definite orthogonal complement. This
argument works for arbitrarily large \(A\), and needs no affine-order
cutoff.

Second, an indefinite subdiagram with at most \(n\) nodes is affine-free
in the present simple finite-volume setting. A proper connected affine
subdiagram would have fewer than \(n\) nodes; an affine subdiagram of
order \(n\) would be the whole diagram and could not be indefinite. The
same assertion applies componentwise when appropriate.

These two replacements are stronger than merely observing negative index
one: an abstract block-diagonal matrix could have both an indefinite and
a singular positive-semidefinite block. The strict center of the actual
chamber rules out the singular block here.

\section{Preliminary diagram
decomposition}\label{preliminary-diagram-decomposition}

Use the decomposition \(H=U\cup V\cup W_{\rm shared}\) from §6.5: \(U\)
contains the two \(u\)-roots and the white components unable to reach a
\(v\)-root by a white path; \(V\) is defined symmetrically. The notation
\(W_{\rm shared}\) here distinguishes Vinberg's shared partial diagram
from the whole supporting diagram \(W\) above.

Assume for contradiction that all four corners have weight zero. The
shortest white path between the two black pairs has length at least two,
so \(U,V\) are orthogonal. There is at least one shared white node.
Since each of \(U,V\) contains two black nodes and \(|H|\le n+2\),

\[
|U|,|V|\le n-1,\qquad |H-U|,|H-V|\le n.
\]

The finite corners and the opposite-pair indefiniteness proved above
give the connected indefinite diagrams \(H-U,H-V\), exactly as in §6.5
Lemma 4. They are therefore affine-free by the second replacement. The
diagrams \(U,V\) are affine-free by their strict size bounds. Thus §6.6
Lemma 5 still gives an elliptic member of the orthogonal pair \(U,V\),
and Lemma 12 still supplies the required cyclic Lannér core whenever the
corresponding elliptic member has no high bond.

All the auxiliary \(T_{ij}\) are actual finite corner components.
Therefore Lemmas 1--3 and 6--11, including the end-segment conditions,
the four exceptional \(E_8\) marked positions, the tree property of the
shared white paths, and the classical-versus-\(E_8\) alternatives, apply
to these \(T_{ij}\) literally. None of these finite-corner statements is
asserted for an affine corner.

Lemma 7 is needed before bounding the order of \(U\) or \(V\): if either
contains a high bond, that whole diagram is connected. Thus an
\textbf{elliptic} \(U\) or \(V\) with a high bond is a connected finite
diagram, not an arbitrarily large forest containing a small exceptional
component. Its high bond necessarily has a finite Coxeter label at least
five (multiplicity at least three in Vinberg's convention), and the
finite classification gives order at most four.

Among connected affine diagrams, a \textbf{finite} bond of label at
least five occurs only in the three-node affine \(G_2\) diagram, with
label six. Hence a connected diagram of order at least five containing
such a finite high bond is indefinite, at any order. This statement does
not concern the infinite bond of affine \(A_1\), and does not use a
global affine prohibition.

\section{Audit of the five remaining
cases}\label{audit-of-the-five-remaining-cases}

The following table records the affine-sensitive parts of §6.7--11. The
published local finite-diagram and determinant conclusions are retained.
The cardinalities are deliberately generous carrier bounds, rather than
counts of the minimal offending affine diagram.

{\def\LTcaptype{none} % do not increment counter
\begin{longtable}[]{@{}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 2\tabcolsep) * \real{0.5000}}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 2\tabcolsep) * \real{0.5000}}@{}}
\toprule\noalign{}
\begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright

\end{minipage} & \begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright

\endlastfoot
§6.7: \(U\) elliptic with a high bond, \(V\) indefinite & \(|U|\le4\).
Connected high-bond extensions either become indefinite within a small
extension or belong to the explicitly displayed exceptional
configurations. The latter fit inside \(U\), one \(E_8\) corner

are elliptic by the first replacement. \\
§6.8: \(U\) elliptic without a high bond, \(V\) indefinite & The cyclic

§6.11: neither elliptic diagram has a high bond & The two cyclic Lannér

The implicit affine exclusions used to determine their permitted overlap

Every finite carrier in this table has fewer than \(n\) nodes when
\(n\ge18\). Its affine exclusions therefore remain valid.

For precision in \texttt{\textbackslash{}S}6.11, the small-carrier
assertion concerns restrictions on the induced union of the two cyclic
cores and their connecting edges. It is not a separate assertion that
arbitrary white branches have been excluded by an affine test on that
union. The subsequent determination of the shared paths uses the already
positive-definite \(T_{ij}\) and Lemma 8: a cross-distance-two shared
diagram is linear, and at the other short cross-distances a nonlinear
shared diagram requires the finite \(E_8\) alternative. The published
end-piece arguments then use Lemmas 10--11 and ellipticity of \(U,V\).
Thus extending a displayed core pattern by additional white nodes does
not require a new blanket affine exclusion; the pertinent larger
diagrams are already finite corner diagrams. This distinguishes the
core-overlap affine tests from the later finite classification of
complete shared paths.

There is one additional size point in the long classical branch of §6.9.
Its (O\(U\)) and (O\(V\)) attach every white neighbor of the two black
roots to \(U,V\). Each black root has at most three white neighbors,
because all these neighbors occur in an actual positive-definite corner
diagram. Thus

\texttt{
\textbar{}O\textbackslash{}(U\textbackslash{})\textbar{},\textbar{}O\textbackslash{}(V\textbackslash{})\textbar{}\textbackslash{}le4+2\textbackslash{}cdot3=10\textless{}n.
}

They are orthogonal when the shortest white cross-path has length at
least four, so one is elliptic. After the long corner component is split
into its two end pieces, the high-bond pieces of order at least five are
indefinite by the finite/affine classification stated above. Their
orthogonal complements are elliptic by the first replacement, regardless
of their order. This supplies the ellipticity needed for the final
\(H_4\)-piece and negative-index contradiction in that branch. No
order-\(n\) affine end piece has been silently discarded.

\section{Nonzero determinant polynomial in
§6.10}\label{nonzero-determinant-polynomial-in-6.10}

Let \(e\) be the high bond of \(U\). All the other normalized Gram
entries belong to \(\mathbb Q(\sqrt2)\): the elliptic \(U\) has only
this one high bond, the elliptic \(V\) has none, and every other
relevant bond belongs to the finite corner diagrams covered by Lemma 6.
Varying the entry on \(e\) gives a determinant polynomial of degree at
most two. In the original diagonal-one normalization its quadratic
coefficient is minus the determinant obtained by deleting the endpoints
of \(e\). Its positivity deserves an explicit check in the present
setting.

In the unique dependence of \(H\), every vertex of \(U\) has a nonzero
coefficient of the same sign as its two black \(u\)-coefficients.
Indeed, a private white component has contacts only with the \(u\)-pair
and its own white nodes. Solving its dependence equation using its
entrywise nonnegative positive-definite inverse gives that common sign,
strictly at every node because the component is connected and attached
to the black pair.

Deleting an endpoint of \(e\) therefore destroys the only linear
dependence. The normals remaining after both endpoints are deleted are
independent, and their span still contains the indefinite diagram
\(H-U\). A subspace containing a timelike vector has nondegenerate
Lorentz restriction. Its Gram determinant is consequently strictly
negative. Thus the quadratic coefficient is strictly positive (four
times as large if the variable is \(\cos(\pi/m)\) in diagonal-two
normalization), including when the high bond has private white
endpoints.

The published algebraic angle argument and the subsequent negative-index
contradictions can therefore be used unchanged. This check relies on the
actual compact quadrilateral and its full star; it would not be
justified by deleting an arbitrary white root and pretending the smaller
diagram were another face star.

\section{Conclusion and review scope}\label{conclusion-and-review-scope}

Under the assumption of four zero-payment finite corners, the
preliminary decomposition and all five published cases retain their
required hypotheses. Each case produces the same contradiction. This
proves the claim for four-finite-vertex quadrilaterals in the stated
all-simple finite-volume class, \(n\ge18\).

This note is an independent mathematical/source audit, not a numerical
graph census or an independent rederivation of every determinant table
in the original paper. Separate source and mathematical reads by the
root and frontier agents pass the geometric replacements, Lemma 7
connectedness, carrier-size controls, §6.11 locality, and the nonzero
quadratic coefficient. No remaining compactness gap was identified in
the stated transfer. These internal reviews do not claim to duplicate
the published local tables or constitute external refereeing or formal
verification. This proof note is final and frozen.

The other mixed-corner quadrilateral branches require their separate
proofs. This note alone gives no new ambient dimension bound, and
changes none of the frozen 61/127/163 proofs or arithmetic certificates.

\clearpage

\chapter{Small-cusp defects and a one-cusp
consequence}\label{small-cusp-defects-and-a-one-cusp-consequence}

This package proves a local refinement of the fine-payment theorem and
an exact cusp-incidence balance. A deficient triangle or quadrilateral
has a small affine factor in its original wall star. After paying small
ideal corners sufficiently, every remaining carrier cusp lies
\textbf{outside} the defective face. Separately, dimension is at most155
if every cusp has some irreducible factor of rank at most8; in
particular, every one-cusp chamber has dimension at most155.

This package does not improve the unrestricted156 ceiling. Its155
consequence is retained as a historical refinement of that bound; the
separate selective-distance13 proof, once finalized, supersedes it with
a stronger unrestricted result. The local nonincident-defect statement
remains a distinct ingredient. No bound on carrier multiplicity, new
example, or novelty claim is made.

\section{Localizing the fine-payment
failure}\label{localizing-the-fine-payment-failure}

Let P be a finite-sided finite-volume hyperbolic Coxeter n-polytope. For
an actual triangular or quadrilateral two-face F let H(F) consist of its
n−2 supporting walls and its side walls. This is the original wall star,
without artificially adding all walls at nonsimple ideal vertices.

\textbf{If H(F) contains no connected affine subdiagram of order at
most9, then F receives fine payment at least2 for a triangle or at
least1 for a quadrilateral.} Use the finite Vinberg weights and the
distance-three/end-segment rule at ideal corners.

This is the face-local form of the frozen
\href{fresh_cusp_minimum_factor_rank9_dimension29_20261017.md}{rank9
theorem}. The following audits the hypothesis change. The triangle's
minimal indefinite core and its proper affine subdiagrams belong to
H(F), so its Lanner reduction and finite-corner alternatives are
unchanged. At an ideal corner the varying affine factor belongs to H(F),
and thus has order at least10. The
\href{fresh_affine_order10_quad_payment_20261017.md}{ideal-corner proof}
uses only this factor, the other two sides and the supporting
spectators. Every excluded low-contact affine, including the new dual-E8
witnesses, is a principal subdiagram of H(F).

For four finite corners, both complements in the private/shared
decomposition lie in H(F). Every witness in the
\href{fresh_affine_carriers_order10_20261017.md}{carrier proof} uses
only its carrier, the actual white connecting path and the four sides.
The later published cases use the order-at-most9 tests in the
\href{fresh_vinberg_finite_quad_affine_cutoff9_20261017.md}{refined
source audit}; their large orthogonal pieces are positive definite by
the actual Lorentz realization. No affine prohibition elsewhere is used.
The published finite case tables remain inherited inputs, not a new
classification by this checker.

A connected affine diagram in H(F) determines an actual cusp and is one
of its full irreducible factors. Its positive kernel combination is a
nonzero feasible null vector: nonzero follows by pairing with a strict
center, and feasibility follows from acuteness. Strict convexity of the
Klein ball makes its ideal point an actual vertex. The
positive-semidefinite incident Gram then forces every other incident
root right to this affine factor. This is the
\href{fresh_cusp_factor_payment_framework_20261017.md}{actual-factor
lemma}, consistent with the primary unique-ideal-vertex statement in
\href{https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/0502413}{Felikson--Tumarkin, §1, PDF
p.4}, reopened for this package.

\section{A defect demand that charges only nonincident
carriers}\label{a-defect-demand-that-charges-only-nonincident-carriers}

Use this nonnegative rule:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  At finite corners keep Vinberg's weights, whose vertex total is at
  most3n.
\item
  At ideal corners whose varying factor has rank r\textless=8, use
  weight2.
\item
  At other ideal corners retain the fine distance-three/end-segment
  rule.
\end{itemize}

Let s\_large(v) count the factors of rank at least9,
V\_v=product\_i(r\_vi+1), and

\texttt{b(v)=3\ s\_large(v)+sum\_(r\_vi\textless{}=8)\ r\_vi.}

The total cusp weight is at most V\_v b(v). Each marked pair in factor i
occurs in exactly V\_v/(r\_vi+1) link fibers, so a small factor costs
\texttt{2\ binom(r+1,2)V\_v/(r+1)=rV\_v}. A large factor costs at
most3V\_v by the
\href{fresh_cusp_spectator_role_payments_20261017.md}{all-rank affine
cost proof}.

Call a triangle or quadrilateral deficient when its weight is below2 or1
respectively. Such a face has no small varying-factor corner, since that
corner alone pays2. The local theorem nevertheless forces a small affine
factor C inside H(F).

\textbf{The cusp determined by C is not on F.} Otherwise all its walls
contain some ideal vertex v of F. The walls of H(F) containing v are
exactly its supporting whites and the two incident sides. The
factor-fiber description of this corner star has one complete affine
varying factor and one-node-deleted finite pieces from every other
factor. Thus C must be the complete varying factor, contradicting the
absence of a small varying-factor corner. This allows nonsimple ideal
vertices.

Writing T\_bad,Q\_bad for the deficient counts, the weight upper bound
and \href{fresh_cusp_link_shape_curvature_20261017.md}{exact link-shape
curvature} imply

\texttt{2T\_bad+Q\_bad\ \textgreater{}=\ (beta\_n−3n)v\_f\ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ +sum\_v\ {[}kappa(L\_v)−V\_v\ b(v){]}+5(n−1).}

Here beta\_n=n(n−6)/8 for even n and (n−1)(n−5)/8 for odd n, and v\_f
counts finite vertices. A deficient triangle is short by at most2 and a
deficient quadrilateral by at most1; polygons with at least five sides
need no positive payment. This proves the inequality directly, without
assuming all deficient payments are equal to their maximum shortfall.

A positive right side forces face-star charges to \textbf{nonincident}
small cusps. No multiplicity bound for these charges follows from the
argument. In particular, counting only corners of faces actually passing
through the carrier cusp does not finish a dimension proof.

\section{Exact example distinguishing carriers from incident
cusps}\label{exact-example-distinguishing-carriers-from-incident-cusps}

In upper half-space H3 consider

\texttt{−1\textless{}=X\textless{}=1,\ −1\textless{}=Y\textless{}=1,\ X²+Y²+Z²\textgreater{}=4,\ Z\textgreater{}0.}

This Coxeter square pyramid has four finite base vertices (±1,±1,sqrt2)
and one ideal apex at infinity. Adjacent vertical walls are right,
opposite ones parallel, and the base hemisphere has angle pi/3 to each.
In metric diag(−1,1,1,1), outward normals of square one are

\begin{verbatim}
R=(1, 1, 0,1), L=(1,−1, 0,1),
U=(1, 0, 1,1), D=(1, 0,−1,1),
B=(−3/4,0,0,−5/4).
\end{verbatim}

The strict center (5,0,0,4) has square−9. The full cone has exactly the
rays (5,±2,±2,3) and (1,0,0,1). The checker exhausts all ten triple
frames in the section defined by the timelike sum of the normals. That
section is bounded: its recession direction would pair nonpositively
with every normal and zero with their sum, hence zero with all five;
they span the Lorentz space. Every facet has an explicit
relative-interior point from a positive sum of its vertex rays. There
are no exterior rays.

The relations R+L=U+D=2(1,0,0,1) certify the two affine A1 factors and
the proper rectangular cusp link. The bounded link and complete
finite/ideal cone give finite volume.

The compact base's full star contains both affine factors although their
cusp is not on that base. This disproves identifying a carrier in a face
star with a cusp on the face. \textbf{It is not an unpaid-face example:}
each base corner is A3 marked at its two end roots, and the published
rank3 rule pays that pair weight2, total8. No adjacency-only finite rule
is being substituted for Vinberg's actual weights.

\section{Exact cusp-type balance at
dimension156}\label{exact-cusp-type-balance-at-dimension156}

A separate consequence uses the
\href{fresh_distance14_unrestricted_dimension156_20261017.md}{unrestricted
distance14 theorem}, rather than the unbounded nonincident charge. Its
cusp cost per link vertex is

\texttt{c(r)=sum\_i\ min(14,r\_i/2).}

At n=156 the total link rank is155. The frozen convex-order transfer
(a,b)-\textgreater(a−1,b+1), applied when both ranks are strictly
below28 or both strictly above28, preserves c and cannot increase
normalized curvature. Thus a reduced profile has copies of28, at most
one positive rank below28 and at most one above28. All128 reduced shapes
of total155 give

\texttt{kappa(L)/V−c(r)\ \textgreater{}=\ −4172075/82044596.}

If a cusp has a rank at most8, hold one such rank a fixed and transfer
only the other factors. For a=1,\ldots,8 this gives988 marked reduced
shapes, proving

\texttt{kappa(L)/V−c(r)\ \textgreater{}=\ 1395158/20511149\ \textgreater{}0.}

This does not assume that unrestricted transfers preserve a small
factor. The exact minima occur at (15,28,28,28,28,28) and
(1,14,28,28,28,28,28). Standalone rational convolution and independent
inclusion-exclusion for the centered absolute moment agree on all1116
profiles. Completeness comes from the proved concentration reduction,
not a sampled partition cutoff.

\chapter{The discrete spectator-energy spectrum through three
quarters}\label{the-discrete-spectator-energy-spectrum-through-three-quarters}

\textbf{FINAL/FROZEN: exact generation, fresh saved replay and a
separate full mathematical/source review PASS.}

Let G be a positive-definite norm-two acute Coxeter Gram matrix. Let x,y
be nonnegative vectors of native contact magnitudes with disjoint
supports. Assume both separate augmented Grams

\begin{verbatim}
[[G,-x],[-x^T,2]],  [[G,-y],[-y^T,2]]
\end{verbatim}

are \textbf{positive definite}. This is the strict actual-edge
hypothesis, not merely semidefiniteness at a corner. Put D=(x-y)\^{}T
G\^{}(-1)(x-y). Then

\begin{verbatim}
D<=3/4 implies
D in {0,1/2,2/3,3/4,2-sqrt(2),1-sqrt(5)/5}.
\end{verbatim}

In particular \textbf{D cannot equal4/7}. Equality D=3/4 has only two
forms, up to swapping x,y and diagram symmetries: one unit contact at an
endpoint of a whole simple A3 component, or one unit contact from each
side at adjacent vertices of a whole simple A3 component. Every other
spectator contact vanishes.

The
\href{../scripts/fresh_small_spectator_difference_gap_20261017.py}{source}
and
\href{fresh_small_spectator_difference_gap_20261017.json}{certificate}
verify the seven nonzero literal patterns, their separate strict edge
extensions, Schur identities and exact values. Completeness follows from
the argument below, which permits arbitrary spectator rank and native
finite labels. No ambient dimension or complete face-payment theorem is
asserted.

\section{Preliminary positive-definite
facts}\label{preliminary-positive-definite-facts}

Every nonzero native magnitude is at least1; if greater than1 it is at
least sqrt2. A positive-definite acute Coxeter graph is a forest: on any
cycle, the vector with entries1 on that cycle has square at most0, since
each cycle bond has magnitude at least1 and extra bonds only decrease
the square. This applies to G and to each of the two strict augmented
Grams, even if their graph is disconnected.

The inverse of G is entrywise nonnegative and has diagonal at least1/2.
One proof writes G=2I-A with A nonnegative and expands the convergent
Neumann series. Restricting to a principal diagram cannot increase the
corresponding inverse quadratic energy: the full inverse adds a
positive-semidefinite Schur correction. We also use the inherited
\href{fresh_selective_distance9_dimension108_20261017.md}{rank bound}: a
connected positive-definite norm-two Coxeter component of rank r has
every inverse diagonal at least r/(r+1). That argument covers all finite
labels and indirect tails, not a finite diagram sample.

\section{One nonempty support}\label{one-nonempty-support}

If y=0, nonnegative inverse entries give D\textgreater=sum\_i
x\_i\^{}2/2. Thus D\textless=3/4 allows only one nonzero coordinate, and
its native magnitude must be1. The rank bound forces its whole component
to have rank at most3.

Rank1 gives A1 and D=1/2. At rank2, the inverse diagonal is
2/(4-t\^{}2), where t\textgreater=1 is its bond magnitude. Being at
most3/4 forces t\^{}2\textless=4/3, hence t=1 and D=2/3. At rank3 the
graph is a path. Its middle inverse diagonal is at least1. At a leaf,
the minimum is3/4, attained only when both bonds are simple: increasing
either bond strictly increases that diagonal. This is the whole simple
A3 endpoint case. Swapping the two supports gives the same list. If both
supports vanish, D=0.

\section{Two nonempty supports must be
singletons}\label{two-nonempty-supports-must-be-singletons}

For any i in the x-support and j in the y-support, Cauchy in the Gram
metric gives

\begin{verbatim}
D >= (x_i+y_j)^2/(4-2G_ij).
\end{verbatim}

If i and j are not adjacent, this is at least1. Hence under
D\textless=3/4, every vertex of one support is adjacent to every vertex
of the other. If one support had two vertices i1,i2 and the other
contained j, adjoining the root with contacts to i1,i2 would create the
cycle i1-j-i2-new-i1 in its strict positive-definite edge diagram. This
is impossible. Thus x=p\emph{e\_i and y=q}e\_j for adjacent i,j.

Put t=-G\_ij. Positive definiteness of each separate extension gives
(G\textsuperscript{(-1))\_ii\textless2/p}2\textless=2 and
(G\textsuperscript{(-1))\_jj\textless2/q}2\textless=2. The two-node
principal inverse is2/(4-t\^{}2), so t\textless sqrt3. If either p or q
exceeded1, the native gap and the Cauchy bound would give

\begin{verbatim}
D >= (1+sqrt2)^2/(4+2t) > 96/125 > 3/4.
\end{verbatim}

The displayed rational lower bound uses sqrt2\textgreater7/5 and
sqrt3\textless7/4. Consequently p=q=1.

\section{A nonsimple spectator bond is
isolated}\label{a-nonsimple-spectator-bond-is-isolated}

Suppose t\textgreater=sqrt2. If either endpoint of i-j had another
neighbor with bond magnitude u\textgreater=1, its inverse diagonal in
that three-node principal path would be

\begin{verbatim}
2/(4-t^2-u^2) >= 2/(3-t^2) >= 2,
\end{verbatim}

contradicting the strict edge-extension inequality. The denominator is
positive because that principal path is positive definite. Therefore i-j
is a whole rank-two component. The native conditions
sqrt2\textless=t\textless sqrt3 leave exactly labels4 and5. For the two
unit contacts,

\begin{verbatim}
D=2/(2+t),
\end{verbatim}

giving2-sqrt2 and1-sqrt5/5 respectively. This excludes arbitrary high
labels by a proved inequality, not an imposed cutoff.

\section{A simple spectator bond has at most one additional
root}\label{a-simple-spectator-bond-has-at-most-one-additional-root}

Now t=1. If i-j is the whole component, it is A2 and D=2/3. Otherwise
choose a third node adjoining one of its endpoints, with bond magnitude
u\textgreater=1. It cannot adjoin both endpoints because G is a forest.
On A2, G\_A2\^{}(-1)(e\_i-e\_j)=(1/3,-1/3). Schur complementation
therefore gives the three-node principal energy

\begin{verbatim}
2/3 + u^2/[6(3-u^2)],
energy-3/4=(u^2-1)/[4(3-u^2)].
\end{verbatim}

Positive definiteness ensures u\^{}2\textless3. Hence the energy is at
least3/4, with equality only at u=1. The principal diagram is then
simple A3, and the two contacts occupy adjacent vertices. In one
orientation its inverse difference vector is

\begin{verbatim}
G_A3^(-1)(e_0-e_1)=(1/4,-1/2,-1/4),
\end{verbatim}

which has no zero coordinate. Any additional root attached to this A3
can meet only one of its nodes, since a second attachment would create a
cycle. Its product with the displayed inverse difference is nonzero. The
positive Schur correction is then strictly positive. Thus D=3/4 forces
this A3 to be the whole connected component, including all tails. Every
other component has zero contact from both sides.

This proves the stated list and the sealed A3 equality classification.
The exact values2-sqrt2 and1-sqrt5/5 lie on opposite sides of4/7; none
of the other listed values equals4/7. The latter exclusion is useful for
the cycle14 resistance calculation, while the A3 equality description is
a possible input to a smaller affine-D transfer. Those face arguments
remain separate obligations.

\section{Verification scope}\label{verification-scope-90}

The literal matrices and separate edge extensions are checked exactly
over the relevant quadratic fields. The source also verifies the
three-node Schur identity, its positive derivative, the nonvanishing A3
inverse difference, the rational nonunit-contact bound and the4/7
exclusion. Generation and a separate fresh saved replay both terminated

\chapter{The complete strict spectator spectrum below
one}\label{the-complete-strict-spectator-spectrum-below-one}

The new all-rank assertion is as follows. Let G be a positive-definite
norm-two acute Coxeter Gram matrix, and let x,y be nonnegative native
contact vectors with disjoint supports. Require both separate augmented
Grams G+x and G+y to be strictly positive definite. For

\begin{verbatim}
D=(x-y)^T G^(-1)(x-y)<1,
\end{verbatim}

the complete set of possible values is

\begin{verbatim}
0; r/(r+1) for integers r>=1; 2-sqrt2; 1-sqrt5/5.
\end{verbatim}

At the rational nonzero value r/(r+1), the contacts lie on one whole
simple A\_r component: either one unit contact at a leaf, or two unit
contacts at adjacent vertices. Both separate extensions must still be
positive definite; this excludes some interior adjacent positions in
large A\_r. Every other component has zero contacts. The two irrational
values have two unit contacts at the endpoints of a whole I2(4) or
I2(5), respectively. Conversely all the listed energies occur: the
one-contact A\_r leaf realizes every rational value.

The
\href{../scripts/fresh_spectator_energy_below_one_20261017.py}{source}
and \href{fresh_spectator_energy_below_one_20261017.json}{certificate}
check the exact identities below. This strengthens the
\href{fresh_small_spectator_difference_gap_20261017.md}{spectrum through
three quarters}. It is a local lemma, without a new ambient dimension or
construction claim.

\section{Two elementary obstructions in arbitrary
rank}\label{two-elementary-obstructions-in-arbitrary-rank}

All positive-definite acute Coxeter diagrams are forests. A cycle's
all-ones vector would otherwise have nonpositive square. Their inverses
are entrywise nonnegative, and an inverse diagonal cannot decrease when
a principal diagram is enlarged or its bond magnitudes are increased.
The principal comparison is a positive Schur correction; bond
monotonicity follows from the nonnegative Neumann series, or
differentiation of the inverse along the positive-definite line segment.

Two explicit principal subtrees detect any branching or nonsimple bond.
On a simple path ending in a bond of magnitude sqrt2 (type B), the
inverse diagonal at its remote leaf is1. At the next vertex it is2 if
that next vertex precedes the doubled bond. On a simple path ending in a
fork with two short simple leaves (type D), the remote leaf and next
vertex again have inverse diagonals1 and2. This includes D4 with the
fork center as the second vertex.

Here is an all-rank calculation. For B, scale the terminal root by
sqrt2. The rational congruent Gram has last diagonal4 and last bond
magnitude2. Eliminating the last root makes the preceding diagonal1;
eliminating successive roots repeats the diagonal1. The first inverse
column is (1,\ldots,1,1/2). The second is(1,2,\ldots,2,1) when the path
has at least3 nodes. The first two diagonal entries are unaffected by
the terminal congruence. For D, eliminating the two short leaves changes
the fork diagonal to1, and the same recurrence applies. The first
inverse column is (1,\ldots,1,1/2,1/2); the second is(1,2,\ldots,2,1,1).
These vector identities and the positive elimination pivots prove the
assertions for all ranks.

From any vertex of a tree that is not a simple A path, follow a path to
the first nonsimple bond or branching node. Keeping the terminal doubled
bond, or two outgoing fork leaves, gives one of these subtrees; larger
native bonds only increase inverse diagonals. Hence every inverse
diagonal of a component that is not a simple path is at least1. If the
starting vertex itself is a branch, retain two of its neighbors instead:
the resulting simple A3 has inverse diagonal1 at that middle vertex, and
larger bonds only increase it. Thus this zero-length path case does not
require an incoming edge for the fork construction.

There is a stronger statement for an adjacent simple marked edge i-j. If
its component has a nonsimple bond or branch anywhere, it lies in one of
the two sides of that edge. Retain a path from the opposite marked
endpoint to that feature, together with its doubled bond or fork leaves.
The opposite endpoint becomes the remote leaf and the other marked
endpoint becomes its next vertex. One marked inverse diagonal is
therefore at least2. This contradicts strict positive definiteness of
that marked root's separate unit-contact extension.

\section{One nonempty contact
support}\label{one-nonempty-contact-support}

Nonnegative inverse entries and diagonal lower bound1/2 give
D\textgreater=sum\_i x\_i\^{}2/2 when y=0. Under D\textless1, the
support has only one coordinate, with native magnitude1. A nonsimple
magnitude is at least sqrt2 and would already give D\textgreater=1.

The subtree obstruction forces the whole contacted component to be a
simple A\_r path. Its inverse is, in one-based indices,

\begin{verbatim}
(G_A_r^(-1))ij=min(i,j)*(r+1-max(i,j))/(r+1).
\end{verbatim}

Every interior diagonal is at least1. Thus the contact is at a leaf and
D=r/(r+1). The same argument applies after interchanging x and y. If
both supports vanish then D=0; conversely positive definiteness and
disjoint supports force both to vanish when D=0.

\section{Two nonempty supports}\label{two-nonempty-supports}

For any i in the x-support and j in the y-support, Gram-metric Cauchy
gives

\begin{verbatim}
D >= (x_i+y_j)^2/(4-2G_ij).
\end{verbatim}

Nonadjacent support nodes would give D\textgreater=1. Every
opposite-support pair is therefore adjacent. If one support had two
vertices, adjoining its new root would create a cycle through a vertex

\end{verbatim}

then below sqrt3\textless2. On the two-node principal Gram the

\begin{verbatim}
2*(p^2+q^2-p*q)/3.
\end{verbatim}

energy2/(2+t) is exactly one of the two listed irrational values.

bond and branch in the whole component. It is A\_r. For adjacent

\begin{verbatim}
j/(r+1) for j<=k;
-(r+1-j)/(r+1) for j>=k+1.
\end{verbatim}

Every entry is nonzero and the difference energy is r/(r+1), independent
of k. The remaining strict extension conditions are the two explicit
diagonal inequalities(G\^{}(-1))kk\textless2
and(G\^{}(-1))k+1,k+1\textless2. This completes the all-rank
classification; no cutoff on spectator rank or native labels is imposed.

\chapter{The strict spectator boundary at energy
one}\label{the-strict-spectator-boundary-at-energy-one}

Let G be a positive-definite norm-two acute Coxeter Gram matrix, and let
x,y be nonnegative native contact vectors with disjoint supports. Both
separate augmented Grams G+x and G+y are required to be strictly
positive definite. The equality

\begin{verbatim}
(x-y)^T G^(-1)(x-y)=1
\end{verbatim}

has exactly the following possibilities, up to exchanging x and y and
diagram automorphism. Components not mentioned have no contacts.

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  If only one support is nonempty: one sqrt2 contact on a whole A1; two
  unit contacts on two distinct whole A1 components; one unit contact at
  the middle of a whole A3; one unit contact at the remote leaf of a
  whole B\_r, r\textgreater=2; or one unit contact at the long leaf of a
  whole D\_r, r\textgreater=4. In B2 either endpoint is allowed, and in
  D4 any leaf is allowed.
\item
  If both supports are nonempty: one unit contact from each side, on two
  distinct whole A1 components, on the two endpoints of a whole A3, or
  on the two short fork leaves of a whole D\_r
  with4\textless=r\textless=7.
\end{itemize}

Together with the
\href{fresh_spectator_energy_below_one_20261017.md}{strict spectrum
below one}, this classifies the complete
interval0\textless=D\textless=1. The
\href{../scripts/fresh_spectator_energy_one_boundary_20261017.py}{source}
and
\href{fresh_spectator_energy_one_boundary_20261017.json}{certificate}
check exact identities. This local statement does not by itself prove a
new corner transfer or lower an ambient dimension bound.

\section{One nonempty support}\label{one-nonempty-support-1}

As in the preceding proof, inverse entries are nonnegative and inverse
diagonals are at least1/2. Thus at most two contacts are possible. If
there are two, both are unit contacts, both inverse diagonals equal1/2
and their inverse cross entry vanishes. An inverse diagonal equals1/2
only for an isolated root: any incident bond gives a strictly positive
Schur correction. This gives the two whole A1 components.

For one contact of magnitude p, the bound p\^{}2/2\textless=1 and the
native alphabet give p=1 or sqrt2. The latter forces a whole A1. For p=1
the contacted inverse diagonal equals1. On A\_r the formula
i(r+1-i)/(r+1)=1 is equivalent to (i-1)(r-i)=1, so only the middle of A3
occurs.

For a component that is not a simple path, take the principal B or D
obstruction from the preceding proof, beginning at the marked vertex.
The remote-leaf inverse diagonal is1, and its entire inverse column is
strictly positive. Adding any connected vertex therefore increases that
diagonal strictly: the Schur correction contains the nonzero product of
this positive column with a nonnegative nonzero contact vector.
Increasing any bond likewise increases it strictly, by the inverse
derivative formula and positivity of that column. Consequently the
principal obstruction must already be the whole component, with exactly
its minimal bond labels. This gives B\_r or D\_r at their stated leaves.
If the marked vertex is itself a branch, its principal A3 middle already
has inverse diagonal1, and the third neighbor makes it strictly greater,
excluding this case.

All these one-sided cases have projection norm1\textless2, so their
separate edge extensions are strictly positive definite.

\section{Two nonempty supports}\label{two-nonempty-supports-1}

Suppose first that an x-support node i and a y-support node j are
nonadjacent. Gram-metric Cauchy gives

\begin{verbatim}
1 >= (x_i+y_j)^2/4 >= 1.
\end{verbatim}

Equality forces x\_i=y\_j=1 and

\begin{verbatim}
G^(-1)(x-y)=(e_i-e_j)/2.
\end{verbatim}

Hence every other coordinate of x-y is (G\_ki-G\_kj)/2. Since G is
positive definite, all off-diagonal entries are in(-2,0{]}. Their
half-differences are strictly between-1 and1. A nonzero native contact
has magnitude at least1, so every other coordinate vanishes. Disjoint
supports now imply x=e\_i, y=e\_j, and i,j have identical neighbor sets
with identical bonds.

If there are no neighbors, they are two whole A1 components. Otherwise
the forest condition permits exactly one common neighbor k. The two
equal bonds must be simple: a three-node principal Gram with equal
magnitude t has determinant8-4t\^{}2\textgreater0, hence
t\textless sqrt2. Thus i,j are simple twin leaves.

The remaining connected component is A3 or D\_r. Here is an elementary
all-rank argument. The common neighbor has at most one further neighbor,
since four simple leaves would contain an affine D4 subdiagram. Follow
the remaining simple path. A first doubled bond or second fork would
contain an affine B or D principal subdiagram, contradicting positive
definiteness. Explicitly, give the first two fork leaves coefficient1/2
and every stem vertex coefficient1. At a terminal doubled bond give the
terminal vertex coefficient1/sqrt2; at a terminal fork give its two
leaves coefficient1/2. The resulting minimal diagram has positive null
vector. Larger bond magnitudes make its quadratic form negative. Hence
the remaining path ends at a leaf without a nonsimple bond or second
branch.

For D\_r with short leaves i,j, including D3=A3, the inverse column at i
has stem coordinates1/2,2/2,\ldots,(r-2)/2, short-leaf coordinate r/4 at
i and (r-2)/4 at j. Multiplying by G verifies this in every rank. Thus
the two separate projection norms are r/4. Strict edge positivity
requires r\textless8, giving precisely A3 and D4,\ldots,D7. Their
inverse difference is (e\_i-e\_j)/2, so the energy is1.

It remains to exclude the case in which every cross-support pair is
adjacent. Either support having two nodes would make a cycle in its
separate augmented Gram. Thus x=p\emph{e\_i,y=q}e\_j for adjacent i,j.
The preceding below-one proof actually shows that any nonunit p or q
gives energy strictly greater than1. For p=q=1, a simple marked bond
forces the whole component to be A\_r by the strict marked-edge
obstruction, giving energy r/(r+1)\textless1. A nonsimple marked bond
forces a whole I2(4) or I2(5), also with energy strictly below1. No
adjacent case remains.

\section{Verification scope}\label{verification-scope-91}

The written identities and sealing arguments are in arbitrary rank. The
checker corroborates125 one-contact B/D identities through rank64, 62

\chapter{A short-path alternative at spectator energy five
quarters}\label{a-short-path-alternative-at-spectator-energy-five-quarters}

Let G be a positive-definite norm-two acute Coxeter Gram matrix. Let x,y
be nonnegative native contact vectors with disjoint nonempty supports,
and require both separately augmented diagrams G+x and G+y to be
strictly positive definite. If

\begin{verbatim}
(x-y)^T G^(-1)(x-y) = 5/4,
\end{verbatim}

then either an x-contact and a y-contact have distance at most3 in one
connected spectator component, or the only contacted components are
whole A1 and whole A3, with one unit leaf contact in each and opposite
contact sides. The first alternative gives a path of length at most5
between the two new roots. No bound on spectator rank or native labels
is imposed.

The
\href{../scripts/fresh_spectator_five_quarters_transfer_20261017.py}{source}
and
\href{fresh_spectator_five_quarters_transfer_20261017.json}{certificate}
check the exact identities below. The finite Coxeter classification and
the \href{fresh_spectator_energy_below_one_20261017.md}{one-sided
spectrum below1} are inherited inputs. This is a local spectator lemma,
not a complete face-transfer or dimension theorem.

\section{Contacts in the same
component}\label{contacts-in-the-same-component}

Every finite Coxeter diagram is a forest. Thus a new root can contact at
most one node in each connected component: two contacts would make a
cycle in its separately positive-definite augmented diagram. Write two
opposite contacts in one component as p at i and q at j, with
p,q\textgreater=1 and i different from j. Put J=G\^{}(-1), a=Jii, b=Jjj,
c=Jij. Strict extension positivity forces a\textless2 and b\textless2,
even before accounting for other components. The contribution to the
difference energy is

\begin{verbatim}
E(p,q)=a*p^2+b*q^2-2*c*p*q.
\end{verbatim}

When a-c and b-c are nonnegative, expand around p=q=1. The linear terms
are nonnegative and the remaining quadratic form is positive
semidefinite, so E(p,q)\textgreater=a+b-2c for every p,q\textgreater=1.
This does not assume coordinatewise monotonicity at arbitrary p,q.

For A\_r, put N=r+1 and use one-based indices. The all-rank inverse is

\begin{verbatim}
Jij=min(i,j)*(N-max(i,j))/N.
\end{verbatim}

For i\textless j and d=j-i, the row sums are a-c=i\emph{d/N and
b-c=(N-j)}d/N, both positive. The unit-contact energy is d*(N-d)/N.
Since N\textgreater=d+2, for d\textgreater=4 we have

\begin{verbatim}
d*(N-d)/N >= 2d/(d+2) >= 4/3.
\end{verbatim}

The two differences are respectively d\^{}2\emph{(N-d-2)/(N}(d+2)) and
2\emph{(d-4)/(3}(d+2)). These identities prove the assertion in
arbitrary rank. The certificate separately multiplies the proposed
inverse by each Gram and checks every far pair in ranks5 through32 as
corroborating examples.

For B\_r number the simple spine0,\ldots,r-2 and the terminal
doubled-bond node r-1. Its native norm-two inverse is

\begin{verbatim}
Jij=min(i+1,j+1)                      (i,j<r-1),
Ji,r-1=(i+1)/sqrt2                    (i<r-1),
Jr-1,r-1=r/2.
\end{verbatim}

Thus a possible unit contact lies only at0, or at r-1 when r\textless=3.
Two distinct allowed positions never have distance at least4. The
formula follows by direct multiplication with the tridiagonal Gram,
including the two terminal equations, for every r\textgreater=2.

For D\_r number the long spine0,\ldots,r-3 and the two short leaves
r-2,r-1. Its inverse has Jij=min(i+1,j+1) on the spine, Ji,leaf=(i+1)/2,
diagonal r/4 at each short leaf and off-diagonal (r-2)/4 between the
short leaves. Direct multiplication at the spine and fork proves these
identities for every r\textgreater=4. The only positions of diagonal
below2 are0 and, when r\textless=7, the two short leaves. Short leaves
are distance2 apart. A long/short pair of distance at least4 therefore
has r=6 or7; its row sums are1/2 and r/4-1/2, and its unit energy is
r/4\textgreater=3/2. The certificate verifies both inverse families
through rank24, without using that sample as a rank cutoff.

For E6,E7,E8 the entire finite case is checked exactly. E6 has two
possible contact nodes, at distance4, with a=b=4/3 and c=2/3; their
energy is at least4/3. E7 has only one possible contact node and E8 has
none. The complete Grams and inverses are saved. F4,H3,H4 and every
I2(m) have diagram diameter at most3 and need no energy estimate.

Every connected component contributes nonnegative energy. Consequently
one mixed component with its contact nodes at distance at least4 would
already contribute at least4/3\textgreater5/4. Every mixed component
instead yields the stated short-path alternative.

\section{No component has contacts on both
sides}\label{no-component-has-contacts-on-both-sides}

Suppose the short-path alternative does not occur. Every active
component has contacts from only one side. Its energy is at least1/2: a
nonzero native contact is at least1 and an inverse diagonal is at
least1/2. Since both supports are nonempty, there are at least two
active components; three would contribute at least3/2. There are exactly
two, one per side, and each has energy between1/2 and3/4.

The inherited one-sided spectrum below1 forces a unit leaf contact on a
whole A\_r, with energy r/(r+1). Here r\textless=3. The only two such
energies summing to5/4 are1/2 and3/4, from A1 and A3. Every other
spectator component has zero contacts. This proves the second
alternative.

\chapter{A universal short-path alternative for deep finite
distance-eight
pairs}\label{a-universal-short-path-alternative-for-deep-finite-distance-eight-pairs}

Let an actual quadrilateral face of a finite-sided finite-volume real
hyperbolic Coxeter polytope have a finite corner whose two marked roots
lie in one whole finite A/B/D component at graph distance8. Suppose both
marks have distance at least17 from every endpoint, branch and endpoint
of a nonsimple bond of that whole component. Then the \textbf{full
actual supporting star contains a path of length at most7 between the
two opposite black pairs, with white internal roots}.

This statement covers all low/high, disjoint/overlapping minimal-core
cases, all native labels and arbitrary additional supporting roots. It
does not assume the old no-short8 condition. It is a conditional
short-path theorem, not a claim that every low or disjoint configuration
is impossible. Only in the explicit full-star no-short7 branch does it
exclude a deep finite-distance8 pair.

The
\href{../scripts/fresh_universal_deep_finite8_corridor_20261018.py}{source}
and
\href{fresh_universal_deep_finite8_corridor_20261018.json}{certificate}
check the exact rational inequalities below. No contact-profile or
low/high joining census is needed. A complete changed payment rule, its
finite-forest budget and any dimension consequence require their
separate composition. The unrestricted ceiling stays65 in this report.

\section{Actual-face inputs and the forced
path}\label{actual-face-inputs-and-the-forced-path}

Write the star as W+a+b+c+d, with opposite black pairs \{a,c\} and
\{b,d\}. Every root of W is white. The actual white diagram and each W
plus one black are positive definite. Each W plus an opposite pair is
indefinite; these are the inherited strict-edge and closed-opposite-side
facts of the
\href{fresh_selective_distance9_dimension108_20261017.md}{complete face
reduction}. The corner under consideration is W+a+b. Roots are
normalized to squared norm2, so every nonzero native acute contact has
magnitude at least1, including arbitrarily large finite labels, parallel
or dotted contacts. All distinct-root products are nonpositive.

Assume there is no full-star path of the stated length. In particular
c.d=c.b=d.a=0. The products c.a and d.b are unrestricted nonpositive
native products; they may vanish or have arbitrarily large magnitude.

The whole finite A/B/D component is a tree. Feature depth17 gives a
simple eight-edge path from a to b and two disjoint simple outward arms
of17 whites. A feature exactly at outward distance17 is allowed: every
bond inside the corresponding17-white arm is still simple. Keep15

\begin{verbatim}
a at15,     b at23.

\section{Four possible contact positions on each

For a norm-two A\_n path the positive inverse entries are

\begin{verbatim}
J_n[i,j]=(min(i,j)+1)(n-max(i,j))/(n+1),  0<=i,j<n.

(A17 inverse)[j-1,j-1]=j(18-j)/18 >=5/2>2.

The native contact is at least1; all further contacts have nonnegative

If c meets an inner white at distance j\textgreater=2 from a, following

\href{fresh_high_rank_quasilanner_census_20261017.md}{minimal-indefinite

(240/529)q*r -2(q+r)+4.
\end{verbatim}

Write q=91/10+u and r=91/10+v, where u,v\textgreater=0. This lower bound
becomes

\begin{verbatim}
13674/2645 +(1126/529)(u+v) +(240/529)u*v >0.
\end{verbatim}

Thus the Schur matrix is negative definite. By congruence, the full Gram
matrix has two negative directions. Actual wall roots lie in a Lorentz
space with only one negative direction, a contradiction. Additional
roots or contacts outside this principal matrix cannot repair it. The
argument does not require a nonsingular old core, a rational gauge for
that core, or any finite cutoff on supporting components or contact
labels.

This proves the universal full-star short7 alternative. It supplies the
missing conditional low-core and high-disjoint coverage for a future
deep-distance8 payment change. It does not prove a general finite7
quadrilateral theorem, and it does not itself assign a full unit to an
ideal short6/7 pair: the existing ideal-cycle/tree transfers must still
be composed with it.
